begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to keep up a load for a long time.
The good interplay of muscles, nerves and senses.
Fair behaviour in sport, that is, keeping to the rules and respecting your opponent.
The federal sports promotion programme for children and young people.

gewusst: The ancient Olympic Games already took place over 2,700 years ago in Olympia in Greece.
The International Olympic Committee has its seat in Lausanne, which is why Lausanne calls itself the “Olympic Capital”.

teile.einleitung: Basal cell carcinoma, also called basalioma, is a skin cancer. In people with fair skin it is the most common cancer of all. Fortunately it mostly grows slowly and can be treated well.
wichtigste: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in fair-skinned people.
It destroys tissue locally, but only very rarely forms metastases.
It occurs most often on the head and face.
The most important risk factor is the UV dose accumulated over a lifetime.
In most tumours, the Hedgehog signalling pathway is misregulated.
The standard treatment is surgical removal.

abschnitte.text: The risk of **basal cell carcinoma** rises with the **UV dose** that builds up over a whole lifetime. That is why it mainly affects older people and people who work a lot outdoors. Most tumours arise where a lot of sun has reached over decades: on the **head and face**, especially on the **nose**, **forehead** and **ears**.

A nodular basalioma is often a skin-coloured to reddish, **glassy shiny nodule**. Typical is a **pearly, beaded rim**. On the surface you often see fine, widened **little vessels**. Later a small sore can form in the middle that does not heal. Anyone who notices something like this should have a skin doctor look at it.

Basal cell carcinoma can destroy the surrounding tissue right down to the **bone**. **Metastases**, that is, secondary tumours, it forms only extremely rarely. That is why it is sometimes called **semi-malignant**, half malignant. In most tumours, genes such as **PTCH1** are altered. As a result the **Hedgehog signalling pathway** is permanently active. Medicines such as **vismodegib** block this pathway in advanced tumours.

Usually the tumour is **cut out** completely. Under the microscope it is checked whether the cut edges are clear. In **micrographically controlled surgery**, for example by Mohs’ method, the surgeon keeps cutting until the edges are free of tumour. In this way a lot of healthy skin is kept on the face. Protection is offered by **shade**, clothing, a hat and **sun cream**. In the mountains UV radiation is stronger, which is especially important in Switzerland.

gewusst: Basal cell carcinoma is common, but almost never forms secondary tumours.
With every metre of altitude UV radiation gets stronger, so you need especially good sun protection in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: So that we can look in all directions, **eye muscles** move the eyeball. Each eye has six outer eye muscles. They work fast and precisely, and mostly quite automatically.
wichtigste: Each eye has six outer eye muscles, which makes 12 in both eyes together.
The eye muscles are among the fastest muscles in the body.
Both eyes turn in the same direction at the same time.
When reading, the eyes move in small jumps.
The eyes also move in sleep, especially during dreaming.
Looking into the distance helps the eyes to recover.

abschnitte.text: An adult’s **eyeball** is almost a sphere and about **2.5 centimetres** across. It lies well protected in the eye socket of the skull. The **outer eye muscles** are attached to it. Each eye has **six** of them: four straight and two slanting muscles. In both eyes together that makes **12**.

When you look to the left, **both eyes turn to the left at the same time**. The brain controls the muscles of both eyes so that they work together. Only in this way do you see a single, clear picture. Unlike a **chameleon**, a human cannot turn their eyes **independently** in different directions.

The eye muscles are among the **fastest muscles** in the body. When **reading**, the eyes do not glide smoothly along the line. They move **in small jumps**, called saccades, and stop briefly in between. The **blink** is fast too: it lasts **less than half a second**.

The eyes also move **in sleep**, **especially during dreaming**. There is a phase of sleep with fast eye movements behind the closed lids. It is called **REM sleep**, after the English “rapid eye movement”. In this phase we dream especially vividly.

When reading or at a screen, the eyes look at something near for a long time. This strains the muscles in the eye. It helps to take a break regularly and **look into the distance**, for example out of the window. Blinking on purpose is also good for the eyes, because otherwise they can dry out.

gewusst: The eyes make a great many jumps every day without us noticing.
In someone with a squint, the two eyes do not look in exactly the same direction.

teile.einleitung: A base pair consists of two bases that face each other in DNA and hold together. Like the rungs of a ladder, they join the two strands of the double helix.
wichtigste: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine.
An adenine-thymine pair has two hydrogen bonds, a guanine-cytosine pair three.
Adenine and guanine are purines, cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines.
Each base pair consists of one purine and one pyrimidine.
In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.
According to Chargaff’s rule, adenine and thymine occur equally often.
On heating above 90 degrees, the strands separate.

abschnitte.text: DNA is a **double helix**, a twisted ladder. The rungs are **base pairs**. There are four bases: **adenine** (A), **thymine** (T), **guanine** (G) and **cytosine** (C). A always pairs with T, G always with C. This is called **complementary base pairing**. A and T hold together with **two hydrogen bonds**, G and C with three. Stretches rich in AT are therefore easier to separate.

**Purines** have a double ring system. These include adenine and guanine. **Pyrimidines** such as cytosine and thymine have only one ring. Each base pair consists of a large purine and a small pyrimidine. So every pair is about the same length and the helix is **the same width everywhere**. **Erwin Chargaff** found out that in double-stranded DNA there is as much adenine as thymine and as much guanine as cytosine.

With Chargaff’s rule you can do sums. If a piece of DNA contains **20 per cent adenine**, then it also has 20 per cent thymine. The remaining 60 per cent is shared between guanine and cytosine, so **30 per cent** each. The two strands run in opposite directions. The opposite strand to 5'-ATGC-3' is therefore, also read from 5' to 3', **5'-GCAT-3'**.

In **RNA**, the base **uracil** occurs instead of thymine. It also pairs with adenine. When the genetic information is read, **guanine can also pair with uracil** at the third position of a codon. This is described by Francis Crick’s **wobble hypothesis**. If DNA is heated to above 90 degrees, the bonds break and the strands separate. This **denaturing** is used in **PCR**, a method for copying DNA many times over.

gewusst: A person’s genetic material consists of about three billion base pairs.
In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix of DNA.

teile.einleitung: The intestine is a long tube in our belly. It digests the food, takes out the nutrients and brings them into the blood. What is left over leaves the body by way of the toilet.
wichtigste: After the stomach, the food goes into the **intestine**.
The first, long and thin part is called the **small intestine**.
The intestine of an adult is much longer than the person is tall.
The small intestine takes **nutrients** into the blood, the **large intestine** takes water back.
Very many **bacteria** live in the intestine.
Fibre from wholemeal bread and vegetables is good for the intestine.

abschnitte.text: First we chew the food in the mouth and swallow it. Through the gullet it reaches the **stomach**, where it becomes a pulp. After that the food pulp travels into the **intestine**. Muscles in the wall of the intestine push it slowly onwards. This happens all by itself, you do not have to think about it.

The intestine lies folded in many loops in the belly. In an adult it is **several metres long**, so much longer than the person is tall. The first part is the **small intestine**: it is long and thin. After that comes the **large intestine**, which is shorter, but wider.

In the small intestine the food is broken into tiny pieces. These **nutrients** pass through the wall of the intestine into the **blood**. The blood brings them to all parts of the body. To make this work well, the small intestine has many tiny **villi** on the inside. They look like little fingers and make the surface much larger.

In the **large intestine** arrives what the small intestine has not taken up. The large intestine takes back mainly **water**, so that the body does not lose too much of it. In this way the pulp becomes firmer. What is left in the end is the **stool**. It leaves the intestine by way of the toilet.

In the intestine live countless tiny helpers, the **bacteria**. Many of them are useful and help with digestion. **Fibre** from wholemeal bread, vegetables and fruit is good for the intestine, because it keeps it moving. Drinking enough and getting plenty of exercise also help digestion.

gewusst: The tummy noises you sometimes hear come from air and pulp being pushed through the intestine.
The path of food through the whole intestine often takes more than a day.

teile.einleitung: A **booster vaccination** refreshes the protection of an earlier vaccination. It makes use of the memory of the immune system. As a result it works faster and more strongly than the first vaccination.
wichtigste: The primary vaccination builds up the first protection.
In a booster vaccination, memory cells are reactivated.
In the response to the booster, antibodies of the IgG class dominate.
Through affinity maturation, the antibodies bind better and better.
In Switzerland, a tetanus booster is recommended every 20 years for adults aged 25 to 65.
For tick-borne encephalitis, a booster is given every 10 years, while flu vaccination is repeated every year.

abschnitte.text: For many diseases you first get a series of vaccinations. This series is called the **primary vaccination** and builds up the first protection. Over time, the protection from some vaccinations fades. This is called **waning immunity**. A **booster vaccination** brings the protection back to a high level.

abschnitte.titel: The memory of the immune system
abschnitte.text: After the first vaccination, the immune system makes **memory cells**. They remember the germ. In the booster vaccination, they are **reactivated** and multiply quickly. This second reaction is called the **secondary response**. It is faster and stronger than the first. In it, antibodies of the **IgG** class dominate.

With repeated contact with an antigen, the antibodies get better. The defence cells change their blueprint slightly, and the cells with the best fitting antibodies win out. This process is called **affinity maturation**. In this way the antibodies bind ever more firmly to the germ.

The **Swiss vaccination schedule** is published by the Federal Office of Public Health and the Federal Commission for Vaccination. For adults **between 25 and 65 years old**, a booster against **tetanus** is recommended **every 20 years**, and more often after that. Against **tick-borne encephalitis**, which is passed on by ticks, a booster is given **every 10 years**.

The **flu vaccination** is a special case. Flu viruses constantly change their **surface proteins**. So the immune system no longer recognises new variants well. Every year a new vaccine is therefore made to match the viruses that are expected. So you are vaccinated anew every autumn.

gewusst: The English word “booster” means something that strengthens.
Whether a vaccination has to be refreshed depends on the germ and on the vaccine.

teile.einleitung: The body mass index, BMI for short, is a simple number that compares body weight and height. Doctors use it as a first rough hint whether someone is rather too light, normal or too heavy.
wichtigste: The BMI is the body mass in kilograms divided by the square of the height in metres.
In adults, a BMI of 18.5 to under 25 counts as normal weight.
From a BMI of 25 the WHO speaks of overweight, from 30 of obesity.
The basis of the BMI comes from the Belgian scholar Adolphe Quetelet.
The BMI does not distinguish between muscle and fat.
For children and young people, percentiles by age and sex are used.

abschnitte.text: For the BMI you divide the **body mass** in kilograms by the **height** in metres squared. An example: a person weighs 72 kg and is 1.80 m tall. You calculate 1.80 times 1.80, which gives 3.24. Then you divide 72 by 3.24 and get, rounded, **22.2**. The unit is kilograms per square metre.

The **World Health Organization** (WHO) divides the BMI for adults into groups. Below 18.5 counts as **underweight**, 18.5 to under 25 as **normal weight**. From 25 to under 30 you speak of **overweight** or pre-obesity. From 30, **obesity** begins, that is, severe overweight. Someone who weighs 90 kg and is 1.75 m tall has a BMI of about 29.4 and so lies in the overweight range.

The Belgian mathematician and astronomer **Adolphe Quetelet** studied in the 19th century how weight and height are related in many people. He found that in adults weight grows roughly with the square of height. That is why the formula was also long called the **Quetelet index**. It only got the name body mass index in the 20th century.

The BMI is practical, but imprecise. It does not distinguish between **muscle mass** and **fat mass**. A very muscular sportswoman can therefore have a high BMI although she has hardly any fat. The BMI also does not show where the fat sits. That is why professionals sometimes also measure the **waist circumference**.

Children and young people are still growing, so no fixed limits apply to them as for adults. Their BMI is compared with **percentiles**, that is, with curves for children of the same age and sex. If a child is, for example, on the 50th percentile, half of children of the same age have a lower and half a higher value. This assessment is best left to the paediatrician.

gewusst: Adolphe Quetelet is also regarded as one of the founders of modern statistics.
By the BMI, many top strength athletes would be overweight, although they are very fit.

teile.einleitung: The antidiuretic hormone, ADH for short, controls how much water the kidneys keep in the body. “Antidiuretic” means that it slows down the passing of urine. In this way ADH helps to keep the body’s water balance steady.
wichtigste: ADH is made in the hypothalamus.
It is released into the blood in the posterior pituitary.
Another name for ADH is vasopressin.
It is a peptide hormone made of nine amino acids.
Mainly a rise in the osmolality of the blood plasma triggers its release.
Alcohol blocks the release of ADH, so you have to pass water more often.
If ADH is missing, central diabetes insipidus develops.

abschnitte.text: ADH is made by nerve cells in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. Along long nerve fibres it reaches the **posterior pituitary**. There it is stored and, when needed, released into the blood. ADH is a **peptide hormone** and consists of only **nine amino acids**. Its second name is **vasopressin**, because in large amounts it also narrows the blood vessels.

The most important trigger is a **rise in the osmolality of the plasma**. That means that the blood has too many dissolved particles, such as salt, in proportion to the water. This happens, for example, when you have not drunk anything for a long time or have sweated a lot. Special sensor cells in the brain notice this. Then more ADH is released, and at the same time you feel thirsty. Heavy blood loss also leads to its release.

ADH works in the **collecting ducts** of the kidney. There it binds to the **V2 receptors** of the cells. The cells then build water channels, the **aquaporins**, into their wall. Through these channels, water is taken back from the urine into the blood. You then pass less urine, but it is darker and more concentrated.

**Alcohol blocks** the release of ADH. The kidneys then keep back less water, and you have to **pass water** more often. As a result the body loses fluid. This is one reason why alcohol can dry the body out.

If the body makes too little ADH, **central diabetes insipidus** develops. People with it pass very large amounts of pale, dilute urine, often several litres a day. They are constantly very thirsty. Despite the similar name, this disease has nothing to do with diabetes of the sugar kind. It is usually treated with an artificial substance that works in a similar way to ADH.

gewusst: “Diabetes insipidus” means roughly “tasteless flow”, because, unlike in sugar diabetes, the urine is not sweet.
In the morning the urine is often darker, because the body releases more ADH during the night.

teile.einleitung: Brown fat tissue is a special kind of body fat. Unlike ordinary white fat, it does not primarily store energy but burns it to produce heat. It helps newborns and hibernating animals not to freeze.
wichtigste: Brown fat tissue produces heat instead of storing energy.
Its brown colour comes from very many mitochondria.
The protein UCP1, also called thermogenin, makes heat production possible.
Newborns have a lot of brown fat between the shoulder blades and at the neck.
In the cold it is activated through the sympathetic system with noradrenaline.
Adults too still have active brown fat.

abschnitte.text: White fat cells contain **one large fat droplet** and serve as an energy store. Brown fat cells, on the other hand, contain **many small fat droplets**. They also have very many **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. These contain pigments with iron that give the tissue its brownish colour. Brown fat is also well supplied with blood vessels.

Normally mitochondria use the energy from food to make an energy carrier for the cell. In brown fat, though, there is the protein **UCP1**, also called **thermogenin**. It makes sure that the energy is released directly as **heat**. In the cold, the **sympathetic system**, a part of the nervous system, sends the messenger substance **noradrenaline** to the cells. Then heat production starts up.

**Newborns** cannot yet shiver well to warm themselves. That is why they have a lot of brown fat, above all **between the shoulder blades** and at the **neck**. Animals in hibernation such as **marmots** also use brown fat. When they wake in spring, they use it to heat their body up quickly. In this way they get back to normal temperature in a short time.

For a long time it was thought that adults hardly have any brown fat. With **PET-CT**, an imaging method using radioactively labelled glucose, active brown fat was made visible in adults too. There are also **beige fat cells**. These are cells in white fat that take on heat-producing properties through cold. Researchers are studying whether this knowledge can one day be used against overweight.

gewusst: Brown fat occurs only in mammals.
Active brown fat lights up in the PET-CT, because in the cold it takes up a lot of sugar.

teile.einleitung: Broca’s area is a region of the cerebral cortex that is very important for speaking. It helps to form words into sentences and to plan the movements of speech. If it is injured, speaking suddenly becomes hard.
wichtigste: Broca’s area is named after the French doctor Paul Broca.
In most right-handers it lies in the left half of the brain.
It corresponds to Brodmann areas 44 and 45.
Broca’s famous patient could only say the syllable “Tan”.
In Broca’s aphasia, you speak haltingly and in telegram style.
The most common cause is a blockage of the middle cerebral artery.

abschnitte.text: Broca’s area lies in the **frontal lobe** of the cerebrum, in the lower part of the front folds of the brain. In most right-handers it is in the **left half of the brain**. The researcher Korbinian Brodmann divided the cerebral cortex into numbered fields. Broca’s area corresponds to **Brodmann areas 44 and 45**. It works closely with other language regions, for example with **Wernicke’s area**, which is important mainly for understanding language.

The French doctor **Paul Broca** examined in 1861 a patient called **Louis Leborgne**. He understood language, but could hardly say anything any more except the syllable **“Tan”**. That is why he was also called “Tan” in the hospital. After his death Broca found damage in the left frontal lobe of the brain. In this way he showed that particular regions of the brain are responsible for particular tasks.

An **aphasia** is a language disorder after brain damage. In **Broca’s aphasia**, those affected speak **haltingly**, with effort and in **telegram style**. Because mainly the production of speech is disturbed, it is also called **motor aphasia**. Typical is **agrammatism**: small function words and endings drop out. Instead of “I am going to the doctor tomorrow”, someone might say only “tomorrow doctor”.

Most often, Broca’s aphasia arises through a **stroke**. In it the **middle cerebral artery** often becomes blocked. Then the tissue gets too little oxygen. With **speech therapy**, many of those affected can learn to speak better again. The earlier the therapy begins, the better the chances often are.

gewusst: The brain of Louis Leborgne is still kept in Paris today.
Sign language is also processed in Broca’s area.

teile.einleitung: CRISPR is a method with which researchers can change the genetic material very precisely. It is also called “gene scissors”. The system originally comes from bacteria, which use it to defend themselves against viruses.
wichtigste: The protein Cas9 is often used as the “gene scissors”.
A guide RNA steers Cas9 to the right place on the DNA.
Next to the target site there has to be a short PAM sequence.
In bacteria, CRISPR originally serves to defend against viruses.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
In 2023 the first CRISPR therapy, against sickle cell anaemia, was approved.

abschnitte.text: Bacteria are often attacked by viruses. Many bacteria therefore store small pieces of the virus’s genetic material in their own DNA. These places have a special pattern of repeating sections. That is where the name **CRISPR** comes from, the abbreviation for **Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats**. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium recognises it and cuts up its genetic material.

The scissors are usually the protein **Cas9**. A **guide RNA** leads Cas9 to exactly the place on the DNA that you want to change. For Cas9 to be able to cut, a short **PAM sequence** has to lie next to the target site. Then Cas9 cuts through both strands of the DNA. After that the cell tries to repair the cut.

If the cell repairs the cut **without a template**, small mistakes often happen. Small **insertions** or **deletions** arise, that is, added or missing building blocks. In this way a gene can be switched off. If you give the cell a suitable **template** as well, you can also change a gene in a targeted way. In this way, for example, plants, bacteria or cells can be studied in the laboratory.

The Frenchwoman **Emmanuelle Charpentier** and the American **Jennifer Doudna** showed in 2012 how CRISPR/Cas9 can be used as a tool. For this they received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in **2020**. In **2023** the first CRISPR therapy was approved, against the hereditary disease **sickle cell anaemia**. Because the method is so powerful, there is also much debate about where its limits should lie.

gewusst: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna were the first all-female team to win a Nobel Prize in a natural science.
Cas9 originally comes from a bacterium that can cause sore throats in humans.

teile.einleitung: Braille is a writing of raised dots that you can feel with your fingers. It makes it possible for blind and severely visually impaired people to read and write independently. It was invented by the Frenchman Louis Braille.
wichtigste: Braille is made for blind people.
Each character consists of up to six dots.
The dots feel like little hills.
Louis Braille invented his writing at about 16.
You can write it with a Braille writer.
Books in Braille are much thicker than ordinary books.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Braille** was born in France in 1809. His father was a **saddler** and made leather goods. As a small boy, Louis injured his eye in the workshop with a pointed tool. Through an inflammation he soon went blind in both eyes. Later he attended a school for blind children in Paris.

At school Louis got to know a writing that an officer had developed for **soldiers**. It was meant to make **reading in the dark** possible, entirely without light. This night writing was complicated, though, and needed many dots. Louis simplified it and, at about **16 years old**, developed his own dot writing. It was much easier to learn.

Each character stands in a small **cell** with six possible dots, arranged in two columns of three. Depending on which dots are raised, a letter, a number or a punctuation mark results. This gives **64 possibilities**. The dots feel like **little hills**. Practised readers glide their fingertips quickly over the lines.

Braille can be written with a **Braille writer**, which presses the dots into the paper. Today there are also computers with a **Braille display** that shows text as tactile dots. Because the dots need a lot of space and the paper is thick, books in Braille are much **thicker** than others. An ordinary novel can fill several volumes.

gewusst: Braille is often found on lift buttons and on medicine packs.
Louis Braille died in 1852, and only after his death did his writing become established worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Computed tomography, CT for short, is a method that lets doctors look inside the body. A machine takes many pictures with X-rays, and a computer puts them together into cross-sectional images. In this way organs, bones and blood vessels can be seen very precisely.
wichtigste: A CT works with **X-rays**.
It produces **cross-sectional images** through the body.
The Greek word “tome” means **cut**.
**Godfrey Hounsfield** developed the first CT scanner and received the Nobel Prize in 1979.
A **contrast medium** makes blood vessels and organs easier to see.
A CT is quicker than an MRI, but the radiation dose is higher than for a single X-ray.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary X-ray shows everything on top of each other, like a shadow. A CT, by contrast, produces **cross-sectional images**, as if the body were cut into thin slices, without any knife at all. The word **tomography** comes from the Greek “tome”, which means **cut**. The computer can also put the slices together into a three-dimensional picture.

The patient lies on a **couch** that moves slowly through a large **ring**. In this ring an X-ray tube turns around the body. On the opposite side, **detectors** measure how much radiation gets through the body. From many measurements from all directions, the computer calculates the images. You have to lie still, and sometimes hold your breath for a moment.

Some tissues look similar in a CT. That is why a **contrast medium** is sometimes injected into a vein. It weakens the X-rays more strongly and so makes **blood vessels** and organs easier to see. With it, doctors can recognise, for example, narrowed vessels or inflammation.

A big advantage of the CT is speed: the examination is much **quicker** than a **magnetic resonance imaging** scan (MRI). That is why the CT is especially important after accidents, when every minute counts. A disadvantage is the **radiation dose**, which is higher than for a single ordinary X-ray. That is why a CT is done only when it is really necessary.

The first CT scanner was developed by the British engineer **Godfrey Hounsfield** in the early 1970s. The mathematical foundations had been worked out by the physicist **Allan Cormack**. Together they received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in **1979**. At first only the head could be examined, soon afterwards the whole body.

gewusst: The values used to give the density of tissue in a CT are called Hounsfield units, after the inventor.
Hounsfield worked at the firm EMI, which also released records.

teile.einleitung: Surgery is the field of medicine that treats diseases and injuries with operations. Surgeons open the body, repair or remove something and close the wound again. Thanks to anaesthesia and hygiene, this is much safer today than in the past.
wichtigste: Surgery means: treating diseases and injuries through **operations**.
**Trauma surgery** deals with injuries after accidents.
Sterile clothing, gloves and masks prevent germs from getting into the wound.
In a **transplant**, a donor organ is put in.
Before a planned operation, the patient’s **consent** is needed.
In 1967 the first heart transplant from human to human succeeded in Cape Town.

abschnitte.text: In the past, many people died after an operation from wound infections. In the 19th century the British surgeon **Joseph Lister** introduced **antisepsis**, that is, the killing of germs in operations. Today people work **sterile** in the operating theatre: everything that touches the wound is free of germs. That is why everyone wears gloves, a mask, a cap and special clothing. The instruments are also thoroughly sterilised beforehand.

A very common operation is the **appendix operation**. In it, the inflamed **appendix** is usually removed, a small attachment on the large intestine. In an **amputation**, a part of the body is cut off, for example when it is badly injured or diseased. **Trauma surgery** sets broken bones and treats injuries. Besides these there are many specialities, for example heart surgery or paediatric surgery.

In **minimally invasive** surgery, only very small cuts are needed. Through them a tiny camera and slim instruments are pushed into the body. The surgeon sees the inside on a screen and operates with a steady hand. This technique is also called **keyhole surgery**. The wounds heal faster and smaller scars are left.

In a **transplant**, an organ from a donor is put into the body of a sick person, for example a kidney or a heart. In 1967 the first heart transplant from human to human succeeded in **Cape Town** in South Africa. One problem is that the immune system can reject the foreign organ. That is why the recipients are given medicines that dampen the defence. In Switzerland, the foundation Swisstransplant coordinates the allocation of donor organs.

Before a planned operation there is an **information talk**. The doctor explains what will be done and what risks there are. Then the patient has to give their **consent**, usually with a signature. During the operation, the **anaesthetic** makes sure that you sleep and feel no pain. Anaesthesia specialists monitor breathing and heartbeat throughout.

gewusst: The Bernese surgeon Theodor Kocher received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1909, as the first surgeon, for his work on the thyroid gland.
To kill germs, Lister used carbolic acid, which he even sprayed as a fine mist in the operating room.

teile.einleitung: COPD is a lasting lung disease in which the airways are narrowed. The abbreviation stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The most important cause is smoking.
wichtigste: The most important cause of COPD is tobacco smoking.
Typical are sputum, cough and breathlessness, the AHA symptoms in German.
Often a lung emphysema with destroyed air sacs is part of it.
An obstruction counts as confirmed when the ratio of FEV1 to FVC is below 0.7.
In GOLD 4, the FEV1 value is below 30 per cent of the expected value.
Pursed-lip breathing helps with breathing out.

abschnitte.text: In COPD the **airways are permanently narrowed**. This is called an **obstruction**. The bronchi are inflamed, and a lot of mucus forms. Often a **lung emphysema** is part of it: the walls of the air sacs are destroyed, and large, floppy bubbles arise. The lung can then take up less oxygen.

The most important cause is **tobacco smoking**, in Switzerland as in other industrialised countries. Dust and harmful substances at work can also play a part. Rarely, an inherited **alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency** is the cause. In it a protective substance for the lung tissue is missing, and even young people can develop an emphysema. The most important thing against COPD is never to start smoking, or to give it up.

The three main symptoms are called the **AHA symptoms** in German: **A**uswurf (sputum), **H**usten (cough) and **A**temnot (breathlessness). Lung function is measured with a breathing test, **spirometry**. If the ratio of **FEV1** to **FVC** after a medicine that widens the airways is **below 0.7**, the obstruction counts as confirmed according to **GOLD**. FEV1 is the amount of air you can breathe out in one second. In **GOLD 4**, the very severe form, this value is below 30 per cent of the expected value.

In the past, two types were distinguished. The **pink puffer** is lean, breathes hard and has mainly an emphysema. The **blue bloater** is rather overweight and has a bluish skin colour. COPD cannot be cured, but it can be treated well. Medicines to inhale widen the bronchi. With **pursed-lip breathing** you breathe out against slightly closed lips, so the bronchi collapse less when breathing out.

gewusst: GOLD stands for an international initiative that issues recommendations on COPD.
Anyone who gives up smoking clearly slows the progress of COPD.

teile.einleitung: Every day we breathe in **air** thousands of times. It is made up of several gases that you cannot see. Clean air to breathe is important for our health.
wichtigste: Air consists mainly of nitrogen and oxygen.
About one fifth of the air is oxygen.
Carbon dioxide is only a very small part of the air.
Even breathed-out air still contains quite a lot of oxygen.
Exhaust fumes pollute the air in cities.
Cigarette smoke harms the lungs.

abschnitte.text: Air is a mixture of gases. About four fifths is **nitrogen**, and about **one fifth is oxygen**. There are also small amounts of argon and only a very little **carbon dioxide**. There is also water vapour in the air. You cannot see air, but you can feel it when it moves: outdoors you notice this as **wind**.

When you breathe in, the lungs take **oxygen** from the air. The blood carries it to all the cells in the body. When you breathe out, we give off **carbon dioxide**. But in the air we breathe out there is still **quite a lot of oxygen**. That is why rescue breaths work in first aid.

If many people are in a closed room for a long time, the air becomes **stuffy**. It then contains more carbon dioxide and moisture. Then it helps to **open the window** and air the room well for a short time. In winter, the air indoors is often very dry. A **humidifier** makes the air moister.

In cities, the air is polluted mainly by **exhaust fumes** from cars, heating systems and factories. This also includes fine dust, **particulate matter**. In the **forest** the air is usually cleaner, because trees filter dust out of the air. **Cigarette smoke** is especially harmful. It harms the lungs, even in people who only breathe in the smoke from others.

gewusst: An adult breathes in many thousands of litres of air in one day.
In Switzerland, many stations constantly measure how clean the air is.

teile.einleitung: Molars sit at the back of the mouth and are the strongest chewing tools we have. They grind up food so that we can swallow and digest it well.
wichtigste: The molars stand at the back on the left and right of the mouth.
They grind food like a mill.
Their chewing surface is broad and has cusps and grooves.
Another word for molar is grinding tooth, and the technical term is molar.
At about 6 years old the first big permanent molar comes.
The very last molars are called wisdom teeth.

abschnitte.text: The **molars** stand at the back on the left and right of the mouth, near the cheeks. In German they are called “Backenzähne”, or cheek teeth, for this reason. At the front of the mouth the incisors cut, and the canines hold things fast. The molars are broad and strong. With them you chew a hard **nut** into small pieces.

The **chewing surface** of a molar is broad and has **cusps** and small **grooves**. Top and bottom, the teeth fit into each other. In this way the food is ground fine, as in a mill. That is why they are also called **grinding teeth**. The technical term is **molar**, from the Latin word for millstone.

At about **6 years old**, the first big permanent molar grows behind the milk teeth. It is also called the **six-year molar**. No milk tooth falls out for it, it simply comes in addition. More molars follow later. The very last ones are the **wisdom teeth**. They often come only at 17 or later, and sometimes not at all.

Bits of food easily stick in the **grooves** of the chewing surface. There, bacteria can cause **tooth decay**, that is, holes in the tooth. That is why you have to clean the molars especially thoroughly. Dentists can **seal** the grooves with a thin protective varnish. In many Swiss municipalities there is a **school dental service** that regularly checks children’s teeth.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole human body.
The first permanent molar comes without a milk tooth falling out for it.
Some people never get wisdom teeth.

teile.einleitung: Blind people can see little or nothing at all. With aids such as the white cane, Braille and screen readers, they manage their everyday life. Hearing and the sense of touch play a big part in this.
wichtigste: Braille, the writing made of dots, was invented by Louis Braille of France.
One character has at most six dots in two columns.
The white cane shows others that someone is blind.
In Switzerland, white guide lines with grooves on the ground help.
Screen readers read out texts on the computer.
On many medicine packs the name is given in Braille.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Braille** was born in **France** in 1809. He went blind as a small boy. At about **15 years old** he developed a writing of raised **dots** that is named after him. One character consists of at most **six dots** in two columns. Depending on which dots are raised, a different letter results. You read the writing with your fingertips.

The **white cane** shows other people that someone is blind. With it you feel the way ahead. In Switzerland, on pavements and in stations there are **white guide lines** with **grooves** on the ground. You feel them with the cane or your feet. They lead, for example, to platforms or pedestrian crossings.

Blind people pay close attention to **sounds** and feel their surroundings. In this way they replace part of seeing. From the sound they can tell, for example, whether a room is big or small. Smell also helps with orientation. Some also have a guide dog.

A **screen reader** reads out text on the screen with a computer voice. Some devices also show the text in Braille on a **Braille display**. On many **medicine packs** the name is given in Braille. In this way blind people can tell them apart. Phones too can be operated by voice.

gewusst: Braille developed his writing from a night writing of dots and dashes that was meant for soldiers.
On some banknotes and lift buttons there are tactile marks for blind people.

teile.einleitung: Chromosomes are the packaging of your genetic material. In almost every one of your body cells there are 46 of them, neatly arranged in the cell nucleus. They contain the construction plan that decides how you look and how your body works.
wichtigste: Chromosomes consist of DNA and proteins and carry the genes.
A normal human body cell has 46 chromosomes, that is, 23 pairs.
A mature egg cell and a sperm have only 23 chromosomes each.
Sex is partly determined by the chromosomes X and Y.
The two chromatids of a chromosome are joined at the centromere.
The end pieces are called telomeres and become a little shorter with every cell division.
In Down syndrome, chromosome 21 is present three times, which is called trisomy 21.

abschnitte.text: A **chromosome** is a long thread of DNA that is wound round proteins and tightly packed. On it lie many genes, that is, single sections of the genetic information. The name comes from Greek and means colour body, because they can be stained well. Under the microscope they are clearly visible mainly during cell division.

A normal human body cell has 46 chromosomes, which form 23 **pairs**. From each pair, one chromosome comes from the mother and one from the father. Egg and sperm cells have only a single set of 23 chromosomes. At fertilisation, a cell with 46 chromosomes arises again.

Before a cell division, each chromosome is doubled and then consists of two identical halves, the **chromatids**. These are joined at a narrow place, the **centromere**. The ends of the chromosomes are called **telomeres** and protect them like the plastic caps on shoelaces. With every cell division the telomeres become a little shorter.

Experts can photograph all the chromosomes of a cell and arrange them by size and shape. This presentation is called a **karyogram**. The pairs are numbered from 1 to 22, and then there are the two sex chromosomes. Women usually have two X chromosomes, men one X and one Y.

Sometimes something has gone wrong in the making of egg or sperm cells. Then a chromosome can be missing or there can be one too many. In **Down syndrome**, chromosome 21 is present three times instead of twice, which is called trisomy 21. People with Down syndrome can lead a full life and need more or less support depending on the person.

The number of chromosomes is different in every species. Chimpanzees have 48, dogs 78 and fruit flies only 8. The number says nothing about how complicated a living thing is. Some ferns have over a thousand chromosomes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of DNA with the construction plan for a particular feature.
One of the two identical halves of a doubled chromosome.
An ordered picture of all the chromosomes of a cell.
A chromosome is present three times instead of twice.

gewusst: If you unrolled the DNA of all 46 chromosomes of a single cell, it would be about 2 metres long.
The Y chromosome is one of the smallest human chromosomes.
That humans have 46 chromosomes has only been known since 1956.

teile.einleitung: **Bronchial asthma** is a long-lasting inflammation of the airways. In an attack, the bronchi narrow and breathing becomes hard. Asthma is not infectious and can now usually be treated well.
wichtigste: Asthma is a chronic inflammation of the airways.
In an attack, the airways narrow.
A wheezing sound when breathing out is typical.
Pollen, animal hair or dust can trigger an attack.
A reliever inhaler quickly widens the bronchi.
Asthma is not infectious, and children whose asthma is well treated can usually do sport.

abschnitte.text: Air reaches the lungs by way of the windpipe and the **bronchi**. In asthma, these airways are permanently slightly inflamed and react very sensitively. In an attack, the muscles around the bronchi tighten, the lining swells and sticky mucus forms. The airways **narrow**, and breathing out in particular becomes hard.

In **allergic asthma**, for example, **flower pollen**, animal hair or house dust mites set off an attack. Cold air, smoke, infections or heavy exertion can also cause symptoms. Typical are coughing, difficulty breathing, a feeling of tightness in the chest and a **wheeze** when breathing out. Asthma is **not infectious**.

Many people with asthma take a medicine every day that dampens the **inflammation**, often as a spray to inhale. In an attack, a **reliever inhaler** helps, which quickly widens the bronchi. An inhaling aid, the so-called **spacer**, is a tube between the inhaler and the mouth. With it, more of the drug reaches the lungs and less stays behind in the mouth.

With a **peak flow meter** you measure how fast you can breathe out at most. If the value falls, the airways are narrower than usual. In this way you can notice early when the asthma is getting worse. Asthma differs from the lung disease **COPD** mainly in that the narrowing of the airways is largely **reversible**.

A child whose asthma is well treated can usually **do sport without problems**. It is important to warm up well and to have the reliever inhaler with you. Teachers and coaches should know what to do in an attack. Many top athletes have asthma and still win medals.

gewusst: Asthma is one of the most common chronic illnesses in children.
The word asthma comes from Greek and means panting or hard breathing.

teile.einleitung: Bronchioles are the finest branches of the airways in the lungs. They lie between the bronchi and the air sacs. Through them the air reaches the place where oxygen passes into the blood.
wichtigste: Bronchioles are the finest branches of the bronchi.
Their diameter is less than a millimetre.
There is no cartilage in their wall.
Smooth muscles can make the bronchioles narrower or wider.
They open into the alveolar ducts.
An inflammation of the bronchioles is called bronchiolitis.

abschnitte.text: The airways in the lungs branch like a tree. The smallest branches before the air sacs are called **bronchioles**. Their diameter is **smaller than a millimetre**. Unlike the large bronchi, they have **no cartilage** in the wall. They are held open by the surrounding, elastic lung tissue.

In the wall of the bronchioles lie **smooth muscles**. They work by themselves, without our controlling them. When they contract, the airways become **narrower**. When they relax, they become **wider**. In **asthma**, the bronchioles narrow too much, and breathing becomes hard. Medicines to inhale can relax the muscles again.

abschnitte.titel: The way to the air sacs
abschnitte.text: Right at the end there are the **respiratory bronchioles**. On their wall sit single **air sacs**, so gas exchange already begins here. After that the bronchioles open into the **alveolar ducts**. These are densely covered with air sacs. There oxygen gets into the blood, and carbon dioxide is given off.

An inflammation of the bronchioles is called **bronchiolitis**. It affects mainly **infants** and small children, whose airways are still very narrow. It is most often caused by the **RS virus**. Typical are coughing, fast breathing and sometimes whistling sounds. The illness occurs mainly in the winter half of the year.

gewusst: A human lung contains tens of thousands of bronchioles.
In adults the RS virus usually causes only a cold.

teile.einleitung: Before sport you do a **warm-up**. In it you prepare the body for the effort. The muscles, heart and joints slowly get going, and you are less likely to hurt yourself.
wichtigste: In a warm-up the muscles become warm and loose.
The pulse rises slowly as you do it.
In school sport, the warm-up lasts about 10 minutes.
Gentle running and hopping are good exercises for warming up.
With arm circles you loosen the shoulders.
After training comes the cool-down.

abschnitte.text: In a warm-up the **muscles** become warm and loose. They can then contract and stretch better. The **joints** also become more mobile. The mind also gets ready for the sport. Anyone who warms up well can do more and is **less likely to hurt themselves**, for example with a pulled muscle.

In a warm-up the **pulse rises slowly**. The heart pumps more blood, and breathing becomes faster. In this way the muscles get more oxygen. Body temperature rises slightly. It is important not to start at full strength straight away, but to increase the effort bit by bit.

**Gentle running and hopping** are good for warming up. In **jumping jacks**, you jump and clap your hands together above your head while your legs move apart. With **arm circles** you loosen the shoulders. High knees, skipping and little games of tag are also good. In school sport, the warm-up usually lasts **about 10 minutes**.

After training it is best not to stop at once. In a **cool-down**, you jog slowly for a few more minutes. In this way the heart and breathing calm down bit by bit. After that you can stretch the muscles gently and drink enough.

gewusst: Professional sportspeople also warm up thoroughly before every match or race.
In cold weather, the warm-up is best a little longer.

teile.einleitung: The apple is the most popular fruit in Switzerland. It is crisp, juicy and full of vitamins. Apples grow on trees and are harvested mainly in autumn.
wichtigste: The apple is the most popular fruit in Switzerland.
Many vitamins are in and just under the skin.
Before eating an apple with its skin, you should wash it.
A cut apple turns brown because it reacts with the air.
Thurgau is jokingly called “Mostindien” because of its many apple trees.
Süssmost is fresh apple juice.
Most apples are harvested in autumn.

abschnitte.text: Apples contain a lot of **water**, fruit sugar, vitamins and **fibre**. Especially many vitamins are **in and just under the skin**. So it is worth eating the apple with its skin. But first you should **wash** it well, so that dirt and residues come off. An English saying goes: **“An apple a day keeps the doctor away”**.

In Switzerland, the **apple** is the **most popular fruit**. Many apples grow in eastern Switzerland. The canton of **Thurgau** has so many apple trees that it is jokingly called **“Mostindien”**, roughly “Cider India”. Most apples are harvested in **autumn**. Stored well in cool rooms, however, Swiss apples can be bought almost all year round. Well-known varieties are, for example, Gala, Golden Delicious, Braeburn and Boskoop.

Juice is pressed from apples. Fresh apple juice is called **Süssmost** in Switzerland. If you let the juice ferment, you get **Most**, also called cider, which contains alcohol. Apples are also used to make apple sauce, dried fruit or cakes such as the popular apple tart, the “Apfelwähe”.

If you cut an apple open, the cut surface turns **brown** after a short time. This is because substances in the flesh **react with the oxygen in the air**. A particular enzyme in the apple speeds this process up. The brown apple is still perfectly good to eat. A few drops of **lemon juice** slow the browning.

gewusst: Worldwide there are thousands of different apple varieties.
Apples float on water because they contain a lot of air in the flesh.

teile.einleitung: In appendicitis, usually the appendix is inflamed, a small attachment on the caecum. Typical are stomach pains at the lower right. Often the appendix has to be removed in an operation.
wichtigste: Usually it is not the caecum itself but the appendix that is inflamed.
The caecum is the start of the large intestine, at the lower right of the belly.
Typical are pains at the lower right, often with feeling sick and fever.
Often the appendix is operated out.
With bad stomach pains, you go quickly to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: The **caecum**, in German “Blinddarm”, is the start of the **large intestine**. It lies at the lower right of the belly, where the small intestine opens into the large intestine. From it hangs a small, narrow tube, the **appendix**. When people speak of “Blinddarmentzündung”, it is usually really the appendix that is inflamed. The technical term for this is **appendicitis**.

It often begins with stomach ache around the navel. Later the pain usually moves to the **lower right**. Often **feeling sick**, vomiting, little hunger and a mild **fever** come with it. Walking, coughing or hopping can make the pain worse. With such symptoms you go quickly to the doctor, because an inflamed appendix can burst.

Often the inflamed appendix is removed in an **operation**. Nowadays this is often done with **keyhole surgery** through small cuts. People can live well without an appendix. After a few days you can usually go home. Sometimes mild cases are also treated with medicines against bacteria.

gewusst: Appendicitis is one of the most common reasons for an abdominal operation in children and young people.
The appendix contains a lot of defence tissue and probably helps the immune system in the gut.

teile.einleitung: The organ of Corti is the actual organ of hearing in our ear. It lies well protected in the cochlea of the inner ear. There sound waves are turned into electrical nerve signals that travel to the brain.
wichtigste: The organ of Corti lies in the **cochlea** of the inner ear.
It is named after the anatomist **Alfonso Corti**.
Above the sensory cells lies the **tectorial membrane**.
The cochlea has about **two and a half turns**.
The signals reach the brain by way of the **auditory nerve**.
Young people hear from about **20 Hz to 20 kHz**.

abschnitte.text: Deep in the skull lies the inner ear with the **cochlea**, which looks like a snail shell. In humans it has about **two and a half turns**. Inside, it is divided into three channels filled with fluid. **Reissner’s membrane** separates the **scala media** from the **scala vestibuli**. In the scala media sits the organ of Corti.

The organ of Corti rests on the **basilar membrane**. It contains sensory cells with fine hairs, the **hair cells**. A distinction is made between inner and outer hair cells. Above them lies the **tectorial membrane** like a roof. The organ is named after the Italian anatomist **Alfonso Corti**, who described it in the 19th century.

Sound makes the eardrum and the small bones of the ear vibrate. This vibration reaches the fluid in the cochlea. There a **travelling wave** arises along the basilar membrane. The hairs of the hair cells are bent against the tectorial membrane. This produces an electrical signal that runs to the brain by way of the **auditory nerve** (cochlear nerve).

Each place in the cochlea reacts to a different pitch. High tones are processed near the entrance, low tones further in at the tip. A young person hears from about **20 hertz** to **20 kilohertz**. With age, it is mainly the high tones that are lost. The travelling wave was researched by **Georg von Békésy**, who received the Nobel Prize for it in **1961**.

In humans, destroyed hair cells do not grow back. Very loud music, bangers or machine noise can damage them permanently. That is why it is worth wearing **ear protection** at concerts or during noisy work. Headphones, too, should not be turned up too loud.

gewusst: The cochlea is about as big as a pea.
Georg von Békésy was originally an engineer and first worked on telephone lines.

teile.einleitung: A burn arises when heat injures the skin, for example from a hot hob, fire or hot water. With proper first aid, small burns usually heal well. Large burns are an emergency.
wichtigste: You cool a small burn for about 10 to 20 minutes with lukewarm water.
Butter, flour or oil never belong on a burn.
You do not prick burn blisters.
Hot water or steam also cause injuries, called scalds.
Sunburn is also a mild burn of the skin.
With large burns, dial the emergency number 144 at once.

abschnitte.text: In the kitchen you easily burn yourself on the **hot cooker**, on pans or on the oven. Hot water, tea or steam lead to a **scald**. The **sun** can also damage the skin: sunburn is a mild burn. Experts divide burns into **degrees**. In the first degree the skin is reddened, in the second blisters form, in the third the skin is destroyed deeply.

The most important thing with a small burn is **cooling**. You hold the spot for about **10 to 20 minutes** under running, lukewarm water. Ice-cold water or ice directly on the skin are not good, because they can damage the skin further. With large burns you cool only briefly, so that the body does not get too cold. You can also ease sunburn with damp, cool cloths.

Old home remedies such as **butter**, **flour** or oil never belong on a burn. They keep the heat in the skin and can bring germs into the wound. You do not prick a **burn blister**, because the skin of the blister protects the wound. Afterwards you cover the spot loosely and cleanly. Clothing that sticks to the skin is not torn away.

If a person’s **clothing** is on fire, they should roll on the ground. You can also smother the flames with a blanket and must fetch help at once. With large burns, burns on the face or in small children, in Switzerland you dial the **emergency number 144** at once. You reach the fire brigade on **118**. Until help comes, you stay with the injured person.

gewusst: Sunburn often shows only some hours after sunbathing.
For people with severe burns there are specialised burn centres in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Capsaicin is the substance that makes chillies hot. It produces the burning feeling in the mouth. Capsaicin is used not only in the kitchen, but also in medicine and in pepper spray.
wichtigste: Capsaicin occurs naturally in chilli pods.
Most capsaicin is in the pale partitions inside the pod.
The heat of chillies is measured with the Scoville scale.
Capsaicin irritates the same sensors that also react to heat.
Milk eases the burning better than water.
Birds hardly feel the heat and spread the seeds of chillies.

abschnitte.text: Capsaicin occurs naturally in **chilli pods**. Most of it is not in the seeds, but in the **pale partitions** inside the pod, to which the seeds are attached. Anyone who removes them makes a dish milder. Sweet peppers, on the other hand, contain almost no capsaicin. The heat is measured with the **Scoville scale**, named after the American pharmacist Wilbur Scoville.

Chilli feels **hot** in the mouth, although it is not warm at all. The reason: capsaicin irritates the same **sensors** in the skin and mucous membranes that also react to **heat**. The brain therefore reports burning. Hot is thus really not a taste like sweet or salty, but a **pain stimulus**. The body often reacts with sweating and a runny nose.

Capsaicin dissolves well in **fat**, but hardly in **water**. Water therefore only spreads it about in the mouth. **Milk**, yoghurt or a piece of bread help better against the burning. They take up the capsaicin and wash it away. Care is also needed when cutting chillies, because afterwards your hands must not get into your eyes.

**Birds** hardly feel the heat of capsaicin. They eat the fruits and so **spread** the seeds of chillies far and wide. Mammals, on the other hand, tend to avoid hot fruits. In **medicine**, capsaicin is used in **plasters and ointments** against pain. It is also often the active substance in **pepper spray**, which irritates the eyes strongly.

gewusst: Pure capsaicin has a value of about 16 million units on the Scoville scale.
The hottest kinds of chilli in the world reach over a million units on the Scoville scale.

teile.einleitung: Bacteria are tiny living things that consist of only a single cell. They live almost everywhere: in the soil, in water, in the air and also in and on our body. Most are harmless or even useful, but some can cause illnesses.
wichtigste: Bacteria are single-celled living things without a cell nucleus.
They are usually only a few thousandths of a millimetre in size.
Bacteria multiply by dividing in two.
Lactic acid bacteria help in making yoghurt.
The many bacteria in our gut help with digestion.
Antibiotics such as penicillin help against bacteria that cause disease.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
Resistant bacteria are bacteria against which an antibiotic no longer works.

abschnitte.text: Bacteria are so small that you can only see them under a **microscope**. There are spherical, rod-shaped and spiral-shaped bacteria. Unlike human cells, they have no **cell nucleus**, and their genetic material lies free in the cell. Many have a firm cell wall and some a flagellum, with which they move about.

Bacteria multiply by **dividing in two**: one cell splits into two identical daughter cells. Under good conditions, in some species this can happen every 20 minutes. So a single bacterium turns into millions in a few hours. Warmth, moisture and food speed up growth, and cold slows it down, which is why the fridge keeps food fresh.

Bacteria are among the oldest living things on Earth and have existed for more than 3 billion years. You find them in hot springs, in eternal ice and deep in the sea. A handful of soil contains billions of bacteria. In the ground they break down dead plants and animals and so make nutrients available again.

In the human gut live countless bacteria, which together are called the **gut flora** or microbiome. They help with digestion and protect against harmful germs. **Lactic acid bacteria** turn milk into yoghurt and also provide the flavour in sauerkraut and some kinds of cheese. In Swiss cheesemaking, bacteria play an important part, and in Emmental they even make the holes.

Some bacteria cause diseases, for example tonsillitis, pneumonia, tuberculosis or Lyme disease after a tick bite. In 1928 **Alexander Fleming** discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic. Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth. If they are used too often, **resistant** bacteria arise, against which the drug no longer works.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a cell in which the genetic material is packed; bacteria do not have one.
Multiplication in which one cell splits into two.
All the bacteria in the gut, also called the microbiome.
When an antibiotic no longer works against bacteria.

gewusst: In and on a person live about as many bacteria as the body has cells of its own.
The holes in Emmental come from gases made by propionic acid bacteria.
The Dutchman Antoni van Leeuwenhoek was one of the first to see bacteria, under his self-built microscope in the 17th century.

teile.einleitung: A blood pressure monitor measures how strongly the blood presses in the vessels. The device shows two values and often the pulse too. You find it in doctors’ surgeries, chemists and many homes.
wichtigste: The device measures the pressure of the blood against the vessel walls.
The cuff is a band with air cushions, usually on the upper arm.
The cuff is pumped up and lets the air out slowly again.
Blood pressure has two values and is given in mmHg.
About 120 over 80 counts as a good value in adults.
When measuring, you sit still and do not talk.
In Switzerland you can also have your blood pressure measured at the chemist’s.

abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through the vessels. In doing so the blood **presses** against the walls of the **blood vessels**. This pressure is measured by the **blood pressure monitor**. Two **values** are always given. One shows the pressure when the heart pumps, the other the pressure between two heartbeats.

The **cuff** is a band with an **air cushion** in it. Usually you put it on the **upper arm**, at about the height of the heart. Some devices also measure at the **wrist**. When measuring, the cuff is **pumped up** with air and presses on the arm. Then the device lets the air out slowly again and measures as it does so.

Blood pressure is given in **millimetres of mercury**, abbreviated **mmHg**. In the past, measuring devices had a column of mercury. A blood pressure of about **120 over 80** counts as a good value in adults. In children it is usually a little lower. Electronic devices feel the heartbeats in the arm and therefore often show the **pulse** too.

**Movement** and **talking** change blood pressure. That is why you sit still and relaxed when measuring and do not speak. It is best to rest for a few minutes beforehand. Many **chemists** in Switzerland offer blood pressure measurement without a doctor’s appointment. The professionals there can explain the values.

gewusst: Mercury is hardly used in new measuring devices any more, but the unit mmHg has stayed.
Blood pressure is often a little different in the morning than in the evening.

teile.einleitung: In a slipped disc, soft tissue escapes from an intervertebral disc and can press on nerves. This can cause severe pain, but mostly heals without an operation.
wichtigste: Inside, a disc has a soft gelatinous core and outside a firm fibrous ring.
In a slipped disc the fibrous ring tears and core tissue escapes.
The lumbar spine is most often affected.
Typical are pains that radiate into the leg, or into the arm when the neck spine is affected.
A disturbance of bladder function is an emergency.
Mostly treatment is first conservative, with movement and painkillers.

abschnitte.text: Between the vertebral bodies lie the **intervertebral discs**. They act like shock absorbers and make the spine flexible. Inside they have a soft **gelatinous core** (nucleus pulposus) and outside a firm **fibrous ring** (anulus fibrosus). If the disc only bulges and the ring stays whole, it is called a **protrusion**. If the ring tears and core tissue escapes, it is a **prolapse**, that is, a slipped disc.

Most common are slipped discs in the **lumbar spine**, especially between L4 and L5 and between L5 and S1. This part carries a lot of weight and is very mobile. If the tissue presses on a nerve root, the pain radiates **into the leg**. Numbness or tingling often come with it. In a slipped disc in the **neck spine**, the pains radiate into the **arm**.

In the **Lasègue test**, the doctor lifts the straightened leg while you lie down. This stretches the sciatic nerve. If pain shoots into the leg, this points to an irritated nerve root. If a piece of tissue has come completely loose and lies free in the spinal canal, it is called a **sequestrum**. Exact pictures are often provided by magnetic resonance imaging.

Without paralysis, treatment is usually **conservative**, that is, without an operation. Painkillers, **physiotherapy** and movement that is as normal as possible are recommended. Most symptoms improve within weeks. An **emergency** is a sudden disturbance of the bladder or bowel. It can point to **cauda equina syndrome**, in which many nerve roots are crushed. Then a rapid operation is needed.

gewusst: A human spine has 23 intervertebral discs.
Intervertebral discs have no blood vessels of their own and are supplied with nutrients through movement.
In the evening you are a little shorter than in the morning, because the discs are squeezed together a little in the course of the day.

teile.einleitung: Many processes in the body run in a regular beat. These biological rhythms are controlled by an inner clock. The science that studies them is called chronobiology.
wichtigste: Circadian rhythms last about a day, like the sleep-wake rhythm.
Ultradian rhythms are shorter, for example the sleep cycle of about 90 minutes.
Infradian rhythms last longer than a day, such as hibernation.
Early risers are called larks, night people owls.
In many teenagers the inner clock shifts later.
Body temperature is lowest in the early hours of the morning.
The biorhythm theory with fixed cycles from birth is not proven.

abschnitte.text: **Chronobiology** studies the timing of processes in living things. The word comes from the Greek “chronos” for time. The best-known rhythm is the **circadian rhythm**. The name comes from the Latin “circa dies”, about a day. The **sleep-wake rhythm** is part of it. Daylight helps to reset the inner clock every day.

**Ultradian** rhythms are clearly shorter than a day and repeat several times daily. One example is the **sleep cycle** of about 90 minutes. **Infradian** rhythms last longer than a day, sometimes weeks or a whole year. Examples are the **hibernation** of many animals or bird migration. Body temperature also follows a beat: it varies by just under one degree during the day and is lowest in the **early hours of the morning**.

Not all people tick the same way. Anyone who likes to get up early and gets tired early is a **lark**. Anyone who stays awake late in the evening and prefers to sleep in the morning is an **owl**. These types are called **chronotypes** and are partly inborn. In many **teenagers** the inner clock shifts later. They get tired later in the evening and have trouble getting up in the morning.

By “biorhythm” a particular theory is sometimes meant. It claims that body, feelings and intellect follow fixed cycles of **23, 28 and 33 days** from birth. From this, people wanted to calculate good and bad days. Studies could **not confirm** this. In science this theory counts as **pseudoscience**, that is, as something that only looks scientific.

gewusst: People without daylight and without a clock mostly live in a rhythm that is a little longer than 24 hours.
Plants also have an inner clock: some open and close their flowers at fixed times of day.

teile.einleitung: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment that is formed when old red blood cells are broken down. The liver processes it so that it can be excreted with the bile. If the bilirubin level rises sharply, the skin and eyes turn yellow.
wichtigste: Bilirubin is formed from the haem of the red blood pigment haemoglobin.
The green intermediate product before it is called biliverdin.
In the blood, unconjugated bilirubin is carried to the liver bound to albumin.
In the liver, the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase couples bilirubin to glucuronic acid.
Gut bacteria turn it into stercobilin, which colours the stool brown.
Too much bilirubin leads to yellowing, called jaundice.
Jaundice in newborns is often treated with blue light.

abschnitte.text: Red blood cells live for about 120 days. After that they are broken down mainly in the spleen and liver. In this, the **haem** from the red blood pigment **haemoglobin** is released. The enzyme **haem oxygenase** opens the ring of the haem, producing the green **biliverdin**. Biliverdin reductase turns this into the yellow **bilirubin**.

The freshly made **unconjugated bilirubin** hardly dissolves in water, but dissolves well in fat. So it cannot float freely in the blood. It is bound to the protein **albumin** and carried to the liver in this way. There the liver cells take it up. This form is also called indirect bilirubin.

In the liver, the enzyme **UDP-glucuronosyltransferase**, UGT1A1 for short, couples the bilirubin to **glucuronic acid**. This makes it **water soluble**, and it is now called conjugated bilirubin. It reaches the gut with the **bile**. There gut bacteria break it down to urobilinogen and further to **stercobilin**. Stercobilin gives the stool its brown colour.

If there is too much bilirubin in the blood, it is deposited in the tissue. The skin and the **whites of the eyes** turn yellow, which is called **icterus** or jaundice. Causes can be a heavy breakdown of blood cells, a liver disease or **blocked bile flow**. With blocked bile flow the stool becomes pale, because the stercobilin is missing. Common and harmless is **Gilbert’s syndrome** (in German, Morbus Meulengracht), in which UGT1A1 is less active. The level then rises slightly, mainly in fasting or stress.

Many **newborns** turn slightly yellow in the first days of life, because their liver is not yet working fully. Mostly this disappears by itself. In marked jaundice, **phototherapy** with **blue light** helps. The light converts bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms. The body can excrete these without the detour through the coupling in the liver.

gewusst: The changing colours of a bruise also arise from the breakdown of haem by way of biliverdin to bilirubin.
Gilbert’s syndrome is very widespread and does not harm the liver.

teile.einleitung: The basic reproduction number R0 tells us how infectious a disease is. It gives the average number of people that one sick person infects when nobody is protected yet.
wichtigste: R0 is the average number of infections caused by one case in an unprotected population.
If R0 is greater than 1, a disease can spread.
With about 12 to 18, measles has one of the highest basic reproduction numbers.
The threshold for herd immunity is 1 minus 1 divided by R0.
The effective reproduction number R is R0 times the share of those who are susceptible.
If R is less than 1, an epidemic dies down.
Tetanus has no meaningful R0, because it is not passed from person to person.

abschnitte.text: The **basic reproduction number R0** describes how many people an infected person infects on average when everyone is **susceptible**. If R0 is greater than 1, the disease can spread. With R0 equal to 3, one case infects three, they infect nine, then 27, and in the fourth generation **81**. The growth is therefore **exponential**. **Measles** is extremely infectious and has an R0 of about 12 to 18.

In a simple model, R0 depends on three quantities: the **contact rate**, the **probability of transmission** per contact and the **length of time** that someone is infectious. R0 is roughly the product of these three values. Measures such as keeping your distance, washing your hands or **isolation** lower these factors. **Tetanus** has no meaningful R0: the spores get into wounds from the soil, not from person to person.

If some people are already immune, fewer infections succeed. The **effective reproduction number R** is then R0 times the share s of those who are susceptible. With R0 equal to 3 and s equal to 0.5, R is 1.5. If R is **less than 1**, the number of new infections falls from generation to generation and the epidemic dies down. During the **Covid-19 pandemic**, this value was regularly reported in Switzerland too.

For a disease to stop spreading, a certain share of the population has to be immune. This threshold is **1 minus 1 divided by R0**. With R0 equal to 4, that is 1 minus 0.25, so **75 per cent**. If a vaccination does not protect everyone, more people need to be vaccinated. With R0 equal to 5 and protection of 90 per cent, you calculate 0.8 divided by 0.9, so about **89 per cent**.

gewusst: Because measles is so infectious, herd protection needs an especially high share of immune people.
There is no herd immunity against tetanus, so every person has to protect themselves by vaccination.

teile.einleitung: The **eye doctor** examines and treats the eyes. The technical term is ophthalmologist. You go to the eye doctor for sight problems, inflammation or injuries to the eye.
wichtigste: The eye doctor examines and treats the eyes.
With drops, the doctor makes the pupil wide in order to look into the eye.
With a lamp, the doctor examines the retina at the very back of the eye.
In conjunctivitis, the eye goes red and itches.
In the operation for a cataract, the eye’s lens is replaced.
If something sharp has got into the eye: do not rub it, and go to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: At the eye doctor’s you often first read letters or signs on a chart. In this way the doctor checks how well you see and whether you need **glasses**. Sometimes the doctor puts **drops** into the eye so that the **pupil becomes wide**. Then she can look with a **lamp** and a magnifying glass right to the back of the eye at the **retina**. Afterwards your sight is a little blurred for some hours and you are sensitive to glare.

A common illness is **conjunctivitis**. The eye goes red, itches, waters or is stuck shut. A **stye** is a small, inflamed **lump on the eyelid**. For an inflamed eye, you are often given **eye drops or ointment** by the eye doctor. So that an inflammation does not spread, you should not rub your eyes and should wash your hands often.

In a **cataract**, the **lens of the eye** becomes cloudy. You then see everything as if through fog. This mainly affects older people. In an operation, the cloudy lens is removed and replaced by an **artificial lens**. This operation is one of the most common operations of all.

If something **sharp** has got into the eye, you should **not rub it** and should go **to the doctor** at once. You should not pull the foreign object out yourself. If a **chemical** gets into the eye, you rinse the eye at once for a long time with clean water and then go to the doctor. When doing crafts or experiments, safety goggles protect the eyes.

gewusst: The technical term ophthalmology comes from the Greek word “ophthalmos” for eye.
The retina is the only place where you can look at blood vessels directly from outside without cutting.

teile.einleitung: The respiratory system includes all the organs involved in breathing: from the nose through the windpipe to the air sacs of the lungs. It supplies the body with oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Muscles, cartilage and the finest blood vessels work closely together in it.
wichtigste: The respiratory system includes the nose, throat, larynx, windpipe, bronchi and lungs.
A distinction is made between the upper and lower airways.
Gas exchange takes place in the air sacs of the lungs.
The diaphragm is the most important muscle for breathing in.
The epiglottis stops food from getting into the windpipe when you swallow.
The air we breathe in contains about 21 per cent oxygen.
We breathe out more carbon dioxide than we breathe in.

abschnitte.text: The **upper airways** include the nose, the sinuses and the throat. The lining of the nose warms the air and moistens it. Fine hairs and mucus catch dust and germs. That is why it is healthier to breathe through the nose than through the mouth.

The **larynx** lies at the start of the windpipe and contains the vocal cords with which we speak. Above it sits the **epiglottis**, a movable flap of cartilage. When you swallow, it closes off the windpipe, so that food slides into the gullet. If something gets into the windpipe anyway, we have to cough.

The windpipe is about 10 to 12 centimetres long and is held open by rings of cartilage. It divides into two **bronchi**, which branch further and further like the branches of a tree. This is why people also speak of the bronchial tree. The inner wall is covered with tiny cilia, which carry mucus and dirt upwards.

The right lung has three lobes, the left only two, because the heart needs room there. At the ends of the finest branches sit about 300 million **air sacs**. This is where gas exchange takes place: oxygen goes into the blood, carbon dioxide is given off. The air breathed out still contains about 16 per cent oxygen and around 4 per cent carbon dioxide.

The **diaphragm** is a dome-shaped muscle between the chest and the abdomen. When it contracts, the chest space becomes larger and air flows into the lungs. The muscles between the ribs also help by lifting the ribs. When breathing out at rest, the muscles simply relax again.

Smoking damages the cilia and the air sacs permanently. Fine dust and air pollution also burden the airways. Common diseases of the respiratory system are colds, bronchitis, asthma and pneumonia. Exercise in the fresh air and not smoking keep the lungs healthy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flap of cartilage that closes the windpipe when you swallow.
The branches of the windpipe that lead into the lungs.
Tiny hairs in the airways that carry dirt out.
The most important breathing muscle between the chest and the abdomen.

gewusst: In a sneeze, the air can shoot out of the nose and mouth at very high speed.
Hiccups happen when the diaphragm suddenly contracts with a jerk.
The left lung is smaller than the right because the heart needs room.

teile.einleitung: Intervertebral discs are elastic discs between the vertebral bodies of the spine. They cushion shocks between the vertebrae and make the back flexible. Without them, the bones would crash straight into one another with every step.
