wichtigste: Intervertebral discs lie between the vertebral bodies of the spine.
They cushion shocks between the vertebrae like shock absorbers.
A human being has 23 discs.
Each disc has a firm ring and a soft core.
The discs are supplied with nutrients through movement.
In a slipped disc, core tissue escapes and can press on nerves.
Strong back muscles and good posture protect the discs.

abschnitte.text: The **spine** consists of many single bones, the vertebrae. Between the vertebral bodies lie the **intervertebral discs**, 23 of them in a human being. There are none between the top two neck vertebrae, nor in the sacrum and coccyx. Together the discs make up about a quarter of the length of the spine.

Each disc consists of a firm outer **fibrous ring** of connective tissue and cartilage. Inside lies a soft, jelly-like **gelatinous core**, which contains a lot of water. You can imagine it like a cushion filled with gel. Under pressure, the core spreads the force evenly onto the ring.

When walking, jumping and carrying, the discs absorb shocks. They have no blood vessels of their own, but soak up nutrients from their surroundings like a **sponge**. Under load, fluid is pressed out, and when lying down they take up water again. That is why alternating between movement and rest is important for them.

With age, discs lose water and become less elastic. If the fibrous ring tears, core tissue can escape, which is called a **slipped disc**. If this tissue presses on a nerve, strong pain results, which often radiates down into the leg. Mostly the lumbar spine is affected, and many slipped discs heal with physiotherapy without an operation.

Regular movement keeps the discs well supplied. Strong back and stomach muscles take load off the spine. Heavy things are best lifted with a straight back from the knees. A school bag that is not too heavy and is carried on both shoulders also protects the back.

begriffe.erklaerung: The column of bones in the back that supports the body.
The firm outer part of the disc.
The soft, water-rich core in the disc.
When tissue escapes from the disc and can press on nerves.

gewusst: In the morning you are about 1 to 2 centimetres taller than in the evening, because the discs fill with water at night.
Astronauts grow a few centimetres taller in weightlessness, because the discs are not squeezed together.

teile.einleitung: Covid-19 is an infectious disease caused by a coronavirus. From 2020 it spread all over the world. In Switzerland too it greatly changed everyday life.
wichtigste: Covid-19 is caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2.
The disease was first identified at the end of 2019 in the Chinese city of Wuhan.
On 11 March 2020 the WHO declared it a pandemic.
On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation.
From July 2020 masks were compulsory on public transport.
For Covid-19, mRNA vaccines were used on a large scale for the first time.

abschnitte.text: Covid-19 is caused by the virus **SARS-CoV-2**. It belongs to the **coronaviruses**. Under the microscope, with their projections, they look like a **crown**, in Latin “corona”. The name Covid-19 is an abbreviation for coronavirus disease. The number **19** stands for the year **2019**, in which the disease was discovered.

At the end of 2019 the disease was first identified in the Chinese city of **Wuhan**. It spread quickly all over the world. On **11 March 2020** the World Health Organization declared Covid-19 a **pandemic**, that is, a worldwide epidemic. Later, new variants of the virus appeared. From the end of 2021 the variant **Omicron** spread especially fast.

On **16 March 2020** the Federal Council declared the **extraordinary situation**. Schools, shops and restaurants had to close for a time. From July 2020 **masks were compulsory** on public transport. In 2021 adults had at times to show the **Covid certificate**, for example to eat in a restaurant. It confirmed a vaccination, a recovery or a test.

Vaccines against Covid-19 were developed in a short time. For the first time, **mRNA vaccines** were used on a large scale. They contain a set of building instructions with which body cells briefly make a harmless piece of the virus. The **immune system** learns in this way to recognise the real virus. Vaccinations, distance and hygiene helped to reduce severe courses of the illness.

gewusst: The researchers Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023 for their work on mRNA technology.
The variants of the virus were named after letters of the Greek alphabet, for example Delta and Omicron.

teile.einleitung: A **breath** consists of breathing in and breathing out. We take very many of them every day, usually without noticing. How fast we breathe depends on what we are doing.
wichtigste: A breath consists of breathing in and breathing out.
An adult breathes about 15 times a minute at rest.
Children breathe faster than adults.
In one calm breath, an adult breathes in about half a litre of air.
In one day an adult takes about 20,000 breaths.
We breathe quite automatically even in sleep.

abschnitte.text: A whole breath consists of **breathing in** and **breathing out**. When you breathe in, fresh air flows through the nose or mouth into the lungs. The body takes oxygen from it. When you breathe out, used air goes back out. In one calm breath, an adult breathes in about **half a litre** of air.

An adult breathes about **15 times a minute** at rest. **Children** breathe faster than adults, and babies faster still. When **running** or cycling you breathe faster and deeper, because the muscles need more oxygen. All in all, an adult takes about **20,000 breaths** in a day.

We do not have to think about breathing. An area in the brain controls breathing **quite automatically**, even when we are **asleep**. Even so, you can hold your breath for a moment or breathe in deeply on purpose. You do this, for example, when diving, singing or blowing out candles.

A **sigh** is a deep breath, often with an audible breathing out. People sigh when they are relieved, tired or sad. In a **yawn**, too, you breathe in deeply. In laughing and coughing, on the other hand, the air is breathed out in bursts.

gewusst: People also sigh for no reason several times an hour, which helps the lungs to open out well.
When we speak and sing, we use the air we breathe out to make sounds.

teile.einleitung: In an autoimmune disease, the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue as if it were an enemy. Normally the defence system can tell exactly between “self” and “foreign”. In these diseases, this no longer works properly.
wichtigste: In an autoimmune disease, the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue.
There are more than 80 different autoimmune diseases.
Examples are type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis.
The exact causes have not yet been fully researched.
Inheritance and environmental influences play a part.
Women are affected more often than men.
Most autoimmune diseases cannot be cured, but can be treated well.

abschnitte.text: The **immune system** normally protects us from bacteria, viruses and other invaders. To do this, it learns early on to recognise the body’s own cells and leave them alone. In an **autoimmune disease** this tolerance is lost. Defence cells and so-called **autoantibodies** then turn against the body’s own organs.

In **type 1 diabetes**, the immune system destroys the cells of the pancreas that make insulin. In coeliac disease, the small intestine reacts to gluten from cereals such as wheat. In multiple sclerosis, the protective coverings of nerves are damaged. In rheumatoid arthritis, the joints become inflamed.

Why the immune system turns against the body itself has not been fully explained. Certain genes raise the risk, which is why some diseases run in families. Infections, smoking or hormones can also play a part. Autoimmune diseases are not infectious, though.

The symptoms depend on which organ is being attacked. Tiredness, pain, inflammation or skin changes are common. With blood tests you can look for autoantibodies. It often takes a while until the right diagnosis is made.

Many medicines dampen the overactive immune system; they are called **immunosuppressants**. In type 1 diabetes, the missing insulin has to be injected regularly or delivered through a pump. In coeliac disease, a strictly gluten-free diet helps. Thanks to good treatment, many people with these diseases can lead a largely normal life.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body’s defence system against germs.
Antibodies that are directed against the body itself.
Medicines that slow down the immune system.
An autoimmune disease in which the gut reacts to gluten.

gewusst: Type 1 diabetes often begins already in childhood or youth.
The prefix “auto” comes from Greek and means “self”.

teile.einleitung: Flexibility means being able to move joints through a wide range and stretch muscles well. It helps in sport and play and protects against injuries. Anyone who practises it regularly stays flexible for a long time.
wichtigste: Children are mostly more flexible than older people.
You only stretch after warming up.
Jerky bouncing while stretching can injure muscles.
Anyone who moves little loses flexibility.
Gymnastics, yoga and the bridge need a lot of flexibility.
An octopus has no bones and squeezes through tiny gaps.

abschnitte.text: In **children**, muscles, tendons and ligaments are still very stretchy. That is why they are mostly more flexible than older people. With age, **flexibility** decreases if you do not practise it. If muscles and joints are moved little, they become **stiffer**. Regular movement keeps you flexible, at any age.

Warm muscles can be **stretched** better. That is why you warm up first and stretch only afterwards. You go slowly into the stretch and hold it calmly. **Jerky bouncing** can injure muscles. In **yoga** there are many poses with animal names, for example the “downward dog”. They stretch the body and make you flexible.

In PE lessons you often sit with straight legs and reach for your toes. The further you get, the more flexible are your **back** and **hamstring muscles**. In **artistic gymnastics**, you show exercises on the floor and on apparatus such as the **high bar** and the **parallel bars**. In the **bridge**, the body forms a high arch. For this you need a flexible back. In Switzerland you can learn such exercises in many **gymnastics clubs**.

In the circus, **contortionists** show how far a body can bend. For this they practise for years. In the animal kingdom the **octopus** is a master: it has no skeleton of bones. Only its hard **beak** does not fit through every opening. The rest is quite soft, so it squeezes through tiny gaps.

gewusst: An octopus can squeeze through an opening that is hardly bigger than its beak.
Flexibility can be improved at any age if you practise regularly.

teile.einleitung: The citric acid cycle is a chain of chemical reactions in our cells. It breaks down fragments of sugar, fat and protein further and gains energy in doing so. The cycle runs in a circle and is a centrepiece of metabolism.
wichtigste: The citric acid cycle takes place in the **mitochondrial matrix**.
At the start, acetyl-CoA reacts with **oxaloacetate** to form citrate.
It is also called the Krebs cycle, after **Hans Krebs**.
In each round, **2 molecules of carbon dioxide** are released.
One round yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP or ATP.
Without oxygen the cycle quickly comes to a halt.

abschnitte.titel: In the power station of the cell
abschnitte.text: The citric acid cycle takes place in the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. To be exact, it runs in the **mitochondrial matrix**, the inner space. It is named after the substance **citrate**, the salt of citric acid. The biochemist **Hans Krebs** described the cycle in 1937, which is why it is also called the **Krebs cycle**. For this discovery Krebs received the Nobel Prize in 1953.

When sugar is broken down, **pyruvate** is formed first. The **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex** converts it into **acetyl-CoA** and so links glycolysis with the citric acid cycle. Acetyl-CoA is also formed from fats and some protein building blocks. This makes the citric acid cycle a common hub for many nutrients.

At the start, acetyl-CoA combines with **oxaloacetate** to form citrate. In several steps the citrate is rebuilt, until at the end oxaloacetate is left again. Then the next round can begin. In each round, **2 molecules of carbon dioxide** are released, which we finally breathe out.

Directly, only one energy-rich molecule arises per round, namely **GTP or ATP**. This happens through **substrate-level phosphorylation**. More important are the **reducing equivalents**: 3 NADH and 1 FADH2. These molecules carry energy-rich electrons to the **respiratory chain**, where far more ATP is made from them.

The citric acid cycle itself uses no oxygen. Even so, without oxygen it quickly stops. The reason: only the respiratory chain, which needs oxygen, takes the electrons from NADH and FADH2. Only in this way are **NAD+ and FAD** freed again. If they are missing, the citric acid cycle cannot carry on.

gewusst: Hans Krebs had to leave Germany in 1933 and afterwards did research in England.
The citric acid cycle also supplies building blocks from which the cell makes new substances, for example amino acids.

teile.einleitung: Cortisol is a hormone that is often called the stress hormone. It is made in the adrenal glands and helps the body to cope with strain. A little cortisol is vital, but too much over a long time can do harm.
wichtigste: Cortisol is a hormone from the adrenal cortex.
In stress, more cortisol is released.
It quickly provides the body with energy in the form of sugar.
Cortisol dampens inflammation and the immune system.
The cortisol level is highest in the morning and lowest at night.
Permanently high cortisol can strain health.
Artificially made relatives of cortisol are used as medicines.

abschnitte.text: Cortisol is a **hormone**, that is, a messenger substance that is spread through the body by the blood. It belongs to the steroid hormones. It is made in the cortex of the **adrenal glands**, which sit like little caps on the kidneys. Its release is controlled by the brain by way of the pituitary gland.

In stress, for example before an exam, the body releases more cortisol. First the fast hormone **adrenaline** acts, cortisol follows a little later and acts for longer. It makes sure that more sugar gets into the blood. In this way muscles and brain have enough energy to meet the challenge.

Cortisol follows a fixed **daily rhythm**. In the early morning the level rises sharply and helps with waking up. In the course of the day it slowly falls. At midnight it is lowest, so that the body can sleep well.

Cortisol slows inflammation and the body’s defence reactions. Medicine makes use of this property. Similar active substances, often simply called **cortisone**, help with allergies, asthma or rheumatism. They are given as an ointment, spray or tablets.

Anyone who is under constant stress for a long time often has too much cortisol in the blood. This can lead to sleep problems, weight gain and more frequent infections. If the body makes too little cortisol, it is called **Addison’s disease**, a rare illness. Those affected are weak and have to take the hormone as a medicine.

Against too much stress, enough sleep, exercise and breaks help. Time with friends and hobbies also lowers the stress level. A little stress is normal and can even spur you on. What matters is that the body can recover afterwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that carries messages through the body by way of the blood.
A small gland that sits on each kidney and makes hormones.
A medicine that resembles cortisol and inhibits inflammation.
A fast stress hormone that speeds up heartbeat and breathing.

gewusst: Cortisol can also be measured in saliva and even in hair.
The Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein received a Nobel Prize in 1950 for his research on hormones of the adrenal cortex.

teile.einleitung: Dietary fibre is made up of parts of plants that our body cannot digest. Even so, it is very important for healthy digestion and keeps you full for a long time.
wichtigste: Most dietary fibre is not digested in the small intestine.
Cellulose forms the cell walls of plants.
Adults should eat at least about 30 grams of fibre a day.
Wholemeal bread contains much more fibre than white bread.
Pectin makes jam set.
Fibre binds water, so you have to drink enough.
Gut bacteria break down some of the fibre.

abschnitte.text: Dietary fibre comes from plants. Humans lack the **enzymes** to break it down. That is why it is not digested in the **small intestine** and moves on into the **large intestine**. In the past it was thought to be useless **ballast**, hence the German name “Ballaststoffe”. Today we know that it is very important for health.

The best-known fibre is **cellulose**. It forms the cell walls of plants and gives them firmness. Paper and cotton also consist mostly of it. **Pectin** is a soluble fibre found in fruits such as apples and quinces. With sugar and acid it forms a gel and makes **jam** and jelly set.

A lot of fibre is found in the outer layers of the grain of cereal, the **bran**. For **wholemeal bread** the whole grain is ground, so it contains much more fibre than white bread. Pulses such as lentils and beans, vegetables, fruit and nuts are also rich in it. For adults, at least about **30 grams** a day are recommended. Many people eat clearly less.

Fibre **binds water** and swells. In this way it increases the contents of the gut and helps digestion. Without enough fluid, though, **constipation** can result, which is why you should drink plenty. Foods rich in fibre have to be chewed for longer, they fill the stomach and make blood sugar rise more slowly. So they **keep you full for longer**. In the large intestine, **gut bacteria** ferment some of it. This produces useful substances, but also gases.

gewusst: Cellulose is the most common plant substance on Earth.
The German name “Ballaststoff” comes from the fact that these substances were once thought to be useless ballast.
The gut bacteria live to a good extent on the fibre that we eat.

teile.einleitung: Contact tracing means looking for people who have been in contact with an infected person. The aim is to stop an infectious disease from spreading further.
wichtigste: Contact tracing finds **contacts** and breaks chains of infection.
**Isolation** applies to people who are ill, **quarantine** to people who may have been infected.
The first known infected person in an outbreak is called the **index case**.
In Switzerland during Covid-19 it was mainly the **cantons** that were responsible.
The SwissCovid app recorded encounters by **Bluetooth**.
Infections before symptoms begin make contact tracing harder.

abschnitte.text: With an infectious disease, one person passes the germ on to others, and they pass it on to others again. In this way a **chain of infection** arises. In contact tracing, the infected person is asked whom they have met recently. These **contacts** are informed and watched. If they fall ill, there are no further infections, because they are being careful.

The two words sound similar, but mean different things. **Isolation** applies to people who are proven to be infected or ill. **Quarantine** applies to people who **may** have been infected, but are not yet ill. Both stay at home for a certain time and avoid other people. How long depends on the disease: with Ebola, for example, contacts are monitored for **21 days**.

The first known infected person in an outbreak is called the **index case**. Usually people search forwards: whom might the person have infected? In **backward contact tracing**, by contrast, you ask where they were infected themselves. In this way you sometimes find an event at which many people were infected at the same time. It becomes difficult when infected people infect others **before they have symptoms** and know about their illness.

During the **Covid-19 pandemic**, it was mainly the **cantons** that were responsible for contact tracing in Switzerland. Their teams phoned infected people and contacts and ordered isolation or quarantine. The basis for this is the federal **Epidemics Act**. In addition there was the **SwissCovid app**, which you could install on your smartphone voluntarily.

The app recorded encounters between smartphones by **Bluetooth**. It stored no names and no location, only random codes. The underlying protocol **DP-3T** was developed largely at **EPFL** in Lausanne and **ETH Zurich**. It is **decentralised**: the data stay on the phones and not on a central server.

gewusst: Contact tracing existed long before smartphones, for example for tuberculosis or smallpox.
In 2020 Switzerland was one of the first countries with an app based on the decentralised principle.

teile.einleitung: A cochlear implant is a hearing prosthesis for people who are profoundly hard of hearing or deaf. It does not amplify sound like a hearing aid, but stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrical impulses. In this way many of those affected can hear again and understand speech.
wichtigste: A cochlear implant stimulates the **auditory nerve** directly with electrical impulses.
The electrodes are inserted into the **cochlea**.
The auditory nerve has to work for the implant to help.
The **speech processor** splits the sound into frequency bands.
The signals pass through the skin by induction.
Children are fitted as early as possible, because the hearing pathway matures in the first years of life.

abschnitte.titel: When the hair cells are missing
abschnitte.text: In the inner ear lies the **cochlea**, the snail-shaped organ of hearing. There tiny **hair cells** turn sound into nerve signals. If these hair cells are destroyed, even a strong hearing aid is hardly any use. A cochlear implant **bypasses the hair cells**: it stimulates the auditory nerve directly. For this, though, the **auditory nerve** itself still has to work.

A cochlear implant consists of an outer and an inner part. On the outside, behind the ear, sits the **speech processor** with a microphone. It picks up the sound and splits it into **frequency bands**, that is, high and low tones. A **coil**, held to the head by a **magnet**, sends the signals through the skin by **induction**. Under the skin the implant receives the signals.

In an operation, a thin **electrode carrier** is inserted into the cochlea. It has many small contacts that lie at different places in the cochlea. Each place stands for a different pitch. The electrodes give off fine electric impulses and so stimulate the auditory nerve. The brain interprets these signals as sounds.

The **multichannel** cochlear implant was developed in Australia by **Graeme Clark**. Multichannel means that several electrodes carry different pitches. This made it possible to understand speech much better. Today very many people worldwide wear such an implant, and in Switzerland too they are fitted in specialised hospitals.

Children born deaf receive a cochlear implant as early as possible. The reason: the **hearing pathway** in the brain matures in the first years of life. If it gets no signals during this time, it develops less well. After the operation a lot of practice is needed, because hearing with the implant has to be learned first.

gewusst: When first switched on, voices sound strange to many people, for example like beeping or robot voices. With time the brain gets used to it.
Some people wear a cochlear implant on both sides and so can hear better where a sound comes from.

teile.einleitung: In medicine, a bypass is a diversion for the blood. If a blood vessel is narrowed, surgeons place a replacement vessel around the narrowing. Best known is bypass surgery on the heart.
wichtigste: In bypass surgery, a narrowing is bypassed with a replacement vessel.
On the heart, narrowed coronary vessels are bridged in this way.
The internal thoracic artery is regarded as an especially long-lasting bypass.
For a vein bypass, the great saphenous vein in the leg is often used.
Often a heart-lung machine temporarily takes over the work of the heart and lungs.
In 1967 René Favaloro carried out one of the first systematic vein bypasses in Cleveland.

abschnitte.text: The heart is supplied with blood through the **coronary vessels**. Over the years, deposits can form in them, and the vessels become narrower. Then the heart muscle gets too little oxygen. In **bypass surgery**, a **replacement vessel** is put in that goes around the narrowing. The word bypass comes from English and means going round.

As a replacement you mostly take vessels from the person’s own body. The **internal thoracic artery** is regarded as especially **long-lasting**. For a vein bypass, the **great saphenous vein** in the leg is often used. Such a **coronary artery bypass graft**, abbreviated **CABG**, joins the main artery to the coronary vessel beyond the narrowing. The body copes well even without this leg vein.

For classic bypass surgery, the chest is usually opened by **cutting the breastbone lengthways**. Often a **heart-lung machine** then takes over the work of the heart and lungs temporarily. In this way the heart can stand still while the operation is done. In **off-pump bypass**, on the other hand, the surgeon operates on the **beating heart**. After the operation, a period of recovery is needed and often rehabilitation.

The Argentine heart surgeon **René Favaloro** worked in the 1960s at the clinic in **Cleveland** in the USA. In **1967** he carried out there one of the first systematic **coronary artery vein bypasses**. His method spread quickly all over the world. Today bypass surgery is among the most common heart operations, in Swiss hospitals too.

gewusst: In one operation, several bypasses can be put in at once.
Bypasses are not only on the heart, but for example also in the legs.

teile.einleitung: In **osteoarthritis**, the cartilage in a joint gradually wears away. It is the most common joint disease and mainly affects older people. The knees, hips or fingers are often affected.
wichtigste: In osteoarthritis, the joint cartilage wears away.
Osteoarthritis of the knee is called gonarthrosis, of the hip coxarthrosis.
Typical is pain on the first steps after a rest.
On an X-ray, the joint space has often become narrower.
Being very overweight puts a strain on the knees and hips and encourages osteoarthritis.
Sport that is gentle on the joints, such as cycling and swimming, is often recommended.

abschnitte.text: In a joint, two bones meet. Their ends are covered with smooth **joint cartilage**, which works like a shock absorber. In osteoarthritis this cartilage becomes thinner and rough and can disappear completely. Then the bones rub against each other more. At the edge of the joint, bony spurs called **osteophytes** often grow.

The two words sound similar but mean different things. The ending **“-itis”** means **inflammation**, so arthritis is an inflamed joint. Osteoarthritis, on the other hand, is mainly a **wearing away** of the joint. Depending on the joint, there are special names: osteoarthritis of the knee joint is called **gonarthrosis**, of the hip joint **coxarthrosis**.

A typical early sign is **start-up pain**: after a rest, the first steps hurt, and then it gets better. Later the joint hurts even with longer effort, and sometimes at rest. The joint can become stiff and move less far. On the **X-ray** you often see a narrower **joint space**, because the cartilage is missing.

The risk rises with **age**. **Being very overweight** puts a strain especially on the knees and hips. Earlier injuries, deformities such as knock knees or bow legs, and heavy strain at work or in sport can also play a part. Sometimes osteoarthritis runs in the family.

Exercise is important, because cartilage is nourished by movement. Sports that are gentle on the joints, such as **cycling** and **swimming**, are recommended. **Physiotherapy** strengthens the muscles around the joint. Against pain, medicines, heat or cold help. If the joint is badly destroyed, it can be replaced by an **artificial joint**.

gewusst: An artificial hip joint is now one of the most common operations of all.
Joint cartilage has no blood vessels of its own and so can renew itself only poorly.

teile.einleitung: An antihistamine is a medicine that blocks the effect of the body’s own substance histamine. Histamine is released in allergies and causes itching, sneezing and watering eyes. Antihistamines are among the most commonly used medicines.
wichtigste: In allergies, histamine is released from defence cells, the mast cells.
Classic antihistamines for allergies work at the H1 receptor.
First-generation drugs often make you sleepy.
Cetirizine is a second-generation antihistamine.
H2 antihistamines such as famotidine reduce stomach acid.
Daniel Bovet, who was born in Neuchâtel, received the Nobel Prize in 1957, partly for the first antihistamines.

abschnitte.text: In an allergy, for example to pollen, the defence system overreacts. Certain cells, the **mast cells**, then release **histamine**. Histamine binds to **receptors**, which are docking points on other cells. The results are itching, sneezing, a runny nose, red eyes or wheals on the skin. An **antihistamine** stops histamine from having its effect.

There are different histamine receptors. The classic antihistamines for allergies work at the **H1 receptor**. Strictly speaking, most H1 antihistamines do not just block the receptor but put it into an inactive state. Experts therefore call them **inverse agonists**. At the **H2 receptor** in the stomach, histamine stimulates the making of acid. **H2 antihistamines** such as **famotidine** are therefore used to reduce **stomach acid**.

The older drugs of the **first generation** get into the brain easily. That is why they often make you **sleepy**. This side effect is sometimes even put to use: **diphenhydramine** is found in many **sleeping aids** that you can buy without a prescription. **Dimenhydrinate** is often taken against **travel sickness**. The newer drugs of the **second generation**, for example **cetirizine**, hardly get into the brain and so make you much less sleepy.

The pharmacologist **Daniel Bovet** was born in **Neuchâtel** in 1907. He worked mainly in Paris and later in Rome. He helped to develop the **first antihistamines** and also researched drugs that relax muscles. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine in **1957**.

gewusst: Histamine is also found in some foods, for example in long-matured cheese or red wine.
Stinging nettles also contain histamine, which is why the skin itches after a touch.

teile.einleitung: At the pharmacy you can get medicines and good advice about health. Experts there explain how to take a medicine correctly. In Switzerland you can often recognise pharmacies by a glowing green cross.
wichtigste: A green cross glows outside many Swiss pharmacies.
The pharmacist hands out medicines and explains them.
Some things, such as plasters, can be bought without a prescription.
How to take a medicine is written in the patient information leaflet.
You measure liquid cough syrup with the measuring cup.
Medicines are kept out of children’s reach.
An emergency pharmacy helps at night or on Sundays too.

abschnitte.text: A **green cross** glows outside many pharmacies in Switzerland. That makes them easy to find, even in the evening. In the pharmacy there are experts who know a lot about medicines. The **pharmacist** has studied pharmacy at a university. They are helped by pharmacy assistants, who have learned a trade through an apprenticeship.

Some things can be bought at the pharmacy **without a prescription**, for example **plasters**, throat sweets or sun cream. But many medicines are only available with a **prescription** from the doctor. At the pharmacy, the expert often asks whether you are taking other medicines or have allergies. In this way they can check that everything goes well together.

How to take a medicine correctly is written in the **patient information leaflet**, a slip of paper in the box. There you can read how much and how often you may take it. You measure a **liquid cough syrup** best with the **measuring cup**, not with a tablespoon. On every pack there is also an **expiry date**. It shows **until when** the medicine is good. Out-of-date medicines are taken back to the pharmacy.

At home, you keep medicines **out of children’s reach**, best of all in a locked cupboard. Some tablets look like sweets and can be dangerous. If a child has swallowed something anyway, **Tox Info Suisse** helps in Switzerland round the clock on **145**. If you need a medicine at night or on a Sunday, an **emergency pharmacy** helps. It takes turns with other pharmacies.

gewusst: The word “Apotheke” comes from Greek and originally meant storeroom.
In the past, pharmacists still made many medicines themselves, for example ointments and pills.

teile.einleitung: Blood vessels are tubes that run through the whole body. In them the blood flows away from the heart and back again. In this way oxygen and nutrients reach every cell.
wichtigste: There are three kinds: arteries, veins and capillaries.
Arteries lead away from the heart, veins lead to the heart.
The finest vessels are called capillaries.
The blood always flows in a circle, in the circulation.
In warmth the skin vessels widen, in cold they narrow.
All the blood vessels together are about 100,000 kilometres long.

abschnitte.text: There are three kinds of **blood vessels**. **Arteries** carry the blood **away from the heart**. **Veins** carry it **to the heart**. The **capillaries** join the two to each other. So the blood flows **always in a circle**, which is why we speak of the **circulation**.

The tiniest blood vessels are called **capillaries**. They are even thinner than a hair and can only be seen under the **microscope**. They reach every cell. There they give up oxygen and nutrients. If you hang all the blood vessels of an adult one behind the other, it makes about **100,000 kilometres**.

In **sport** the body gets warm. The blood vessels in the skin become **wider**, so that more blood can give off heat to the outside. That is why the face goes **red**. In great **cold**, the vessels in fingers and toes contract. In this way the body loses less heat, but the skin becomes **pale**.

In a **knock**, small blood vessels under the skin can be injured. Blood escapes and becomes visible as a **bruise**, which slowly disappears again. In a **nosebleed**, too, small vessels are injured. In the nose, many fine vessels lie just under the lining. They can burst easily, for example when picking your nose or in dry air.

gewusst: The largest artery is called the main artery or aorta and is about as thick as a thumb.
At 100,000 kilometres, the blood vessels of an adult could stretch more than twice round the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A bruise appears when you bump yourself. Tiny blood vessels burst under the skin in doing so. It often hurts a little, but is mostly harmless and goes away by itself.
wichtigste: A bruise arises from a knock or blow.
In it small blood vessels burst, and blood runs into the tissue.
Another word for it is haematoma.
As it heals, the mark turns greenish and yellowish.
Cooling straight after the knock keeps it smaller.
After about one to two weeks it is mostly gone.

abschnitte.text: When you **bump yourself**, the tissue under the skin is crushed. In doing so tiny **blood vessels** tear. Some blood runs into the tissue and shows dark through the skin. Another word for it is **haematoma**. When you press on it, the spot often hurts a little.

At first the mark is red, then **blue** or violet. The body slowly breaks down the blood that has leaked out. In doing so the mark changes colour through **green** to **yellow**. These colours arise from breakdown products of the red blood pigment. After about **one to two weeks** the mark has mostly disappeared.

Straight after the knock, **cooling** helps. Cold makes the blood vessels narrower. Then less blood leaks out, and the mark stays smaller. You never put ice directly on the skin, but wrapped in a cloth. If a mark is very big or hurts a lot, you ask a doctor.

Children get bruises especially often on the **shins**. There the bone lies directly under the skin, without a thick pad. Anyone who bumps into something there quickly gets a mark. On the **head**, the spot often swells after a knock. Such a round swelling is called a **bump**.

gewusst: In older people bruises arise more easily, because their skin is thinner.
The green colour of a healing bruise comes from the pigment biliverdin.

teile.einleitung: Calcium, in German often spelled Kalzium, is a mineral without which your body would not be stable. It is found mainly in bones and teeth and makes them hard. But calcium also helps your muscles, your nerves and even your heart.
wichtigste: Calcium is a mineral and a chemical element with the symbol Ca.
It is especially important for strong bones and teeth.
An adult has about 1 kilogram of calcium in the body.
About 99 per cent of it is in bones and teeth.
Calcium is also needed for muscles, nerves and blood clotting.
Good sources are dairy products, green vegetables and some mineral waters.
Vitamin D helps the body to absorb calcium.

abschnitte.text: Calcium is a **chemical element** with the symbol Ca. In pure form it is a silvery metal. In the body and in nature, though, it occurs only in compounds, for example as lime. For humans it is a vital **mineral**.

An adult carries about a kilogram of calcium. Almost all of it is in the **bones** and teeth and makes them hard. The small remainder in the blood is important all the same. It makes sure that muscles contract, nerves pass on signals and the blood clots.

Especially a lot of calcium is contained in **dairy products** such as milk, yoghurt and hard cheese. Broccoli, kale, almonds and hazelnuts also supply calcium. In Switzerland there are also many mineral waters rich in calcium. Children and young people need about 1,000 to 1,200 milligrams a day, depending on age.

For the gut to absorb calcium well, the body needs **vitamin D**. The skin makes this vitamin with the help of sunlight. Exercise outdoors is therefore doubly good for the bones. Sport and jumping also encourage the bones to become stable.

If the body gets too little calcium for a long time, it takes it from the bones. They then become thinner and more brittle. In old age, **osteoporosis** can result, a disease with very fragile bones. Until about the age of 30, the body builds up the most bone mass.

Calcium is very common in the Earth’s crust. Limestone, marble and chalk consist mostly of calcium carbonate. Many mountains of the Swiss Alps and the whole Jura are made of **limestone**. Shells and eggshells also consist of calcium compounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance from nature that the body needs but cannot make itself.
A disease in which the bones become thin and brittle.
A common calcium compound from which rock, shells and eggshells are made.
A vitamin that helps to absorb calcium from food.

gewusst: The white coating in a kettle is limescale, that is, a calcium compound from the tap water.
Calcium is the most common metal in the human body.
The name calcium comes from the Latin word calx for lime.

teile.einleitung: **Autism spectrum disorder** is an inborn difference in the development of the brain. It shows itself mainly in social communication and in repeated behaviour. Autistic people are very different from one another, which is why we speak of a spectrum.
wichtigste: The core features concern social communication and repetitive behaviour.
We speak of a spectrum because how it shows itself and how much support is needed vary greatly.
The Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler introduced the term “autism”.
In the 1940s Leo Kanner described early childhood autism.
In the DSM-5, Asperger syndrome was merged into autism spectrum disorder.
There is no link between vaccinations and autism.

abschnitte.text: In autism spectrum disorder, the core features show themselves in two areas: in **social communication** and in **repetitive behaviour**. Some autistic people find it hard to understand facial expressions or hints. Many have fixed habits and very strong interests. Changes in everyday life can put them under great strain.

Today we speak of a **spectrum** because **how it shows itself and how much support is needed vary greatly**. Some autistic people speak little and need a lot of help in everyday life. Others study, work and live independently. In the diagnostic manual **DSM-5** of 2013, earlier separate diagnoses such as **Asperger syndrome** were combined into autism spectrum disorder.

A **heightened or lowered sensitivity to sensory input** is common. Loud noises, glaring light or scratchy clothes can be very unpleasant. Many autistic people show self-stimulating, repeated behaviour such as **rocking** or **hand flapping**. This is called **stimming**. It can help to calm down or to cope with lots of stimuli.

The Swiss psychiatrist **Eugen Bleuler** introduced the term **“autism”** into technical language. He worked at the Burghölzli clinic in Zurich. In the 1940s the child psychiatrist **Leo Kanner** in the USA described **early childhood autism**. At about the same time, the Viennese doctor **Hans Asperger** described children with similar features.

The claim that vaccinations could cause autism has been thoroughly investigated. Research clearly shows: there is **no link**. The study that had spread this idea was withdrawn. The term **neurodiversity** describes the view that neurological differences such as autism are **natural variations** of humankind. Many experts today rely on understanding and suitable support.

gewusst: The word autism comes from the Greek “autos”, which means self.
For many autistic people, clear routines and advance notice of changes are a great help.

teile.einleitung: Beta oxidation is the pathway by which the body breaks down fatty acids to gain energy. In it the long chain of the fatty acid is cut up bit by bit into small building blocks.
wichtigste: Beta oxidation takes place mainly in the mitochondrial matrix.
First the fatty acid is activated to acyl-CoA.
Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria.
With each round the fatty acid gets 2 carbon atoms shorter.
Each round yields one FADH2 and one NADH.
Palmitic acid with 16 carbon atoms gives 8 acetyl-CoA.
At rest the heart gets most of its energy from fatty acids.

abschnitte.text: Before a fatty acid can be broken down, it is **activated**. The enzyme acyl-CoA synthetase links it to **coenzyme A**, using up ATP. This produces **acyl-CoA**. Long-chain fatty acids cannot simply cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. They are transferred to **carnitine** and smuggled in as acylcarnitine. Inside they are bound to CoA again.

In humans, beta oxidation takes place mainly in the **mitochondrial matrix**. Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell. Very long-chain fatty acids are first shortened in the **peroxisomes**. The **heart muscle** is especially rich in mitochondria and works without a break. At rest, most of its ATP comes from the breakdown of fatty acids.

Each round splits off a unit with **2 carbon atoms** as **acetyl-CoA**. This produces one **FADH2** and one **NADH**. These pass their electrons on to the **respiratory chain**, where ATP is made. The process has its name because oxidation takes place at the **beta carbon atom**. Counting from the carboxyl group, the second carbon atom is the alpha and the third the beta carbon atom.

**Palmitic acid** has 16 carbon atoms. 16 divided by 2 gives **8 acetyl-CoA**. For this only **7 rounds** are needed, because the last step yields two acetyl-CoA at once. The acetyl-CoA are broken down further in the **citric acid cycle**. In fasting, the liver also makes **ketone bodies** from them, which other organs can use as a source of energy.

gewusst: One gram of fat yields more than twice as much energy as one gram of sugar.
At rest the heart works mainly on energy from fat.

teile.einleitung: Antibodies are proteins of the immune system that recognise and fight foreign invaders such as bacteria and viruses. They are made by special white blood cells, the plasma cells. Each antibody fits exactly one particular target.
wichtigste: Antibodies recognise and fight foreign invaders.
They are made by plasma cells and released into the blood.
A typical antibody is shaped like a Y.
In its basic form, an antibody consists of four protein chains.
Antibodies bind to a particular spot on an antigen, the epitope.
Antibodies of the IgG class can pass through the placenta and so protect the newborn baby.
Antibodies of the IgE class are mainly involved in immediate allergic reactions.

abschnitte.text: In technical language, antibodies are also called **immunoglobulins**, abbreviated Ig. They are proteins that float in the blood and in other body fluids. They belong to what is called the acquired defence, which can remember germs. They are made by **plasma cells**, which develop from B lymphocytes.

A typical antibody molecule looks like the letter **Y**. It consists of four polypeptide chains, namely two heavy and two light chains. At the tips of the two arms are the binding sites for the antigen. Because there are two arms, an antibody can grab two identical antigens at once.

An antibody binds exactly to one small spot on an antigen, the **epitope**. As a result, viruses or toxins are blocked and can do no more harm. Antibodies also mark germs so that scavenger cells can find and destroy them more easily. Often they also clump several germs together.

In humans there are five classes of antibody: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE. **IgG** is the most common in the blood and is the only class that can pass through the placenta, which is how a mother protects her baby. IgA is found in saliva, tears and breast milk. **IgE** is involved in immediate allergic reactions and in defence against worms.

After a vaccination or an infection, the body makes antibodies and memory cells. This lets it react quickly the next time it meets the germ. Doctors measure antibodies in the blood to show earlier infections. **Monoclonal antibodies** made in the laboratory are now used as medicines against cancer and other diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for antibody.
A white blood cell that makes antibodies and releases them.
The small spot on an antigen to which an antibody binds.
The organ in the womb that supplies the unborn child.
Completely identical antibodies made in the laboratory, used as medicine.

gewusst: A person can make billions of different antibodies, so that there is one to fit almost every germ.
For discovering how monoclonal antibodies are made, Georges Köhler and César Milstein received the Nobel Prize in 1984, together with Niels Jerne, who did research in Basel for a long time.

teile.einleitung: **Atopy** means an inherited tendency to react to harmless substances in the environment with an allergy. In it, the body makes antibodies of the **IgE** type. Atopic diseases include eczema, hay fever and allergic asthma.
wichtigste: Atopy is an inherited tendency to make IgE against substances in the environment.
The Greek word “atopia” means placelessness or strangeness.
In the “atopic march”, atopic dermatitis is usually at the start.
In atopic immune reactions, Th2 cells predominate.
In 1989 David Strachan put forward the hygiene hypothesis.
Children from traditional farms with livestock have allergies less often.

abschnitte.text: The term comes from the Greek word **“atopia”**, which means **placelessness** or **strangeness**. People with atopy have an **inherited tendency** to make antibodies of the **IgE** type against harmless substances such as pollen, house dust mites or animal hair. In the immune reaction, certain defence cells, the **Th2 cells**, predominate. Atopy often runs in the family.

Atopic diseases often appear one after another. This is called the **“atopic march”**. At the start there is usually **atopic dermatitis**, also called **eczema**, already in infancy. Later, **hay fever** and **allergic asthma** can be added. It does not run like this in all children, and many have only one of the diseases.

In people with atopy, certain features are found more often. One is the **Dennie-Morgan fold**, a double fold on the lower eyelid. Dry, sensitive skin that itches easily is also common. But atopy cannot be recognised for certain from such signs alone; for that you need a medical check.

abschnitte.titel: The hygiene hypothesis and the farm
abschnitte.text: The British epidemiologist **David Strachan** put forward the **hygiene hypothesis** in **1989**. In simple terms, it says that less contact with germs in early childhood could encourage allergies. Studies from **Switzerland**, Austria and Germany showed that **children from traditional farms with livestock** have allergies less often. The exact reasons are still being researched.

Since the middle of the 20th century, allergies have increased sharply in industrialised countries. The term **allergy epidemic** is used for this. Possible reasons are thought to be changes in the way we live, in diet and in the environment. So far no single cause has been pinned down.

gewusst: The term atopy was introduced into medicine in the 1920s.
In Switzerland, a large part of the population suffers from hay fever, a typical atopic disease.

teile.einleitung: An unconscious person no longer reacts to being spoken to or touched. This is dangerous, because their airways can become blocked. With the right moves you can help until the ambulance service arrives.
wichtigste: An unconscious person reacts neither to being spoken to nor to touch.
Lying on the back, the tongue can block the airways.
Unconscious people lack the cough and swallowing reflexes.
You check breathing for at most about 10 seconds.
Tilting the head back and lifting the chin clears the airways.
You never give an unconscious person anything to drink.
A brief unconsciousness of a few seconds is called fainting.

abschnitte.text: You speak to the person loudly and take hold of their shoulders. If they react neither to **being spoken to** nor to **touch**, they are **unconscious**. Closed eyes alone do not yet mean this, because sleepers have them closed too. Then you call loudly for help and alert the ambulance service. In Switzerland you dial **144**.

In unconsciousness the muscles go slack. Lying **on the back**, the **tongue** can sink backwards into the throat and block the airways. In addition, the **cough** and **swallowing reflexes** are missing. Vomit or blood can then get into the lungs. That is why you also **never give an unconscious person anything to drink**: they could breathe in the liquid and choke.

To clear the **airways**, you tilt the **head back** and lift the **chin**. This lifts the tongue away from the throat. Then you check **breathing** for at most about **10 seconds** by looking, listening and feeling. If the person is breathing normally, you put them in the **recovery position**. You stay with them and keep watching their breathing. If they are not breathing, you start chest compressions at once.

A brief unconsciousness of a few seconds is called **fainting**. It usually arises because the brain briefly gets too little blood, for example after standing for a long time in the heat. The person usually comes round by themselves. In people with **diabetes**, **low blood sugar** can lead to unconsciousness. Then the brain gets too little energy. Beforehand, those affected often tremble and become confused.

gewusst: The most common danger for unconscious people is not the cause itself, but their own tongue blocking the airways.
For rescues in the mountains there is Rega in Switzerland, with the emergency number 1414.

teile.einleitung: A baby is a child in its first months of life. It is still small and needs a great deal of help, love and care, but it learns something new every day.
wichtigste: A newborn baby is about 50 centimetres long.
It usually weighs between 3 and 4 kilograms.
A newborn drinks only milk.
By crying, a baby shows that it needs something.
The first tooth often comes at about 6 months.
In the first year of life a baby is also called an infant.
A baby has more bones than an adult.

abschnitte.text: Most babies are about **48 to 54 centimetres** long at birth, so roughly half a metre. They usually weigh between **3 and 4 kilograms**, about as much as a few cartons of milk. In the first year babies grow very fast. A baby in its first year is also called an **infant**, because it sucks milk.

A newborn baby drinks only **milk**, either from its mother or as **formula milk from a bottle**. It contains everything the baby needs to grow. When it is hungry, it usually **cries**, because it cannot talk yet. Later it is given porridge made of vegetables or fruit. At about **6 months** the first **milk tooth** often comes, earlier in some babies and later in others.

A baby has about **300 bones** and parts of bones, while an adult has only about 206. Many parts grow together later. On the head, a baby has soft spots, the **fontanelles**. There the bones of the skull have not yet grown together. Because it cannot yet control its bladder, a baby wears a **nappy**.

Newborns sleep a great deal, often more than half of the day. Even so, they are learning all the time: soon they recognise voices and faces. If you put a finger into a newborn’s hand, it grips it tightly. This is an inborn **reflex**. In Switzerland, experts at the **maternal and child health advice service** advise parents on questions about their baby.

gewusst: At birth a baby has about 300 bones and parts of bones, more than an adult.
Newborns can already grip tightly when you put a finger into their hand.

teile.einleitung: **Arterial hypertension** is the technical term for high blood pressure. In it, the pressure in the arteries is permanently too high. High blood pressure is very common and can damage the heart, brain and kidneys over the years.
wichtigste: In high blood pressure, the pressure in the arteries is permanently raised.
Under the usual European definition, readings of 140/90 mmHg or more at the doctor’s count as high blood pressure.
High blood pressure often causes no symptoms for a long time.
Being very overweight, a lot of salt, a lot of alcohol and little exercise raise the risk.
Untreated, it can lead to stroke, heart attack and kidney damage.
Blood pressure that is too low is called hypotension.

abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood into the arteries. In doing so the blood presses against the vessel walls, and this is the **blood pressure**. It is measured in **millimetres of mercury (mmHg)** and given as two numbers. The first number is the pressure when the heart contracts, the second the pressure when it relaxes. From readings of **140/90 mmHg**, measured at the doctor’s, we speak of high blood pressure under the European definition.

High blood pressure mostly does not hurt. Many people have it for years without noticing. So it is often discovered by chance during a **measurement** at the doctor’s or in the pharmacy. Some people also measure their blood pressure at home with a small device on the upper arm or wrist. Measuring regularly is the best way to spot high blood pressure early.

Often there is no single cause, but several things come together. They include **being very overweight**, little exercise, a lot of **table salt** in food and regularly drinking a lot of **alcohol**. Age and a family tendency also play a part. Salt holds water in the body and can raise the pressure in this way. A lot of hidden salt is found in ready meals, sausage and crisps.

Permanently high pressure damages the **vessel walls** over time. This raises the risk of a **stroke**, in which a vessel in the brain is blocked or bursts. A **heart attack** also becomes more likely, and the heart has to keep pumping against the high pressure. The **kidneys** contain many fine vessels that filter the blood. If these are damaged, the kidneys work less well.

**Regular exercise** is very effective, for example cycling, swimming or brisk walking. A diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit and pulses supplies **potassium**, which helps the body to pass out sodium. Less salt, little alcohol, a healthy weight and not smoking also help. If that is not enough, the doctor prescribes **medicines that lower blood pressure**.

gewusst: High blood pressure is one of the most important risk factors for heart and circulation diseases worldwide.
The prefix “hyper” means over, “hypo” means under: hence hypertension and hypotension.

teile.einleitung: Cholera is a dangerous diarrhoeal disease caused by a bacterium. It spreads mainly through dirty drinking water. In the 19th century it raged in Europe too, today it occurs mainly where clean water is lacking.
wichtigste: Cholera is caused by a **bacterium** that is bent in the shape of a comma.
The main feature is very severe, watery diarrhoea.
You usually catch it through dirty drinking water.
Most important in treatment is replacing fluid and salts.
Clean water supply and sewers have defeated cholera in Europe.
There is a vaccine that you swallow.

abschnitte.text: The germ that causes cholera is called **Vibrio cholerae**. Under the microscope you can see that the bacteria are **comma-shaped**. They get into the gut with water or food and make a poison there. This poison makes the gut wall release huge amounts of water and salts. The German researcher Robert Koch was able to describe the germ more exactly in the 1880s.

The main feature of cholera is very severe, **watery diarrhoea**. Vomiting often comes with it. The body thus loses a great deal of water in a short time. Untreated patients usually die of this great **loss of water**, because the circulation and organs fail. With quick help, on the other hand, almost all survive.

For a long time people believed that diseases arose from bad air. In 1854 the doctor **John Snow** investigated a cholera outbreak in London. He marked on a map where the sick people lived. Almost all had fetched water from the same **water pump** in Broad Street. Snow had the pump handle removed. His map counts as the beginning of modern **epidemiology**, the science of how diseases spread.

In the 19th century there were severe cholera outbreaks in many European cities, in Switzerland too. What helped most was a **clean water supply** together with **sewers** that carry the waste water away. In this way the bacteria no longer got into the drinking water. Today cholera occurs mainly in areas with poverty, war or after natural disasters, where clean water is lacking.

Most important is replacing **fluid and salts**. For this there is a simple drink made of water, sugar and salt, the **oral rehydration solution**. Severely ill patients get the fluid through a drip. Sometimes antibiotics help in addition. For protection there is an **oral vaccine**, which you drink rather than being injected.

gewusst: The simple drink of water, sugar and salt has saved millions of lives worldwide.
The pump in Broad Street in London stands today as a replica in memory of John Snow.

teile.einleitung: A blood count is a laboratory test in which the cells in the blood are counted and looked at more closely. It is among the most common tests at the doctor’s. It shows, for example, whether someone has anaemia or an inflammation.
wichtigste: One microlitre of blood contains about 4 to 6 million red blood cells in adults.
Red blood cells are called erythrocytes, from the Greek “erythros” for red.
Hb stands for haemoglobin, the red blood pigment.
The haematocrit gives the share of blood cells in the blood volume.
Normal is about 4,000 to 10,000 white blood cells per microlitre.
The differential blood count shows the shares of the different white blood cells.
Reticulocytes are young red blood cells.

abschnitte.text: The **red blood cells** are called **erythrocytes**, from the Greek “erythros” for red. They are the most common blood cells. A tiny droplet of one **microlitre** contains about **4 to 6 million** of them. In the blood count they are counted, and their size is measured. Young, newly made red blood cells are called **reticulocytes**. Their number shows how strongly the **bone marrow** is currently making new blood.

**Hb** stands for **haemoglobin**, the red blood pigment that carries oxygen. The **haematocrit** shows what percentage of the blood volume consists of cells. If Hb or haematocrit is too low, it can point to **anaemia**. A common cause is a lack of iron.

The **white blood cells** are called **leukocytes** and belong to the defence system. A healthy adult has about **4,000 to 10,000** per microlitre of blood. So there are far fewer white than red blood cells. In an infection their number often rises. In the blood count the **platelets** are also counted, which help in blood clotting.

In the **differential blood count**, the white blood cells are counted by type. Most common are the **neutrophil granulocytes**. They make up about half to two thirds and eat mainly **bacteria**. The **lymphocytes** include B cells and T cells. B cells can develop into cells that make **antibodies**. In this way you can recognise, for example, bacterial infections or allergies.

gewusst: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days, after that it is broken down.
Today laboratory machines count the blood cells automatically, in the past they were counted by hand under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: In **burping**, also called **belching**, air escapes from the stomach through the mouth. It happens to everybody and is quite natural. Sometimes, though, it is loud and a little embarrassing.
wichtigste: When you burp, air comes up from the stomach.
The air rises up through the gullet.
After fizzy mineral water, you often have to burp.
Drinking slowly in small sips helps against it.
A baby’s burp after feeding is called a “Bäuerchen” in German.
When cows burp, they give off the gas methane.

abschnitte.text: When we eat and drink, we always swallow some **air** too. It collects in the **stomach**. If there gets to be too much there, the air rises up through the **gullet** and escapes through the mouth. This is **burping** or **belching**. It is a natural process and mostly harmless.

You especially often have to burp after drinks with **carbon dioxide gas in them**, for example after **fizzy mineral water** or sweet drinks. The gas forms bubbles in the stomach. People who eat in a hurry, talk a lot while eating or chew gum also swallow more air. So it helps to drink **slowly in small sips** and to eat calmly.

Babies swallow a lot of air when they feed. Afterwards, parents hold the baby upright against the shoulder and gently pat its back. This lets the air escape. This burp is called a **“Bäuerchen”** in German. Afterwards the baby usually feels more comfortable.

Where we live, loud burping at the table is seen as rude. If you have to burp, you politely hold your **hand** in front of your mouth and turn away a little. Afterwards you can say “excuse me”. In other countries and cultures there are sometimes different rules.

Animals burp too. **Cows** digest grass in several stomachs with the help of tiny living things. This produces the gas **methane**, which cows give off mainly by burping. Methane is a **greenhouse gas** that adds to the warming of the climate. Researchers are therefore looking for feed that produces less methane.

gewusst: The technical word for burping is ructus.
Anyone who burps often and with a sour taste should have it checked by a doctor, because heartburn may be behind it.

teile.einleitung: The **breathing centre** is a group of nerve cells in the brainstem. It controls breathing automatically, day and night. To do this it constantly evaluates signals from sensors in the body.
wichtigste: The breathing centre lies mainly in the medulla oblongata.
The pre-Bötzinger complex is regarded as the most important pacemaker of the breathing rhythm.
The strongest drive to breathe is a rising partial pressure of CO2.
Central chemoreceptors react mainly to a fall in pH in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies mainly report a lack of oxygen.
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm.

abschnitte.text: The breathing centre lies mainly in the **medulla oblongata**, the lower part of the brainstem. There, a group of nerve cells, the **pre-Bötzinger complex**, sets the rhythm. These cells produce regular signals for breathing in by themselves. Other areas in the brainstem fine-tune breathing, for example when speaking or swallowing.

In a healthy person, a **rising partial pressure of CO2** in the blood is the strongest drive to breathe. Carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the **cerebrospinal fluid**, the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. There it makes the fluid more acidic. The **central chemoreceptors** in the brainstem react mainly to this **fall in pH** and make us breathe deeper and faster.

The **peripheral chemoreceptors** sit in the **carotid bodies** at the carotid artery and in the **aortic bodies** at the main artery. They mainly report a **lack of oxygen** to the breathing centre. There are also stretch receptors in the lungs. In the **Hering-Breuer reflex**, they slow breathing in when the lungs are stretched a lot.

abschnitte.titel: From the brain to the diaphragm
abschnitte.text: The breathing centre sends its orders along nerves to the breathing muscles. The most important breathing muscle is the **diaphragm**. It is supplied by the **phrenic nerve**, which comes from the cervical spinal cord. When the diaphragm contracts, it moves down and air flows into the lungs. The muscles between the ribs also help with breathing.

Anyone who **hyperventilates** a lot before diving breathes out a lot of carbon dioxide. As a result, the **urge to breathe comes late**. The oxygen in the blood can then fall so far that you lose consciousness underwater before you feel the urge to breathe. That is why hyperventilating hard before diving is very dangerous.

gewusst: The pre-Bötzinger complex was only described in more detail in 1991.
You can hold your breath, but at some point the breathing centre forces the body to breathe again.

teile.einleitung: Almost every child has a stomach ache now and then. Mostly it is harmless and goes away by itself. Sometimes, though, something is behind it that a doctor has to look at.
wichtigste: Eating too much can cause stomach ache.
A hot water bottle often helps with a mild stomach ache.
Fennel tea and camomile tea are good for the stomach.
With a bad stomach ache, you tell a grown-up.
In constipation, the stool stays in the gut too long.
In appendicitis, it usually hurts at the lower right.
Excitement and worries can cause stomach ache too.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who **eats too much** has a very full stomach. This can press and hurt. **Constipation** also causes stomach ache: the stool stays in the gut too long and becomes hard. Sometimes stomach ache comes from a **stomach bug**. And even **excitement** or worries, for example before a test, can make the belly feel tight. The belly and feelings are closely connected.

Warmth relaxes the belly. A **hot water bottle** or a warm cushion often helps with a mild stomach ache. Many people then drink **fennel tea** or **camomile tea**, because they are mild and warm. Rest and a gentle belly massage can help too. Afterwards you eat something light instead.

To keep the stool nice and soft, **drinking plenty** helps. **Vegetables**, fruit and wholegrain foods also keep digestion going. **Exercise** helps the gut too. Anyone who takes time over eating and chews well has a full, tight belly less often.

With a **bad stomach ache**, you always tell a **grown-up**. If necessary, you go to the doctor. The **appendix** lies at the lower right of the belly. In **appendicitis** it usually hurts there, often with a fever and feeling sick. Then you must go to the doctor quickly. In an emergency in Switzerland you dial **144**.

gewusst: The gut has so many nerve cells that it is sometimes called the “belly brain”.
Feelings such as fear or excitement can also cause real stomach ache.

teile.einleitung: A bee sting hurts, but is mostly harmless. Anyone who knows why bees sting and what to do afterwards stays calm and helps themselves and others properly.
wichtigste: Bees sting only when they feel threatened, themselves or their colony.
The honeybee’s sting has barbs and often stays in the skin together with the venom sac.
You remove the sting quickly, best by scraping it away sideways with a fingernail.
Cooling eases pain and swelling.
A sting in the mouth or throat can be dangerous: dial the emergency number 144 at once.
In an allergy with difficulty breathing, help is needed at once.
Anyone who stays calm gets stung less often.

abschnitte.text: Bees are peaceful animals that collect nectar and pollen. They sting only to defend themselves or their **colony**. Hectic movements, hitting out or stepping on a bee can set off a sting. Anyone who stays calm and does not swat the bee gets stung less often. Mostly it flies off by itself after a short time.

The sting of the **honeybee** has small **barbs**. That is why it stays stuck in the skin, often together with the **venom sac**. The venom sac can go on releasing venom for a while. Wasps have a smooth sting and can pull it out again. Only the honeybee usually loses its sting when it stings.

Most important is to remove the sting **quickly**. You best scrape it away sideways with a fingernail or a card. Then you cool the spot, for example with a cold, damp cloth. The skin goes red, swells a little and often itches. After some hours to days this goes away again.

A sting in the **mouth** or **throat** can swell so much that it is hard to breathe. Then you dial the emergency number **144** at once and give the person ice to suck. An **allergy** to bee venom is also dangerous. Then the whole body reacts, for example with difficulty breathing, dizziness or a rash. Here too you get help at once by calling 144.

Wasps and bees like **sweet things**. Outdoors, an insect can crawl unnoticed into an open can or a glass. That is why you look inside before drinking or use a straw. Walking barefoot across a flowering meadow raises the risk of a sting. It is best to cover food outdoors.

gewusst: A honeybee mostly dies after it has stung a person, because the sting tears off with the venom sac.
When stinging, bees release a scent that can warn other bees nearby.

teile.einleitung: A bath in the bathtub cleans you, warms you and relaxes you. So that bathing is fun and stays safe, there are a few important rules.
wichtigste: Before bathing, you check the water temperature.
With your hand or elbow you can feel whether the water is too hot.
Small children must never be alone in the bath.
Hollow bath toys have to dry well, otherwise mould grows.
After bathing you dry yourself well, between the toes too.
At the end you pull out the plug.

abschnitte.text: Before you climb into the tub, you check the **water temperature**. If the water is too hot, you can **scald** yourself. You briefly hold your **hand** or **elbow** in the water. The elbow is especially sensitive, which is why parents use it to test the water for babies. Water that is about as warm as the body is pleasant.

Small children can **drown** even in a little water, and it often happens quite silently. So a grown-up always stays there. Even a quick look at a phone can be too long. The wet floor of the tub is slippery, and a **non-slip mat** helps. In Switzerland the **BFU**, the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention, gives tips on how to avoid accidents at home.

A **bubble bath** is a bath additive that you add to the running water. Then lots of mountains of foam form. Many children like to play with rubber ducks and other **bath toys**. In hollow toys, though, water often stays inside. **Mould** can form there. That is why you squeeze them out and let them dry well.

At the end you pull out the **plug**, and the water runs away. Then you rinse the tub out briefly. With a big **bath towel** you dry yourself so that you do not get cold. The places **between the toes** are important too. If they stay damp, **athlete’s foot** can develop, because it likes to grow in damp, warm places.

gewusst: The elbow feels warmth better than the hand, which is why it is used to test bath water for babies.
Small children can drown in just a few centimetres of water.

teile.einleitung: Blood clotting is your body’s emergency plan when you get hurt. If you cut your finger slightly, it bleeds a little at first, but after a few minutes the bleeding stops by itself. The blood closes the wound like a natural plaster.
wichtigste: Blood clotting stops bleeding after an injury.
First the injured blood vessels contract.
Then platelets stick together and form a first plug.
A protein called fibrin forms a fine net that firms up the plug.
From the clotted blood the scab later forms.
With small wounds, clotting usually takes only a few minutes.
In the disease haemophilia, the blood clots only badly.

abschnitte.text: Blood clotting means that liquid blood becomes solid at a wound. Experts also speak of **haemostasis**, that is, stopping bleeding. Without this process even a small scratch could become dangerous. The body would otherwise lose too much blood.

If a blood vessel is injured, it contracts at once so that less blood escapes. Then the **platelets** rush in, which are also called thrombocytes. They stick to the wound and to one another. In this way a first, still loose seal forms within seconds to minutes.

Now a chain of reactions starts with many clotting factors. At the end, the dissolved substance fibrinogen is converted into **fibrin**. Fibrin forms long threads that catch blood cells like a net. The plug becomes firm and dense as a result.

The clotted blood dries on the surface into a hard crust, the **scab**. Underneath, the body forms new tissue and new skin. When the wound has healed, the scab falls off by itself. You should not pick it off, otherwise the wound can bleed again.

In the inherited disease **haemophilia**, a clotting factor is missing. Those affected bleed much longer when injured. Conversely, blood can also clot inside a vessel, and then a **thrombosis** forms. In such cases doctors give medicines that thin the blood.

A small cut is best rinsed out with clean water. Then you press a clean cloth on the wound for several minutes. A plaster protects it from dirt. If a wound bleeds heavily or does not stop, medical help is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny particles in the blood that stick together at wounds.
A protein that forms a firm net of threads at the wound.
The hard crust of dried blood on a wound.
A blood clot that blocks a blood vessel in the body.

gewusst: One microlitre of blood, which is a tiny droplet, contains several hundred thousand platelets.
Haemophilia used to occur in several European royal families, for example in descendants of Queen Victoria.
When sucking, leeches release a substance that inhibits blood clotting.

teile.einleitung: Bitter is one of the basic tastes, besides sweet, sour, salty and umami. Bitter things often warn us of poison. Even so, many adults like bitter foods such as coffee or dark chocolate.
wichtigste: Bitter is one of the five basic tastes.
Many poisonous plants taste bitter, so the taste warns us.
Children taste bitter things more strongly than adults.
Coffee, dark chocolate and grapefruit taste bitter.
Chicory and radicchio contain bitter substances.
Black tea becomes bitter if it steeps too long.

abschnitte.text: On the tongue lie **taste buds**. With them we taste sweet, sour, salty, umami and **bitter**. Bitter is tasted from certain substances called **bitter compounds**. Many **poisonous plants** taste bitter. That is why you often prefer to spit out something bitter. The taste is therefore a kind of warning signal.

**Children** react more strongly to bitter things than adults. That is why many children like bitter foods less. With age, many people **get used** to the taste. Some even learn to really like it. It is worth trying new things again and again in small amounts.

**Coffee** contains bitter substances such as **caffeine** and tastes bitter without sugar. **Dark chocolate** has a lot of cocoa and little sugar, so it is more bitter than milk chocolate. **Black tea** becomes bitter if it steeps too long. Then many **tannins** dissolve out of the leaves.

**Chicory** and the red **radicchio** with its white veins contain bitter substances. **Grapefruits** also taste bitter and a little sour. The white skin under the **orange peel** is bitter too, which is why you often pick it off. Many bitter substances in vegetables are harmless for people.

gewusst: Humans have many different kinds of bitter receptors, but only very few for sweet.
Chicory grows in the dark, so its leaves stay almost white.

teile.einleitung: In **breathing out**, air flows out of the lungs through the nose or mouth. In doing so the body gives off carbon dioxide. With the air we breathe out we can also speak, whistle and make music.
wichtigste: In calm breathing out, the diaphragm relaxes.
The air we breathe out is warm and moist.
In winter you can see your breath, because the water in it forms droplets.
With air we breathe out, we speak, whistle and sing.
By blowing you can inflate balloons and blow out candles.
A recorder sounds because air is blown into it.

abschnitte.text: When you breathe in, the **diaphragm** contracts and the lungs fill with air. In calm breathing out, the **diaphragm relaxes** again. The chest becomes smaller, and the air flows out by itself. If you blow hard, the stomach muscles and the muscles between the ribs help as well.

If you breathe onto your hand, the breath feels **warm**. The air was warmed to body temperature in the lungs. It also contains a lot of **water vapour**. In winter the air outdoors is cold. Then the breath cools quickly, and the **water in the breath forms tiny droplets**. That is why you can see your breath like a little cloud.

We also need the air we breathe out **for speaking**. It flows through the larynx and makes the **vocal cords** vibrate there. In this way sounds are made. If you breathe out and purse your lips, you can **whistle**. A **recorder** sounds because you blow air into it, and the air begins to vibrate at a sharp edge.

With air you breathe out, you can inflate a **balloon** or make soap bubbles. On a birthday cake you blow out the **candles**. If there is no wind outdoors, **blowing hard** makes a **pinwheel** turn. If you want to blow for a long time and hard, you have to breathe in deeply first.

gewusst: Air that is breathed out contains about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than the air outside, but still a lot of oxygen.
Air is also breathed out when laughing, coughing and sneezing, especially fast in a sneeze.
