teile.einleitung: The blood volume is the amount of blood that a person has in the body. It depends mainly on body weight. An adult therefore has much more blood than a baby.
wichtigste: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight.
Heavier people have more blood.
A newborn has about 3 decilitres of blood.
Blood plasma is liquid, yellowish and consists of about 90 per cent water.
Losing a lot of blood is dangerous, because organs get too little oxygen.
Every day the body makes new blood in the bone marrow.

abschnitte.text: How much blood a person has depends mainly on **body weight**. Blood makes up about **7 to 8 per cent** of body weight. An **adult** is heavier and therefore has more blood than a child. A **newborn** weighs about 3.5 kilograms and has about **3 decilitres** of blood. That is roughly one big glassful.

Blood consists of **blood cells** and the liquid **blood plasma**. If you remove the cells, a yellowish fluid is left over. Plasma consists of about **90 per cent** **water**. In it nutrients and other substances are dissolved. The red blood cells bring **oxygen** to all the organs.

With a small **prick** in the finger, only a few drops come out. This is no problem for the body. What is dangerous is losing **a lot of blood**. Then the **organs** get too little oxygen. With heavy bleeding, you press on the wound and call the emergency number **144**.

The body makes **new blood all the time**. This happens every day in the **bone marrow**, inside many bones. Old blood cells are broken down and replaced by new ones. That is why a healthy person can also donate blood. After a while the amount is topped up again.

gewusst: An adult weighing 70 kilograms has about 5 litres of blood.
In the bone marrow, millions of new red blood cells are made every second.

teile.einleitung: The corpus callosum, in German “Balken”, is the largest connection between the left and the right half of the brain. Through it the two halves constantly exchange information. How important it is was shown especially by experiments with people whose corpus callosum had been cut through.
wichtigste: The corpus callosum connects the two **halves of the brain**.
It consists of around **200 million** nerve fibres.
It belongs to the **white matter** of the brain.
Its thickened rear end is called the **splenium**.
In severe **epilepsy** it is sometimes cut through in an operation.
Kim Peek, the model for the film “Rain Man”, had no corpus callosum.

abschnitte.text: The cerebrum consists of two halves. The **corpus callosum** lies deep between them and joins them like a broad bridge. It consists of around **200 million nerve fibres**. Because these fibres are surrounded by a light, fatty sheath, the corpus callosum belongs to the **white matter**. Its thickened rear end is called the **splenium**.

In very severe **epilepsy**, seizures spread from one half of the brain to the other. When medicines do not help, the corpus callosum is sometimes **cut through** in an operation. In this way the seizures spread less easily. People after this operation are called **split-brain patients**. In everyday life they often notice surprisingly few changes.

Researchers such as Roger Sperry and **Michael Gazzaniga** examined such patients closely. Each half of the brain processes the visual field of the opposite side. If a patient sees an object only in the **left visual field**, the picture ends up in the right half of the brain. Language, however, sits mostly on the left. That is why the patient **cannot name** the object, but can feel for it with the **left hand**.

Gazzaniga observed something else astonishing. When the right half of the brain did something, the left half at once invented a fitting explanation, although it did not know the real reason. He therefore ascribed to the left half of the brain an **“interpreter”** that invents explanations. After damage to the corpus callosum, the **alien hand syndrome** can also occur: one hand then seems to act on its own.

Some people are born without a corpus callosum. A well-known example is **Kim Peek** from the USA, the model for the film **“Rain Man”**. He lacked the corpus callosum. He had an extraordinary memory and could remember the contents of very many books. In people without a corpus callosum, other connections often take over part of its tasks.

gewusst: In 1981 Roger Sperry received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on the halves of the brain.
The word “callosum” comes from Latin and means roughly “callused” or “hardened”.

teile.einleitung: An **automated external defibrillator**, or **AED** for short, is a device that can save lives in a cardiac arrest. It analyses the heart rhythm by itself and, if needed, delivers an electric shock. Even lay people can use it, because the device announces every step with spoken instructions.
wichtigste: An AED recognises ventricular fibrillation and then delivers an electric shock.
Without defibrillation, the chance of survival falls by about 7 to 10 per cent every minute.
The electrodes go on the right below the collarbone and on the left at the side of the chest.
After the shock, chest compressions carry on at once.
In asystole, the flat line, the AED does not deliver a shock.
Child electrodes or a child mode reduce the energy.

abschnitte.text: In a sudden cardiac arrest, there is often **ventricular fibrillation**. The heart twitches in a disorderly way and no longer pumps blood. An electric shock can end this state, so that the heart can beat properly again. Time is vital: without defibrillation, the **chance of survival falls by about 7 to 10 per cent every minute**. That is why AEDs hang in many places such as railway stations, schools and sports grounds.

In adults, you stick the electrodes in the standard position **on the right below the collarbone** and **on the left at the side of the chest**. If the chest is **wet**, you dry it quickly so that the electrodes stick well. If there is a **medicine patch** at that spot, you **remove** it and wipe the skin. If the person has an implanted **pacemaker**, you do **not** stick the electrode **directly over the device**.

After it is switched on, the AED gives clear **spoken instructions**. It analyses the heart rhythm by itself. During the analysis and the shock, nobody may touch the person. Modern AEDs usually deliver a **biphasic pulse**, in which the current flows briefly in both directions. In **asystole**, the so-called **flat line**, the AED gives **no shock**, because current does not help there.

**Straight after a shock**, the helpers **carry on at once with chest compressions**. The AED speaks again after about two minutes and analyses once more. It is also important to call the **emergency number 144** at once. Chest compressions and the AED bridge the time until the ambulance arrives.

For children there are special **child electrodes** or a **child mode**. They **reduce the energy delivered**, because children are smaller. If no child electrodes are available, the normal electrodes can also be used on children. An AED does no harm if you use it on an unconscious person who is not breathing normally, because it only shocks when it is needed.

gewusst: In Switzerland, apps alert volunteer first aiders who are near a cardiac arrest and show the way to the nearest AED.
You cannot set off an AED wrongly: it only gives a shock if it recognises a suitable rhythm.

teile.einleitung: Connective tissue joins, supports and pads the parts of our body. Tendons, ligaments, cartilage, bone and fatty tissue belong to it. Typical is that the cells lie loosely in a lot of intercellular substance.
wichtigste: In connective tissue, the cells lie in an extracellular matrix of fibres and ground substance.
Fibroblasts make the fibres and the ground substance.
Collagen is the most common protein in the body and makes tendons resistant to pulling.
Elastic fibres of elastin let skin and arteries spring back into shape.
For stable collagen fibres the body needs vitamin C, otherwise scurvy threatens.
Adipocytes store fat, brown fat tissue produces heat.

abschnitte.text: Unlike in skin or muscles, the cells in connective tissue do not lie tightly against one another. Between them there is a lot of **extracellular matrix**, that is, intercellular substance. It consists of **fibres** and a **ground substance** that can bind a lot of water. Its composition decides whether a tissue is firm, elastic or soft. The typical cells are called **fibroblasts**. They make fibres and ground substance and are important in wound healing.

**Collagen** is the most common protein in the human body. It forms tear-resistant fibres found in **tendons**, ligaments, bone and skin. Tendons are therefore very **resistant to pulling**. For stable collagen fibres the body needs **vitamin C**. If it is missing for long, **scurvy** results, with bleeding gums, badly healing wounds and bleeding. In the past, sailors on long voyages without fresh fruit often suffered from it.

**Elastic fibres** consist mainly of **elastin**. They can be stretched like rubber and afterwards return to their shape. They are found, for example, in the skin, in the lungs and in the walls of the **arteries**. With age their amount decreases. That is why the skin becomes less firm and more wrinkled.

**Fatty tissue** is also a form of connective tissue. Its cells are called **adipocytes** and store fat in large droplets. Fatty tissue serves as an **energy store**, as protection against the cold and as padding, for example on the soles of the feet. Special is the **brown fat tissue**, which mainly infants have. Its cells contain very many mitochondria with the protein **thermogenin** and burn fat directly into heat.

gewusst: Collagen makes up about a third of all proteins in the human body.
The word collagen means “glue forming”, because in the past glue was boiled from bones and skin.

teile.einleitung: Blood sugar is the amount of glucose in the blood. Glucose is the most important fuel for the brain and muscles. The body keeps blood sugar within a narrow range with two hormones.
wichtigste: Glucose is the most important source of energy for the cells.
The hormone insulin lowers blood sugar, the hormone glucagon raises it.
Both hormones are made in the pancreas.
Fasting, blood sugar in healthy people is about 4 to 6 mmol/l.
If blood sugar is permanently too high, it is called diabetes mellitus.
Low blood sugar is called hypoglycaemia in technical language.

abschnitte.text: When we eat bread, pasta or fruit, the gut breaks the carbohydrates down into **glucose**. This gets into the blood and is carried to all the cells. The **brain** in particular needs glucose constantly. Surplus sugar is stored in the liver and muscles as **glycogen**. In this way the body has a supply for later.

The **pancreas** lies behind the stomach. In it there are small groups of cells, the **islets of Langerhans**. Their beta cells make **insulin**, which brings sugar from the blood into the cells and lowers blood sugar. Other cells make **glucagon**, the opposite number. Glucagon makes the liver release stored sugar into the blood.

Before breakfast, blood sugar in healthy people is between about 4 and just under 6 **millimoles per litre** (mmol/l). In Switzerland it is usually measured in this unit. In Germany and the USA, **mg/dl**, that is milligrams per decilitre, is often used. One mmol/l corresponds to about 18 mg/dl. Many people with diabetes measure themselves with a **blood glucose meter** or a sensor on the skin.

In **diabetes mellitus**, blood sugar is permanently too high, because insulin is missing or does not work enough. In **type 1 diabetes**, the body’s own immune system destroys the insulin-making cells. It often begins already in childhood or youth, and those affected need insulin all their lives. **Type 2 diabetes** occurs more often in adults. Exercise and a balanced diet help to prevent it.

If blood sugar falls too low, it is called **hypoglycaemia**. “Hypo” means under, “glyc” stands for sweet or sugar. Typical signs are trembling, sweating and ravenous hunger. Then **glucose tablets** or a sweet drink help quickly. In 1921, **Frederick Banting** and **Charles Best** in Toronto managed to obtain insulin, and since then diabetes can be treated.

gewusst: The brain uses a large part of the glucose that the body converts every day.
Banting received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for the discovery of insulin as early as 1923.

teile.einleitung: Cholesterol is a fat-like substance that every person needs to live. It is found in all cells and is a building block for important hormones and for bile. Too much of it in the blood, though, can harm the blood vessels.
wichtigste: Cholesterol belongs to the group of substances called **sterols**.
A cholesterol molecule has **27 carbon atoms**.
The body makes most of it itself, mainly in the **liver**.
Cholesterol regulates the flexibility of the cell membrane.
From cholesterol arise bile acids and hormones such as cortisol.
In the blood it needs transport particles, because it hardly dissolves in water.

abschnitte.text: Cholesterol belongs to the **sterols**, a group of fat-like substances with four rings joined together. A molecule consists of **27 carbon atoms** and many hydrogen atoms. The name comes from Greek: “chole” means bile, “stereos” means solid. The substance was first found in **gallstones**. Cholesterol occurs only in animals and humans, plants have similar substances.

Every cell is surrounded by a thin covering, the **cell membrane**. Cholesterol sits in this covering and regulates its **flexibility**. It makes sure that the membrane is neither too rigid nor too fluid. Without cholesterol our cells could not work properly. That is why it is not a poison, but a vital substance.

The body makes most of the cholesterol itself, mainly in the **liver**. Only a smaller part comes from food, for example from eggs, meat or butter. The liver also makes **bile acids** from cholesterol, which help to digest fats in the gut. Vitamin D and hormones such as the stress hormone **cortisol** also arise from it.

Cholesterol hardly **dissolves in water**, and blood consists largely of water. That is why it travels in small transport particles, the **lipoproteins**. Well known are **LDL**, which brings cholesterol to the cells, and **HDL**, which brings surplus cholesterol back to the liver. If there is a lot of LDL in the blood, deposits can form in the vessel walls. This raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Against too high cholesterol levels, exercise, a balanced diet and giving up smoking help. If that is not enough, doctors often prescribe **statins**. These medicines inhibit the enzyme **HMG-CoA reductase**, which is important in the liver for making cholesterol. The liver then makes less cholesterol and takes more of it out of the blood.

gewusst: The body makes cholesterol in many single steps from small building blocks.
The brain also contains a great deal of cholesterol, mainly in the sheaths of the nerve fibres.

teile.einleitung: The biological value tells us how well the body can convert a protein from food into its own protein. What matters is how well the building blocks, the amino acids, match the body’s needs.
wichtigste: The biological value gives how much body protein can be made from 100 g of dietary protein.
The whole hen’s egg serves as the reference with the value 100.
The limiting essential amino acid mainly decides the value.
Potatoes and egg together reach about 136.
Gelatine has a very low value, because it lacks tryptophan.
Milk and cereal complement each other, because milk supplies lysine.
The FAO today recommends the measure DIAAS.

abschnitte.text: Proteins consist of **amino acids**. The body cannot make some of them itself, and they are called **essential amino acids**. The more similar the amino acid pattern of a dietary protein is to the body’s own protein, the more body protein can be built from it. As the reference, the **whole hen’s egg** was chosen with the value **100**. A value of 80 therefore means: from 100 g of dietary protein, about 80 g of body protein are made. From 50 g it would accordingly be 40 g.

The value is decided mainly by the **limiting amino acid**. This is the essential amino acid that is scarcest in relation to the need. You can imagine it as in building: if one particular building block is missing, you cannot carry on building, even if all the others are there in plenty. **Gelatine** made from collagen contains practically no **tryptophan**. That is why the body can hardly make body protein from it.

Different proteins can **complement** each other. **Potatoes and egg** in a ratio of about 35 to 65 reach about **136**, more than egg alone. Rösti with a fried egg is therefore a meal rich in protein. **Milk and cereal** also go well together, for example in **Birchermüesli**. Cereal protein has little **lysine**, while milk protein has a lot. So the milk makes up for the weakness of the cereal.

The biological value is an older measure. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the **FAO**, today recommends the **DIAAS**. The abbreviation stands for Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score. This measure takes into account how well each single essential amino acid is digested and taken up in the **small intestine**.

gewusst: The combination of potatoes and egg beats egg alone, even though potatoes themselves contain little protein.
Many traditional dishes combine cereals with pulses or milk quite naturally and so complement the proteins.

teile.einleitung: In giving rescue breaths, a helper blows air into the lungs of a person who is no longer breathing by themselves. Together with chest compressions, it can save lives in an emergency.
wichtigste: In mouth-to-nose breathing, you close the person’s mouth and blow into the nose.
You can tell that a breath is effective when the chest rises.
A single breath lasts about a second.
You give an infant breaths over the mouth and nose at the same time.
Air that is breathed out still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.
Anyone who does not want to give breaths does chest compressions without a pause.

abschnitte.text: If a person is no longer breathing, their body gets no oxygen. In **rescue breaths**, the helper blows their own breathed-out air into the person’s lungs. Fresh air contains about **21 per cent** oxygen, and the air we breathe out still about **16 per cent**. That is enough to supply the person. In resuscitation, you usually alternate **30 chest compressions** and **2 breaths**.

In **mouth-to-nose breathing**, you hold the person’s mouth shut with your thumb and blow through the nose. Many experts recommend it, because the nose can be sealed well. In mouth-to-mouth breathing, you hold the nose shut instead. You blow calmly for about **a second**, until the **chest rises**. With an **infant**, you cover mouth and nose at the same time and blow only gently.

If the **belly** swells instead of the chest, the air is going into the **stomach**. This happens if you blow too hard. Then the entrance to the stomach opens. The person can be sick, and stomach contents can get into the lungs. That is why you give breaths calmly and evenly. A **face shield** or a mask protects against direct contact with saliva or blood.

Anyone who does not dare to give breaths to a stranger does **chest compressions without a pause**. This is far better than nothing, because the blood still contains oxygen. It is important to dial the emergency number **144** at once. A **defibrillator** helps as well, and it tells you itself what to do. In Switzerland, you attend a **first aid course** for your driving licence and practise resuscitation there.

gewusst: Even air that is breathed out still contains enough oxygen to give another person breaths.
In Switzerland you have to attend a first aid course before you get your learner driver’s permit.

teile.einleitung: Broccoli is a green vegetable from the cabbage family. It is healthy, tastes mild and can be prepared in many ways. It is also grown in Switzerland.
wichtigste: With broccoli, we eat the flower buds that are still closed.
Broccoli is closely related to cauliflower.
The small, tree-like parts are called florets.
Fresh broccoli is a strong green.
It contains a lot of vitamin C and vitamin K.
The name broccoli comes from Italy.

abschnitte.text: Broccoli belongs to the **cabbage family**, just like cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and white cabbage. It is especially closely related to **cauliflower**. What we eat are the many **flower buds** that have not yet opened. They sit close together on small, tree-like parts, the **florets**. If you leave broccoli standing too long, yellow flowers open, and it becomes tougher.

The name **broccoli** comes from **Italian**. The word “broccoli” is the plural of “broccolo” and means roughly cabbage sprouts. In Italy, broccoli has been grown for a long time. From there it spread to many countries of Europe. Today it grows all over the world.

Fresh broccoli is a **strong green** and firm. It contains a lot of **vitamin C** and **vitamin K**. Vitamin K helps the blood to clot, so that a wound stops bleeding. Broccoli also supplies fibre and minerals. If it turns yellow, it is no longer quite fresh.

So that many vitamins are kept, it is best to **steam** broccoli only briefly. Cooking it too long makes it soft and grey. The **stalk** is edible too: you peel it and cook it along. In Switzerland, broccoli is harvested in the fields from **summer to autumn**. In winter, the broccoli in the shop often comes from countries further south.

gewusst: A close relative of broccoli is Romanesco, whose florets form pointed little towers.
Broccoli, cauliflower, white cabbage and Brussels sprouts all descend from the same wild cabbage.

teile.einleitung: In **arteriosclerosis**, the arteries harden and narrow. In everyday speech people often say “hardening of the arteries”. The disease develops slowly over many years and can cause a heart attack or stroke.
wichtigste: Arteriosclerosis is a hardening and narrowing of the arteries.
In everyday speech it is called hardening of the arteries.
Deposits called plaques form in the vessel walls.
Cholesterol plays an important part in this.
Smoking is one of the strongest risk factors.
The disease develops slowly over many years.

abschnitte.text: Healthy arteries are elastic and smooth inside. In arteriosclerosis, fats, cells and later also calcium build up in the vessel wall. These deposits are called **plaques**. The wall becomes thicker and stiffer as a result, and the space inside the vessel becomes narrower. So less blood can flow through.

**Cholesterol** is a fat-like substance that the body needs, for example for cell walls. But if there is too much of it in the blood, especially the so-called **LDL cholesterol**, it can build up in the vessel walls. That is why doctors often measure the **blood fat levels**. A balanced diet and exercise can improve the levels.

**Smoking** is one of the strongest risk factors. Others are **high blood pressure**, high blood fat levels, **diabetes**, being very overweight and little exercise. Age and a family tendency also play a part. The more risk factors come together, the greater the danger. Many of them can be influenced by the way you live.

If a **coronary vessel** is blocked, part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen any more: a **heart attack** results. If this happens in a vessel of the brain, a **stroke** threatens. If the leg arteries are narrowed, it is called **intermittent claudication**, in German “Schaufensterkrankheit”, or shop window disease. People with it have pain when walking and often have to stop, as if they were looking into a shop window.

Because arteriosclerosis develops **slowly over many years**, a healthy lifestyle is worthwhile even when you are young. Not smoking is especially important. Regular exercise, plenty of vegetables, fruit and wholegrain products and a healthy weight protect the vessels. If needed, medicines that lower blood pressure or cholesterol help.

gewusst: The word arteriosclerosis comes from Greek: “sklerosis” means hardening.
Heart and circulation diseases, often as a result of arteriosclerosis, are among the most common causes of death in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Baroreceptors are small sensors in the walls of large blood vessels. They constantly report to the brain how high the blood pressure is, and so help to adjust it in a flash.
wichtigste: Baroreceptors react to the stretching of the vessel wall.
Important baroreceptors sit in the carotid sinus and in the aortic arch.
The cardiovascular centre in the medulla oblongata processes their signals.
If blood pressure rises suddenly, the reflex lowers the heart rate.
The reflex provides quick adjustments within seconds.
In permanently high blood pressure, the receptors adjust to higher values.

abschnitte.text: Baroreceptors, also called **pressoreceptors**, are **stretch receptors**. If blood pressure rises, the vessel wall is stretched more. Then the receptors send signals more often. The most important arterial baroreceptors sit in the **carotid sinus** at the fork of the carotid artery and in the **aortic arch**, the bend of the great artery of the body.

The signals from the carotid sinus travel along the **glossopharyngeal nerve**, the ninth cranial nerve. The signals from the aortic arch travel along the **vagus nerve**. Both reach the **cardiovascular centre** in the **medulla oblongata**. There the **sympathetic system**, which drives the circulation, and the **parasympathetic system**, which slows it, are adjusted.

If blood pressure rises suddenly, the receptors report more stretch. The cardiovascular centre dampens the sympathetic system and activates the vagus. The **heart rate falls** and the vessels widen, so the pressure drops again. If the pressure falls, for example on **standing up** quickly, it works the other way round. The reflex is responsible mainly for **quick adjustments** within seconds.

If you press on the carotid sinus from outside, for example in a **carotid sinus massage**, it is stretched. The brain wrongly reads this as high blood pressure and slows the heart. Doctors sometimes use this on purpose. In permanently high blood pressure, **hypertension**, the receptors’ **set point** shifts upwards. The high pressure is then no longer reported as a deviation.

gewusst: A brief dizziness on standing up quickly shows that the baroreceptor reflex needs a moment to readjust.
Pressure on the neck from outside can slow the heart by way of the baroreceptors.

teile.einleitung: The basal ganglia are nuclei deep in the brain. They help us to select and control movements, and are important for habits, reward and motivation.
wichtigste: The basal ganglia lie deep in the cerebrum.
They promote wanted movements and inhibit unwanted ones.
The caudate nucleus and putamen together form the striatum.
The globus pallidus means “pale sphere” when translated.
The nucleus accumbens is central to reward and motivation.
In Parkinson’s disease, the subthalamic nucleus is often stimulated.
Huntington’s disease and Tourette syndrome are also linked to the basal ganglia.

abschnitte.text: The **basal ganglia** are collections of nerve cells deep in the **cerebrum**. They include the **striatum**, also called the corpus striatum. It consists of the **caudate nucleus** and the **putamen** and is the most important input station. Other parts are the **globus pallidus** and the **subthalamic nucleus**. Globus means sphere, pallidus pale: because of many myelinated fibres, it looks lighter than its surroundings.

The basal ganglia work in **loops** with the cerebral cortex and the **thalamus**. They help to select the right movement. The **direct pathway** reduces the inhibition of the thalamus, so wanted movements start more easily. The **indirect pathway** acts as a brake and suppresses unwanted movements. Only the interplay makes our movements smooth.

When we repeat actions often, the basal ganglia increasingly take over their control. In this way, for example, **brushing your teeth** becomes an automatic habit. This is called **habit learning**. The **nucleus accumbens** in the lower part of the striatum becomes active with rewards. It is important for motivation and also plays a part in **addiction**.

In **Parkinson’s disease**, nerve cells die that supply the striatum with the messenger substance **dopamine**. Movements become slow and stiff, and trembling often comes with it. If **deep brain stimulation** helps, it is usually the subthalamic nucleus that is stimulated through an electrode. In the inherited disease **Huntington’s disease**, cells in the striatum die, causing wild, flinging movements. In **Tourette syndrome** too, with its tics, a disturbed inhibition in these loops is suspected.

gewusst: Many everyday routines such as cycling or brushing your teeth run almost automatically thanks to the basal ganglia.
The name globus pallidus simply describes its appearance: a pale sphere.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Office of Sport, BASPO for short, is the federal sports office. It promotes sport all over Switzerland, from children’s sport to top-level sport. Its head office is in Magglingen high above Biel.
wichtigste: The BASPO’s head office is in Magglingen above Biel.
Magglingen is called Macolin in French.
The BASPO belongs to the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS).
It runs the promotion programme Youth and Sport.
The Federal University for Sports Magglingen belongs to the BASPO.
In Tenero in Ticino it runs a national youth sports centre.

abschnitte.text: The BASPO’s head office is in **Magglingen**, on a Jura height **above Biel**. In French the place is called **Macolin**, because the region is bilingual. From Biel a funicular railway runs up. There are sports halls, sports fields and accommodation there. Many national teams train here.

The federal school in Magglingen was originally founded as the **Federal Gymnastics and Sports School**. Later it became the Federal Office of Sport. Today it belongs to the **Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport**, DDPS for short. The Confederation’s promotion of sport today rests mainly on the **Sports Promotion Act**. It lays down how the Confederation supports sport and exercise.

The best-known programme of the BASPO is **Youth and Sport**, J+S for short. It supports sports courses and camps for children and young people in many sports. For this, J+S trains **leaders**. Clubs and schools receive contributions if they run J+S activities. In this way very many young people in Switzerland can do sport.

The **Federal University for Sports Magglingen** belongs to the BASPO. There you can study sport and become, for example, a sports teacher or a trainer. Research on sport is also done there. In Ticino, the BASPO runs a **national youth sports centre** in **Tenero** on Lake Maggiore. School classes, clubs and sports camps can use it.

gewusst: Because the region around Biel is bilingual, much in Magglingen is signposted in German and French.
At the Tenero youth sports centre you can also camp.

teile.einleitung: Chondral ossification is one way in which bones arise. In it, the body first forms a model made of cartilage, which is later replaced bit by bit by bone. This is how most bones of our skeleton arise, for example the long bones in arms and legs.
wichtigste: Chondral ossification means bone formation by way of a **cartilage model**.
The model consists of **hyaline cartilage**.
Bones formed in this way are called **replacement bones**.
Growth in length takes place in the **growth plate**.
When the plates have turned to bone, growth in length is finished.
In achondroplasia this process is disturbed.

abschnitte.text: The word **ossification** means turning to bone, “chondral” means that cartilage is involved. First a small model of the later bone arises from **hyaline cartilage**, a smooth, firm tissue. This model is then broken down step by step and replaced by bone. That is why such bones are called **replacement bones**. Other bones, for example parts of the roof of the skull, arise directly from connective tissue without a cartilage model.

In **endochondral ossification**, the cartilage inside the model is broken down. Bone cells, the **osteoblasts**, build new bone tissue in its place. At the same time, in **perichondral ossification**, a bony sleeve arises around the model from outside. Both processes work together until the cartilage model has become a solid bone.

Long bones grow in length in the **growth plate**, a disc of cartilage between the shaft and the end of the bone. Right at the epiphysis lies the **reserve zone** with resting cartilage cells. In the **proliferation zone** the cartilage cells divide and arrange themselves in columns. After that the cells become bigger, the cartilage calcifies and is replaced by bone. In this way the plate keeps pushing the end of the bone further outwards.

As long as the growth plates are open, a person can still grow taller. At some point the plates turn completely to bone, and **growth in length** is finished. In the **X-ray** you can see this well: the dark gaps of the plates have disappeared. Doctors can estimate a child’s **bone age** from an X-ray of the hand.

In the inherited disease **achondroplasia**, endochondral ossification does not work properly. The cartilage cells in the growth plates multiply too little. That is why mainly the arms and legs stay short, while the trunk is almost normal in size. This is called **disproportionate short stature**, and achondroplasia is its most common cause.

gewusst: A newborn has more separate bone parts than an adult, because many grow together later.
The growth plates are among the last places in the skeleton to turn to bone.

teile.einleitung: A barefoot path is a trail on which you walk without shoes. With bare feet you feel grass, sand, stones and mud. This is fun and good for your feet.
wichtigste: On a barefoot path you walk without shoes and socks.
You feel different grounds such as grass, sand, bark or stones.
Moss feels especially soft, fir cones prick.
Walking barefoot strengthens the small muscles in the foot.
A well-known barefoot trail runs from Jakobsbad to Gontenbad in Appenzell Innerrhoden.
After the trail you wash your feet.

abschnitte.text: On a **barefoot path** you take off your shoes and socks. The trail leads over very different grounds: **grass**, **sand**, **stones**, **bark** or **mud**. Every ground feels different. The sole of the foot is very sensitive and feels every little change. So walking becomes an experience for the senses.

**Moss** is a soft, damp cushion of small plants. You walk on it as on a carpet. **Fir cones**, on the other hand, are hard and edgy and prick under the soles of your feet. In the early morning the grass is often wet. In the cool night, little drops of water form out of the air, the **dew**.

Without shoes, the small **foot muscles** work more. This keeps the feet strong and flexible. Balance is practised too, when the ground is uneven. A barefoot path is nicest in **summer**, when the ground is warm. After the trail the feet are often dirty. That is why many barefoot trails have a basin at the end for **washing your feet**.

In Switzerland there are several barefoot trails. Especially well known is the **barefoot trail from Jakobsbad to Gontenbad** in the canton of **Appenzell Innerrhoden**. It is several kilometres long and leads through the hilly landscape near **Gonten**. On the way you walk over meadows, boggy ground and little streams. You also see typical Appenzell farmhouses.

gewusst: Each human foot consists of 26 bones.
The sole of the foot has very many nerve endings, which is why it feels the ground so precisely.

teile.einleitung: In taking blood, a little blood is drawn from the body. It is examined in the laboratory. In this way doctors learn more about a person’s health.
wichtigste: Usually blood is taken from a vein in the crook of the arm.
For this you need a fine needle and a small tube.
A tourniquet on the upper arm makes the veins stand out better.
For a single drop, a prick in the fingertip is enough.
Fasting means that you have eaten nothing beforehand.
After the blood is taken, you press on the spot and put on a plaster.
In the laboratory the blood is examined closely.

abschnitte.text: For a blood sample, blood is almost always taken from a **vein**. Most often the needle goes in at the **crook of the arm**. There clearly visible veins lie just under the skin. A **fine needle** is put into the vein. The blood then flows into a small **tube**. Only **a little** blood is needed.

Before the blood is taken, a **tourniquet** is often tied round the upper arm. It holds the blood back briefly in the veins. Then they stand out better, and you find them more easily. After the needle goes in, the band is loosened again. You feel a short prick, and then it is mostly over quickly.

Sometimes only a single **drop of blood** is needed. Then a small prick in the **fingertip** is enough. This is how, for example, **blood sugar** is measured. In small children, blood is sometimes taken from the heel. After the prick you press briefly on the spot.

For some tests you should come **fasting**. This means you have **eaten nothing** for a while beforehand. Water is usually allowed. After eating, blood sugar and blood fats, for example, change. Without fasting, some values would therefore be **distorted**.

After the blood is taken, you **press** briefly on the puncture site. Then it soon stops bleeding. A **plaster** protects the small puncture. In the **laboratory**, professionals test the blood with machines. In this way you find out, for example, whether there is enough **iron**.

gewusst: The tubes for blood samples have coloured caps that show what they are meant for.
Anyone who is afraid of the needle may lie down and look away.

teile.einleitung: **Eye colour** is the colour of the **iris**, the coloured ring around the pupil. It depends on how much pigment there is in the iris. Eye colour is inherited from the parents.
wichtigste: Eye colour is the colour of the iris.
Brown is the most common eye colour in the world.
Green is one of the rarest eye colours.
Blue eyes are especially common in northern Europe.
Blue eyes do not have a blue pigment, but little pigment.
Two eyes of different colours are called heterochromia.

abschnitte.text: The colour of the eyes arises in the **iris**. There is the pigment **melanin**, which also colours skin and hair. A lot of melanin makes the eyes **brown**. In **blue eyes** there is no blue pigment. They only have **a little pigment**, and the light is scattered in the iris in such a way that they look blue. The sky looks blue in a similar way.

**Brown** is the **most common** eye colour in the world. In Africa, Asia and South America almost all people have brown eyes. Blue eyes are especially common in **northern Europe**, for example in Scandinavia and the Baltic states. **Green** is one of the **rarest** eye colours. There are also grey and hazel eyes and many mixed shades.

You get your eye colour **from your parents**. It is inherited, and several genes work together in it. That is why two parents with brown eyes can also have a child with blue eyes. A child’s eye colour cannot be predicted exactly.

Many fair-skinned babies have **blue or grey** eyes at birth. Their iris only makes pigment bit by bit. So eye colour can still change **in the first years of life** and, for example, turn green or brown. After that it usually stays the same.

Some people have **two eyes of different colours**, for example one blue and one brown. This is called **heterochromia**. It also happens in dogs and cats. People with **albinism** make only very little melanin. Their eyes often look **very pale**, sometimes with a reddish shimmer, and they are sensitive to bright light.

gewusst: Every person’s iris has a unique pattern, which is why people can be recognised with an iris scan.
In dim light, eye colour often looks darker than in sunshine.

teile.einleitung: Blood is a red fluid that flows through the veins and supplies the whole body. It carries oxygen and nutrients to the cells and takes waste substances away. An adult has about 5 litres of blood.
wichtigste: Blood is a fluid that carries oxygen and nutrients.
Our blood is red.
Blood flows through the body in the blood vessels.
An adult has about 5 litres of blood.
Blood consists of blood plasma and blood cells.
When a small wound heals, a scab forms.
The heart pumps the blood round the body without a pause.

abschnitte.text: A little more than half of the blood is **blood plasma**, a yellowish fluid that consists mainly of water. In it float the blood cells. The **red blood cells** carry oxygen, and the white blood cells fight off germs. The **platelets** make sure that blood clots when there is an injury.

The red blood cells contain the pigment **haemoglobin**. It contains iron and binds oxygen in the lungs. Blood rich in oxygen is bright red, blood low in oxygen dark red. That veins under the skin look bluish is only because of how light is scattered in the skin.

The **heart** pumps the blood through a huge network of blood vessels, which are also called veins in everyday speech. Arteries carry the blood away from the heart, and veins carry it back. In the finest vessels, the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients are given up to the cells. Going once round the whole body takes the blood at rest only about a minute.

When you cut yourself, the blood vessels at the spot narrow. The platelets stick together and form a net with a protein called fibrin. This makes a plug that stops the bleeding. It dries into a **scab**, under which the skin grows back.

People have different **blood groups**, the most important being A, B, AB and O. In addition there is the rhesus factor, positive or negative. In a blood transfusion the blood group has to match. In Switzerland, Blood Donation SRK Switzerland organises blood donations, and you may donate from the age of 18.

begriffe.erklaerung: The liquid, yellowish part of the blood.
Blood cells that carry oxygen.
Blood cells that fight germs.
Tiny parts of the blood that help to close wounds.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.

gewusst: Red blood cells live for about 120 days, then they are broken down and replaced by new ones.
In the body, millions of new red blood cells are made in the bone marrow every second.
If you laid all the blood vessels of an adult end to end, they would be many tens of thousands of kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Not all blood is the same: every person has a particular blood group. It depends on tiny features on the surface of the red blood cells. Anyone who needs a blood transfusion has to get matching blood, otherwise it becomes dangerous.
wichtigste: The most important blood groups are called A, B, AB and O.
They are determined by features on the surface of the red blood cells.
Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO system in 1901.
In addition, a distinction is made between rhesus positive and rhesus negative.
The blood group is inherited from the parents.
Blood group O rhesus negative counts as a universal donor for red blood cells.
People with blood group AB can receive red blood cells of all ABO groups.

abschnitte.text: On the covering of the red blood cells sit certain sugar features, the **antigens**. Anyone who has feature A has blood group A, anyone who has B has blood group B. Anyone who has both has AB, and anyone who has neither has O. In the blood plasma there are also **antibodies** against the missing features, so in blood group A, anti-B.

The Austrian doctor **Karl Landsteiner** discovered the ABO blood group system in 1901. He mixed blood samples from different people and saw that they sometimes clumped together. For this discovery he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930. Since then, blood transfusions can be carried out safely.

Besides the ABO system there is the **rhesus system**. Anyone who carries feature D is rhesus positive, anyone who does not have it is rhesus negative. In Europe about 85 in 100 people are rhesus positive. If a rhesus negative mother is expecting a rhesus positive child, she can form antibodies against the child’s blood cells, which is why she is now given a preventive injection.

In a transfusion, the donor blood has to match the recipient, otherwise the blood cells clump together. Red blood cells of group **O rhesus negative** almost always match, which is why it counts as a universal donor. People with AB can receive red blood cells of all ABO groups. In Switzerland, Blood Donation SRK organises blood donation, and you may donate from the age of 18.

Every person inherits one blood group gene from the mother and one from the father. A and B are **dominant**, O is recessive. If the mother has the genotype AO and the father BO, their children can have A, B, AB or O. That is why siblings can have quite different blood groups.

In Switzerland the blood groups A and O are the most common. Blood group AB is rather rare. In other regions of the world the distribution is quite different. In parts of South America, for example, almost all the indigenous people have blood group O.

begriffe.erklaerung: A feature on a cell that the immune system can recognise.
Defence substances in the blood that recognise and attack foreign features.
The transfer of blood or blood components from one person to another.
An additional blood feature that you either have (positive) or do not have (negative).

gewusst: Besides ABO and rhesus, over 40 other blood group systems are known today.
The rhesus factor is named after rhesus monkeys, with whose blood it was researched.
Dogs and cats also have blood groups, but different ones from humans.

teile.einleitung: The **respiratory chain** is the last step of cell respiration. In the mitochondria, electrons are passed along through several protein complexes until they reach oxygen. The cell uses the energy that is released to make the energy carrier **ATP**.
wichtigste: The complexes of the respiratory chain sit in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.
Complexes I, III and IV pump protons across the membrane.
Ubiquinone and cytochrome c carry electrons between the complexes.
Peter Mitchell explained the making of ATP with the chemiosmotic theory.
Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase.
According to current estimates, about 30 to 32 ATP are made per glucose molecule.

abschnitte.text: **Mitochondria** are seen as the power stations of the cell. They have an outer membrane and a strongly folded **inner membrane**. In this inner membrane sit the complexes of the respiratory chain. They receive electrons from the carriers **NADH** and **FADH2**, which were made when sugar and fat were broken down. In the end the electrons are passed to **oxygen**, which produces water.

**Complex I** takes up electrons from NADH. Through **complex II**, succinate dehydrogenase, electrons from FADH2 enter the chain. The mobile molecule **ubiquinone** carries the electrons from complexes I and II to **complex III**. From there the small haem protein **cytochrome c** carries them to **complex IV**, cytochrome c oxidase, which passes them on to oxygen.

Complexes I, III and IV use the energy of the electrons to pump **protons** across the inner membrane. This builds up a gradient, like water behind a dam. The protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, an enzyme that works like a tiny turbine. In the process **ATP** is made. This explanation is called the **chemiosmotic theory**.

The British biochemist **Peter Mitchell** put forward the chemiosmotic theory in 1961. At first many researchers doubted his idea. Later, experiments confirmed his explanation. In 1978 Mitchell received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for it.

When one glucose molecule is broken down completely, according to current estimates **about 30 to 32 ATP** are made, most of them in the respiratory chain. Some poisons block the chain. **Cyanide** blocks **cytochrome c oxidase**. Then the cells can no longer use oxygen, even though there is enough of it in the blood.

gewusst: In one day, a person makes and uses roughly as much ATP as they weigh.
Mitochondria have their own genetic material, which points to their origin from bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart into the body. In German they are also called Schlagadern, “beating vessels”, because you can feel the heartbeat in them as a pulse. The largest artery is the aorta.
wichtigste: Arteries carry blood away from the heart into the body.
In German they are also called Schlagadern.
The largest artery is the aorta, which is about 3 centimetres thick.
In most arteries, bright red, oxygen-rich blood flows.
You feel the pulse because the heart pushes blood into them with every beat.
An injury to a large artery is very dangerous.

abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through a network of tubes, the **blood vessels**. **Arteries** carry the blood **away from the heart** into the body. **Veins** lead it back to the heart. The largest artery is the **aorta**, the main artery. In adults it is **about 3 centimetres** thick. Ever smaller arteries branch off from it, down to tiny capillaries.

In most arteries flows blood that has taken up a lot of **oxygen** in the lungs. It is **bright red**. Blood in the veins has less oxygen and is a darker red. One exception is the **pulmonary artery**: it carries low-oxygen blood from the heart to the lungs. Arteries have a thick, **elastic** wall with muscles, because the pressure in them is high.

With every heartbeat, the **heart pushes blood** into the arteries. Their wall stretches briefly as a result. You feel this wave as the **pulse**, which is why arteries are called **“beating vessels”** in German. You can feel the pulse well at the wrist or at the **carotid artery**, the large artery at the side of the neck. In the groin runs the **femoral artery**, which supplies the leg.

When **blood pressure** is measured, a cuff is put round the upper arm. It is pumped up and squeezes the **brachial artery**. Then the device measures how hard the blood presses against the vessel walls. If a large artery is injured, the **blood spurts out strongly**. Because you lose a lot of blood in a short time, this is very dangerous. You press firmly on the wound and call **144** at once.

gewusst: If you laid all the blood vessels of an adult end to end, they would be many thousands of kilometres long.
In children, too, you can feel the pulse; it is usually faster than in adults.

teile.einleitung: Blood plasma is the liquid part of the blood. It is yellowish and consists for the most part of water. In it float the blood cells and many dissolved substances.
wichtigste: Plasma makes up about 55 per cent of the blood volume.
It carries nutrients, salts and hormones.
Albumin is the most common plasma protein.
Immunoglobulins are antibodies in the plasma.
Without clotting substances, the fluid is called serum.
With a centrifuge you separate plasma and blood cells.
In plasmapheresis only plasma is donated.

abschnitte.text: About **55 per cent** of blood is liquid **plasma**. The rest is made up by the blood cells. Plasma is yellowish and consists for the most part of **water**. In it many substances are dissolved, for example sugar, fats, **salts**, **nutrients** and **hormones**. In this way they reach all the cells of the body.

The most common protein in the plasma is **albumin**. It makes up over half of the plasma proteins. Albumin holds water in the blood vessels and carries many substances. Also important are the **immunoglobulins**. These are **antibodies** that recognise germs and mark them for the defence cells. Other proteins such as **fibrinogen** provide for blood clotting.

In the laboratory, plasma is separated from the blood cells with a **centrifuge**. It spins the tube very fast. The heavy cells sink to the bottom, the lighter plasma stays on top. If you let blood **clot** instead, a fluid without fibrinogen is left over. This fluid is called **serum**.

In **plasma donation**, only the plasma is taken. This method is called **plasmapheresis**. A machine separates off the plasma and gives the blood cells back to the donor. In this way you can donate plasma more often than whole blood. From donor plasma, **medicines** are made, for example albumin, antibodies and **clotting factors**.

gewusst: Plasma consists of about 90 per cent water.
The word plasma comes from Greek and means roughly “that which is formed”.

teile.einleitung: **Endurance** means that you can keep up an effort for a long time. It is important in sport and in everyday life. With regular training, endurance gets better.
wichtigste: Endurance means being able to keep going for a long time.
Cross-country skiing, running, swimming and cycling are typical endurance sports.
Endurance training strengthens the heart and lungs.
You get more endurance through regular training.
In a triathlon you swim, cycle and run one after the other.
In Switzerland, the Tour de Suisse and the Engadin Ski Marathon are well-known endurance races.

abschnitte.text: Someone with **endurance** can **keep up** an effort **for a long time** without quickly getting tired. You need this, for example, when hiking, playing football or cycling to school. Typical **endurance sports** are running, swimming, cycling and **cross-country skiing**. In them you move for a long time at an even pace.

abschnitte.titel: Good for the heart and lungs
abschnitte.text: In endurance training, the **heart and lungs** work harder so that the muscles get enough oxygen. Over time they become stronger as a result. With every beat the heart can pump more blood. People who train endurance often feel fitter and sleep better. You only get more endurance through **regular training**, that is, several times a week.

When running, some people get a **stitch**, a sharp pain in the side of the stomach. Exactly where it comes from has still not been fully explained. It helps to **slow down and breathe calmly**. A big meal shortly before sport can also make a stitch more likely.

The **Tour de Suisse** is a big cycle race through Switzerland that lasts **several days**. It was first held in 1933. In winter the **Engadin Ski Marathon** takes place in the Engadine. Thousands of cross-country skiers ski across the frozen lakes from Maloja to S-chanf.

In a **triathlon** you do three sports straight **one after the other**: first **swimming**, then **cycling** and at the end **running**. There are short courses for beginners and very long races. Triathlon has been an Olympic sport since 2000. Swiss athletes have already been successful in it several times.

gewusst: The Engadin Ski Marathon is about 42 kilometres long, about as long as a running marathon.
In 2000 the Swiss athlete Brigitte McMahon won the first Olympic gold in the women’s triathlon.

teile.einleitung: An antigen is a substance that the immune system recognises as foreign and defends itself against. Antigens set off the immune response, and antibodies fight them. Antigens sit, for example, on the surface of bacteria, viruses or pollen.
wichtigste: Antigens are substances that set off a defence reaction of the immune system.
Antigens set off the immune response, and antibodies fight them.
Antigens are mostly proteins or sugar compounds.
They often sit on the surface of germs.
The exact part to which an antibody binds is called an epitope.
The blood groups A, B, AB and O are also determined by antigens.
Vaccinations teach the body harmless antigens.

abschnitte.text: The name **antigen** is short for “antibody generator” and means roughly “producer of antibodies”. So an antigen is a substance to which the immune system reacts. It is often a large molecule such as a protein. In this way the immune system tells “self” from “foreign”.

An antibody fits its antigen like a key in a lock. But it does not bind to the whole antigen, only to a small spot, the **epitope**. A single bacterium can carry many different epitopes. That is why the body often makes several kinds of antibodies against the same germ.

Antigens are found on bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Pollen, animal hair or parts of foods can also act as antigens. Substances that cause an allergy are also called **allergens**. Foreign organs in a transplant also carry antigens that the immune system can recognise.

Red blood cells carry certain antigens on their surface. Someone with blood group A carries antigen A, with blood group B antigen B. In blood group O both are missing, in AB both are present. So in a **blood transfusion** the blood group has to match, otherwise the immune system attacks the foreign blood.

In a **vaccination**, the body is given weakened or killed germs, or only their antigens. The immune system gets to know them and makes memory cells. If the body later meets the real germ, it can react very quickly. Rapid tests, for example for flu or COVID-19, also detect antigens.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that the immune system recognises as foreign.
A protein of the immune system that binds to antigens.
The small spot on an antigen to which an antibody fits.
The body’s defence reaction against foreign substances.

gewusst: The blood groups were discovered in 1901 by the Austrian Karl Landsteiner.
An antigen rapid test shows after a few minutes whether certain parts of a germ are present.

teile.einleitung: A stomach bug, in German called “Bauchgrippe”, is an inflammation of the stomach and gut. You have diarrhoea, often have to be sick and feel weak. Mostly it is over after a few days.
wichtigste: In a stomach bug, the stomach and gut are inflamed.
Typical are diarrhoea and vomiting.
Most important is drinking plenty, best in small sips.
Often noroviruses or rotaviruses cause a stomach bug.
A stomach bug is very infectious, so clean hands are important.
It usually lasts only a few days.

abschnitte.text: In a **stomach bug**, the **stomach and gut** are inflamed. The technical word is **gastroenteritis**. It has nothing to do with real flu, even if the name sounds like it. You often have **diarrhoea**, have to **be sick**, and sometimes have stomach cramps or a fever. Mostly it is over after **a few days**.

Often **viruses** are behind it, especially **noroviruses** and **rotaviruses**. They spread very quickly, for example in schools, nurseries or care homes. Even tiny amounts are enough to catch it. The germs get into the mouth by way of the hands or dirty objects. That is why thorough **handwashing with soap** is very important.

Through vomiting and diarrhoea, the body loses a lot of **water** and salt. So **drinking** is the most important thing. A sick stomach does not cope well with large amounts, and small **sips** are more likely to stay down. Good are water, tea or a special rehydration drink from the chemist’s. If a small child becomes very weak or hardly drinks, you should go to the doctor.

When hunger comes back, light food is good. **Rusks**, rice, potatoes or bananas are easy to digest. Greasy and very sweet food, on the other hand, puts a heavy strain on the stomach. Even after the stomach bug, the stomach still needs some **taking it easy**. And because you can stay infectious for a while, you keep washing your hands well.

gewusst: A stomach bug has nothing to do with real flu.
There is a vaccine against rotaviruses for babies, given by mouth.

teile.einleitung: Apoptosis is the programmed, natural death of cells in the body. In it, cells take themselves apart in an orderly way when they get a signal, without causing inflammation. This sounds odd, but it is vital for a healthy body.
wichtigste: Apoptosis is programmed, natural cell death.
Every day, billions of cells in an adult die through apoptosis.
The cell shrinks and breaks up into small packages.
Scavenger cells clear up the remains without causing inflammation.
Apoptosis shapes the fingers in the embryo, for example.
It removes damaged or dangerous cells.
If apoptosis does not work properly, cancer can develop.

abschnitte.text: The word **apoptosis** comes from Greek and means “falling off”, like leaves falling from a tree in autumn. It means a cell death that the cell carries out itself according to an exact programme. The opposite is **necrosis**, a disorderly cell death after an injury. In necrosis the cell bursts, and there is often inflammation.

Apoptosis is started by signals from outside or from the cell itself. Then special proteins called **caspases** become active and take the cell apart from the inside. The cell shrinks, its genetic material is cut up, and it breaks up into small sacs wrapped in a membrane. Scavenger cells take up these sacs and put them to use.

In the embryo, hands are at first shaped like little paddles. Only through apoptosis do the cells between the fingers die off, so that separate fingers form. In the brain, too, surplus nerve cells are removed in this way. In tadpoles, apoptosis makes sure that the tail shrinks away.

Apoptosis removes old, damaged or infected cells. If the genetic material of a cell is badly damaged, it can destroy itself before it becomes dangerous. The **immune system** also uses apoptosis to break down defence cells again after an infection. In this way the number of cells stays in balance.

If apoptosis works too weakly, cells can grow out of control and **cancer** can develop. If it is too strong, too many cells die, which plays a part in some diseases of the nervous system. For research on programmed cell death, Sydney Brenner, Robert Horvitz and John Sulston received the Nobel Prize in 2002. They had studied a tiny roundworm for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: Programmed, orderly cell death.
Disorderly cell death, for example after an injury.
Proteins that take a cell apart from the inside during apoptosis.
A living thing in an early phase of its development.

gewusst: In an adult human, about 50 to 70 billion cells die every day through apoptosis.
Without apoptosis we would have webbing between our fingers.

teile.einleitung: Blue light is the part of visible light with a short wavelength. It makes us awake and sets the inner clock. In the morning this is helpful, in the evening it can make it harder to fall asleep.
wichtigste: The light sensor melanopsin in the eye reacts most strongly to light of about 480 nanometres.
The screens of phones and tablets give off a lot of blue light.
Blue light in the evening slows the making of the sleep hormone melatonin.
Night mode makes the screen colour warmer and more yellowish.
The colour temperature of a lamp is measured in kelvin.
For the bedroom, warm white light is better.
In the morning, bright light rich in blue is helpful.

abschnitte.text: White light consists of many colours. Each colour has a different **wavelength**, measured in **nanometres**. Blue light has short waves of about 450 to 490 nanometres, red light long waves of about 700 nanometres. In the eye, besides the visual cells there are special cells with the substance **melanopsin**. They react most strongly to light of about **480 nanometres** and tell the brain whether it is day.

In the evening the body makes the hormone **melatonin**, which makes you tired. Blue light **slows** this production. A lot of it is given off by the white **LEDs** in the **screens** of phones and tablets. Candles and fire, on the other hand, glow yellowish red with little blue. Experts often advise not using screens any more for about **an hour** before sleep. Exciting content also keeps the brain awake.

Many phones have a **night mode**. It reduces the blue share and makes the picture **warmer and more yellowish**. Most effective, though, is to put the screen away altogether. There are also glasses that are meant to filter blue light. Their lenses are mostly **yellowish to orange**, because these colours absorb a lot of blue.

The **colour temperature** of a lamp is given in **kelvin**. **Warm white** light is about 2,700 kelvin, cold daylight white over 5,000 kelvin. The higher the value, the more blue the light contains. For the **bedroom** in the evening, a warm white lamp is therefore suitable. On many lamp packs in Switzerland the kelvin number is printed.

Blue light is not bad. **In the morning**, bright light rich in blue stops the production of melatonin and wakes you up. It sets the **inner clock** to an early start of the day. That is why a walk in the morning in daylight does you good. The blue sky also contains a lot of such light.

gewusst: Melanopsin was only discovered in the eye towards the end of the 20th century.
Even on a cloudy day, the light outdoors is mostly much brighter than in a lit room.

teile.einleitung: The banana is one of the most popular fruits in the world. It is sweet, easy to peel and quickly gives energy. Here with us it is always a well-travelled guest from warm countries.
wichtigste: Bananas grow in bunches on a big plant.
They need a lot of warmth and rain and grow in the tropics.
Bananas contain a lot of potassium and vitamin B6.
They are picked green and ripen on the way to Europe.
Ripe bananas get brown spots and are especially sweet.
A group of joined bananas is called a hand, a single one a finger.
In the fridge the skin quickly turns brown.

abschnitte.text: Bananas grow in bunches on a big **plant**. It looks like a tree, but has no wood. The “trunk” consists of leaves lying tightly on top of one another. Bananas need a lot of **warmth** and **rain**. That is why they grow in tropical countries, for example in South and Central America, Africa and Asia.

A group of joined bananas is called a **hand**, and a single banana a **finger**. That fits well, because they look like fingers on a hand. Several hands hang one above the other on one plant. The bananas that we eat have only tiny dark dots in the middle, but no hard seeds.

Bananas are picked **green**. They travel by ship to Europe, kept cool. Only then do they ripen in special rooms and turn **yellow**. In time they get **brown spots**, and then they are especially sweet. Bananas do not belong in the **fridge**: in the cold their skin quickly turns brown to black. In Swiss shops there are many fair trade bananas.

Bananas contain a lot of **sugar** and **starch**. This gives the body energy quickly, which is why many sportspeople like to eat bananas. Bananas are known for their high content of **potassium**. This mineral is important for muscles and the heart. They also contain **vitamin B6**, which the body needs, among other things, for the nerves.

gewusst: The banana plant is not a kind of tree, but a giant plant without wood.
Bananas are very slightly radioactive, because potassium naturally contains a tiny amount of radioactive potassium. This is completely harmless.

teile.einleitung: A “Coiffeur” or “Coiffeuse” cuts other people’s hair. The word comes from French and is used in Switzerland for this job. In Germany people often say “Friseur”.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the job is called **Coiffeur**, a woman is a **Coiffeuse**.
The hairdresser works in a **hairdressing salon**.
Often the hair is washed first.
Cutting is done with **hair scissors** or the **hair clipper**.
A **cape** protects the clothes from hair.
A **barber** especially looks after men’s beards.

abschnitte.titel: A job with a French name
abschnitte.text: The word **Coiffeur** comes from the French word “coiffer”, which means to do someone’s hair. In Switzerland almost everywhere people say Coiffeur, and a woman in this job is a **Coiffeuse**. The shop is called a **Coiffeursalon**. In Germany the job is mostly called Friseur. The same work is meant, though.

First the hairdresser puts a **cape** round you, so that no hair falls on your clothes. Often they then wash the hair at the **basin**, which has a hollow at the back for the neck. Wet hair is easy to comb and cut exactly. Beforehand the hairdresser asks how the new hairstyle should look.

The most important tool is the **hair scissors**. They are very sharp and lie well in the hand. With the **hair clipper**, hair is cut very short, almost like stubble. Besides these there are combs, brushes and a **hairdryer** for drying. At the end the hairdresser uses a mirror to show how the hairstyle looks at the back.

A **barber** is a hairdresser who especially looks after **men’s beards**. He trims beards into shape and shaves with a sharp knife. In the past, barbers sometimes even pulled teeth and treated small wounds. Today there are barbershops again in many cities.

In Switzerland you learn the job in an **apprenticeship** and finish with the Federal Certificate of Proficiency, **EFZ** for short. You work in the salon and attend vocational school. There you learn cutting, colouring, care and also how to advise customers well. Skilful hands and enjoyment of contact with people are important.

gewusst: Cutting hair does not hurt, because the hairs themselves have no nerves.
Hair on the head grows about a centimetre a month.

teile.einleitung: Chemotherapy is an important treatment against cancer. In it, patients are given medicines that stop cancer cells from growing and dividing. Because these drugs also hit healthy cells, the treatment needs a lot of experience and good support.
wichtigste: The medicines of chemotherapy are called **cytostatics**.
They act especially strongly on cells that divide quickly.
The first cytostatics were developed in the 1940s from the chemical weapon mustard gas.
Common side effects are nausea, hair loss and a weakened defence.
Treatment usually runs in cycles with breaks, so that healthy tissue can recover.
Besides classic cytostatics there are targeted drugs today such as imatinib.

abschnitte.text: Cancer cells often divide much faster than most healthy cells. **Cytostatics** disturb exactly this process: they inhibit the doubling of the **DNA** or cell division itself. Cisplatin, for example, is a compound with the metal **platinum** and cross-links the DNA strands. Methotrexate is an **antimetabolite**: it blocks the folic acid metabolism, so that building blocks for the DNA are missing. Paclitaxel stabilises the microtubules, fine tubes that the cell needs for division.

abschnitte.titel: Where the active substances come from
abschnitte.text: The history of chemotherapy begins with a surprising observation. It was noticed that **mustard gas** sharply lowers the number of white blood cells. From this, in the 1940s, the nitrogen mustard compounds arose, which were used against lymphomas. Other active substances come from nature: **paclitaxel** was originally obtained from the bark of the Pacific yew. Today it is made semi-synthetically.

Newer medicines attack a particular cancer protein in a targeted way. A famous example is **imatinib**, which was developed in Basel and approved in 2001. It inhibits an overactive enzyme in **chronic myeloid leukaemia**, a form of blood cancer. Imatinib is a **tyrosine kinase inhibitor** and counts as a model for many further targeted active substances. Such drugs often spare healthy cells better.

Healthy cells that divide quickly are also damaged, for example in the **bone marrow**, in the hair roots and in the lining of the gut. That is why hair sometimes falls out and the defence against infections becomes weaker. Very common are **nausea and vomiting**. Against these, **antiemetics** such as ondansetron help, which block receptors for the messenger substance serotonin. The breaks between cycles give the body time to recover.

Chemotherapy is often combined with surgery and radiotherapy. **Neoadjuvant** chemotherapy is given before the operation, so that the tumour becomes smaller. **Adjuvant** chemotherapy follows after the operation and is meant to fight remaining cancer cells. Which combination suits is decided by a team of experts together with the patients.

gewusst: The cancer-inhibiting effect of cisplatin was discovered by chance in experiments with bacteria and platinum electrodes.
A whole treatment programme usually consists of several cycles spread over weeks or months.

teile.einleitung: The chronotype describes when a person likes to sleep best and when they are most awake. Some people are bright and early, others only really get going in the evening. The chronotype depends partly on the genes and changes in the course of life.
wichtigste: Early chronotypes are called **larks** in everyday speech, late ones **owls**.
The chronotype depends partly on the **genes**.
At around 20, people on average are at their latest.
In older age the chronotype typically becomes earlier.
Questionnaires such as the Munich ChronoType Questionnaire help to determine the chronotype.

abschnitte.text: People with an early chronotype are called **larks** in everyday speech. They wake early by themselves and soon get tired in the evening. Late types are called **owls**: they like to sleep late and are especially fit in the evening. Most people lie somewhere in between. It is controlled by the **inner clock**, which is set mainly by daylight.

Researchers use questionnaires to determine the chronotype. The **Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire** by Horne and Östberg asks at what times you feel best. The chronobiologist **Till Roenneberg** developed the **Munich ChronoType Questionnaire**. The measure used there is the **midpoint of sleep on free days**, that is, the time in the middle between falling asleep and waking up when no alarm rings.

abschnitte.titel: The chronotype in the course of life
abschnitte.text: Children are often awake early. In the teenage years the chronotype shifts later, and at **around 20** people on average are at their latest. After that the chronotype slowly becomes earlier again. In later adult life many people get up early by themselves. That is why getting up early is often especially hard for teenagers.

The chronotype depends **partly on the genes**, so in families there are often similar types. The environment plays a part too: a lot of daylight in the morning tends to make you earlier, bright light late in the evening tends to make you later. If school or working hours fit your own type badly, you sleep too little during the week. Roenneberg calls this difference between the inner clock and everyday life **social jet lag**.

abschnitte.titel: When the clock is far off
abschnitte.text: Some people can permanently fall asleep only very late and therefore also wake up only late. This is called **delayed sleep phase syndrome**. Those affected are not lazy, their inner clock simply runs strongly shifted. Bright light in the morning and fixed sleeping times can help, for example.

gewusst: At the weekend many people sleep longer, because during the week they have to get up against their inner clock.
Animals and plants also have an inner clock with a rhythm of about 24 hours.

teile.einleitung: Breathing means that we draw air into the lungs and push it out again. In doing so the body takes in oxygen, which all cells need to live, and gives off carbon dioxide. We breathe without a break, mostly without thinking about it.
wichtigste: We need oxygen from the air to live.
What we breathe out is mainly carbon dioxide.
The air flows through the windpipe into the lungs.
In deep breathing, the chest rises and falls.
When running, breathing becomes faster.
At rest, adults breathe about 12 to 20 times a minute.
Breathing is controlled automatically by the brain.

abschnitte.text: Air enters the body through the nose or the mouth. In the nose it is warmed, moistened and cleaned of dust. Then it flows through the throat and the larynx into the **windpipe**. The windpipe divides into two **bronchi**, which lead into the left and right lung.

When you breathe in, the **diaphragm** contracts and flattens, and the chest rises. This stretches the lungs and air flows in. When you breathe out, the muscles relax and the air is pushed out. If you put your hand on your chest, you can feel the chest rise and fall.

Air is about 21 per cent **oxygen**. In the air sacs of the lungs, the oxygen passes into the blood and is carried to all the cells. The cells use it to get energy from food. In the process, **carbon dioxide** is made, which flows back to the lungs with the blood and is breathed out.

When running, the muscles need much more energy and so more oxygen. That is why you breathe faster and deeper. At rest, an adult breathes about 6 to 8 litres of air a minute; with great effort it can be more than ten times as much. Children breathe faster than adults at rest, and babies about 30 to 50 times a minute.

An area in the **brainstem** controls breathing automatically, even in sleep. It mainly measures how much carbon dioxide is in the blood. If the value rises, you breathe faster. You can hold your breath on purpose for a short time, but at some point the brain forces you to breathe again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that all cells need to live.
A gas that is made in the body and breathed out.
The tube through which air flows from the throat into the lungs.
A flat muscle under the lungs that helps with breathing in.

gewusst: A person breathes about 20,000 times a day.
On high mountains such as the Matterhorn the air is thinner, so you get out of breath faster there.
When you yawn, you take a particularly deep breath, but why we yawn has still not been fully explained.

teile.einleitung: The calorific value tells us how much energy is in a food. You find it on every nutrition table, given in kilojoules and kilocalories. It helps to understand how much energy we take in with food.
wichtigste: The calorific value is given in kilojoules (kJ) and kilocalories (kcal).
One kilocalorie corresponds to 4.184 kilojoules.
Fat supplies about 9 kcal per gram, carbohydrates and protein about 4 kcal each.
Alcohol supplies about 7 kcal per gram.
In the EU, fibre is calculated at 8 kJ per gram.
The physical calorific value is measured with a bomb calorimeter.

abschnitte.text: To determine the **physical calorific value**, a food is burned in a **bomb calorimeter**. This is a tightly closed vessel with pure oxygen that stands in water. The heat released warms the water, and from this the energy is calculated. The SI unit of energy is the **joule**. On nutrition tables **kilojoules** usually stand beside the kilocalorie, and 1 kcal corresponds to **4.184 kJ**.

The nutrients supply different amounts of energy. **Fat** gives about 9 kcal per gram, **carbohydrates** and **protein** about 4 kcal each. **Alcohol** supplies about 7 kcal per gram. An example: a snack with 10 g of fat, 30 g of carbohydrates and 5 g of protein supplies 90 plus 120 plus 20, so about **230 kcal**. For **fibre**, EU nutrition labelling calculates 8 kJ per gram.

The **physiological calorific value** tells how much energy the body can really use. For **carbohydrates** and fat, it is almost the same as the physical value. They are broken down completely in the body into **carbon dioxide and water**. For **protein** it is smaller. The nitrogen from protein is excreted as **urea**, and this still contains energy.

The body stores energy in the short term as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles. Glycogen, though, binds a lot of water and is therefore heavy. **Fat**, on the other hand, is stored almost free of water and is much more **energy dense**.
