That is why the body builds up long-term reserves mainly as fat. In this way it can carry a lot of energy for little weight.

gewusst: With the energy from one gram of fat, you could warm about a litre of water by about 9 degrees.
In everyday speech people often say “calories”, but really mean kilocalories.

teile.einleitung: Calcitriol is the active hormone form of vitamin D. It makes sure that the body gets enough calcium for strong bones. For it to be formed, the skin, liver and kidneys work together.
wichtigste: Calcitriol is the active hormone form of vitamin D.
For making vitamin D3, the skin needs UV-B radiation.
In the liver, vitamin D3 is first converted into calcidiol.
In the gut, calcitriol increases the absorption of calcium.
It inhibits the making of parathyroid hormone in the parathyroid glands.
In children, a marked lack of vitamin D leads to rickets.

abschnitte.titel: From the sun to a hormone
abschnitte.text: The body can make **vitamin D3** itself when **UV-B radiation** from the sun hits the skin. This vitamin is not yet active, though. In the **liver** it is first converted into **calcidiol**, which is also called 25-hydroxyvitamin D. In the **kidney** it finally becomes **calcitriol**. Only this form acts as a hormone.

The most important effect of calcitriol is in the **gut**. It increases the **absorption of calcium** from food. The body needs calcium for **bones and teeth**, but also for muscles and nerves. Calcitriol also helps to regulate the phosphate level in the blood. In this way the balance of minerals stays in equilibrium.

Calcitriol works closely with the **parathyroid hormone** of the **parathyroid glands**. It **inhibits** the making of parathyroid hormone, so a feedback loop arises. Bone cells join in too: they make the hormone **FGF23**. It inhibits the making of calcitriol and promotes the excretion of phosphate. In its target cells, calcitriol acts mainly through a **receptor in the cell nucleus** and switches certain genes on or off there.

If vitamin D is badly lacking for a long time, the bones become soft. In children this disease is called **rickets**. The bones can bend, for example the legs. In the **winter months**, the sun in Switzerland is often not enough to make enough vitamin D. That is why **infants** in Switzerland are mostly given vitamin D drops.

gewusst: Vitamin D is really not a proper vitamin at all, because the body can make it itself.
Oily fish such as salmon or herring is among the few foods with a lot of vitamin D.

teile.einleitung: B lymphocytes, or B cells for short, are white blood cells and an important part of our defence. They make antibodies, which help to recognise germs and make them harmless.
wichtigste: B cells are white blood cells that develop in the bone marrow.
Their receptor is an antibody anchored in the cell membrane.
Each naive B cell recognises only a single antigen structure.
Mature naive B cells carry IgM and IgD on their surface.
In a new infection, B cells first make IgM.
V(D)J recombination produces a huge variety of antibodies.
The “B” recalls the bursa of Fabricius in birds.

abschnitte.text: B cells were first studied in chickens. In birds they mature in an organ called the **bursa of Fabricius**, hence the “B”. Mammals do not have this organ. In humans, B cells develop and mature in the **bone marrow**. After that they travel into the blood, the lymph nodes and the spleen.

Every B cell carries the **B cell receptor** on its surface. This is an antibody that sits in the cell membrane. Mature naive B cells carry two classes with the same specificity: **IgM** and **IgD**. According to the **clonal selection theory**, each naive B cell recognises exactly one antigen structure. When it meets its matching antigen, it is activated and multiplies into a **clone** of identical cells.

So that the body can recognise almost any germ, it needs very many different antibodies. This variety arises through **V(D)J recombination**: during maturation, V, D and J gene segments are put together anew at random. For this discovery **Susumu Tonegawa** received the Nobel Prize in 1987. In this way countless combinations arise from a few building blocks.

On first contact with a germ, B cells mainly make **IgM**, a large molecule with ten binding sites. In the **germinal centres** of the lymph nodes, the antibodies improve further: through **somatic hypermutation**, many small changes arise, and the cells that bind best survive. This is called affinity maturation. In **class switching**, B cells change over to other classes such as IgG, IgA or IgE without changing their target.

Activated B cells become **plasma cells**, which release large amounts of antibodies, or **memory cells**, which remember the germ. The effect of many vaccinations rests on this. Sometimes B cells wrongly turn against the body itself or become cancer cells. Then the antibody **rituximab** can help: it binds to the molecule **CD20** and leads to the B cells being broken down.

gewusst: The “B” of B cells comes from an organ that only birds have.
From a single activated B cell, a whole clone of thousands of identical cells can arise.
Memory cells can remember an infection for many years.

teile.einleitung: Burnout means, in German, roughly “burnt out”. It describes a state of deep exhaustion that arises mainly through long-lasting strain at work. You can do a lot to prevent it.
wichtigste: The psychologist Herbert Freudenberger coined the term in the 1970s.
Originally burnout was described mainly in helping professions.
The WHO classes burnout in ICD-11 as an occupational phenomenon.
Christina Maslach describes three core features, including emotional exhaustion.
Burnout is often measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory.
Regular recovery and clear limits help to prevent burnout.

abschnitte.text: The psychologist **Herbert Freudenberger** coined the term **burnout** in the 1970s. He observed people who committed themselves strongly to others and in time became completely exhausted. That is why burnout was first described mainly in **helping professions**, for example in nursing, social work or teaching. Today we know that it can affect people in many jobs.

The psychologist **Christina Maslach** describes three features. The first is **emotional exhaustion**: you feel empty and without strength. The second is called **depersonalisation**, a distant, indifferent attitude towards other people. The third is the feeling of **achieving less** and getting nowhere any more. To measure it she developed the questionnaire **Maslach Burnout Inventory**.

The **World Health Organization** (WHO) lists burnout in its classification **ICD-11**. It does not class it there as a disease in its own right, but as an **occupational phenomenon**. It means chronic stress at the workplace that has not been successfully managed. A burnout can, however, put a heavy strain on health. That is why it is important to take warning signs seriously and to get help.

According to the **Job Demands-Resources model**, the risk rises especially when **demands are high** and **resources are low**. Resources are, for example, support in the team, a say in decisions or recognition. Important for prevention are **regular recovery**, enough sleep and exercise. **Clear limits** also help, such as fixed breaks and free time without work. This applies, by the way, to school and training too.

gewusst: The English word “burn out” originally means that something burns out, for example a candle.
Pupils and students too can suffer from exhaustion similar to burnout.

teile.einleitung: A torn ligament is an injury in which a ligament at a joint tears partly or completely. It often happens in sport, when you twist your ankle or turn awkwardly. Most torn ligaments heal well, but need time.
wichtigste: A ligament joins bone to bone, a tendon joins muscle and bone.
Ligaments consist mainly of tight connective tissue with collagen fibres.
If the ligament is only overstretched, it is called a sprain.
A torn outer ligament at the ankle is usually treated without an operation.
A torn ligament needs about six weeks before it can bear load again.
With an MRI, torn ligaments can be seen especially well.

abschnitte.text: **Ligaments** hold joints together. They join **bone to bone**. **Tendons**, on the other hand, join muscles to bones. Ligaments consist mainly of **tight connective tissue** with strong **collagen fibres**. They resist pulling very well, but stretch only a little.

The most commonly injured is the **outer ligament at the ankle**, when you roll your foot outwards. In **skiing**, it is especially often the **inner ligament** at the knee that is injured. If the ligament is only overstretched, it is called a **sprain**. In a tear it is partly or completely severed. Typical signs are pain, swelling and often a bruise.

Straight after the injury, the **RICE rule** helps: **R**est, **I**ce, **C**ompression with a bandage and **E**levation. You never put ice directly on the skin, but wrapped in a cloth. The doctor checks how stable the joint is. With **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI), torn ligaments can be seen especially well. An X-ray shows whether a bone is also broken.

A **torn outer ligament at the ankle** is nowadays mostly treated **without an operation**. You wear a **splint** and do **physiotherapy** to train muscles and balance. It takes about **six weeks** until a torn ligament can bear load again. If it heals badly, an **unstable joint** can be left behind, which keeps giving way. That is why patient training is important.

gewusst: Ligaments have a poor blood supply, so they heal more slowly than muscles.
Good balance training lowers the risk of twisting your ankle again.

teile.einleitung: A blood bank is a store for donated blood. From there the blood goes to hospitals when patients need it. Without blood donations, no blood bank could work.
wichtigste: Donated blood is stored in a blood bank.
The blood goes into clean plastic bags, called units of blood.
Red blood cells are stored cooled and keep for a few weeks.
The blood group of donor and recipient must match.
In the ABO system there are the blood groups A, B, AB and O.
Because blood does not keep for ever, new donations are needed all the time.
Anyone who receives blood from a bag gets a blood transfusion.

abschnitte.text: In a **blood bank**, **donated blood** is collected, tested and kept. From there it goes to the **hospitals**. It is needed, for example, after an accident, in operations or for certain illnesses. The blood bank must always have enough blood of all blood groups ready. That is why it depends on regular donations.

Donated blood goes into special, clean **plastic bags**. Such a bag is called a **unit of blood**. It is labelled exactly, among other things with the blood group. In this way you always know where the blood comes from and for whom it is suitable. Often a donation is divided into parts such as red blood cells and plasma.

Units with **red blood cells** are stored in a **fridge**. In this way they keep for **a few weeks**. After that they may no longer be used. Blood therefore **does not keep for ever**. That is why the blood bank needs fresh donor blood all the time.

Donor blood must match the **blood group** of the recipient, otherwise it can become dangerous. In the best-known system, the **ABO system**, there are the blood groups **A, B, AB and O**. In addition there is the rhesus factor, positive or negative. When a patient in hospital gets blood from a bag, it is called a **blood transfusion**. The blood flows through a tube into a **vein**.

gewusst: The blood groups A, B and O were discovered by the Austrian doctor Karl Landsteiner around 1900.
Platelets keep for only a few days and are stored at room temperature while being kept in motion.

teile.einleitung: Occupational medicine is a field of medicine that deals with work and health. It studies how work can make people ill, and looks for ways to protect employees. In Switzerland, several laws regulate health protection at work.
wichtigste: Occupational medicine deals with the interactions between work and health.
The Italian doctor Bernardino Ramazzini is regarded as the father of occupational medicine.
Inhaled asbestos dust can cause mesothelioma.
Quartz dust in tunnel building can lead to the lung disease silicosis.
Many years of loud noise can lead to noise-induced hearing loss.
The MAK value gives the highest permitted concentration of a harmful substance in the air at work.
In Switzerland, compulsory accident insurance pays for recognised occupational diseases.

abschnitte.text: **Occupational medicine** deals with the **interactions between work and health**. It asks, for example, which substances, noises or movements at work can do harm. Occupational doctors examine employees, advise firms and help to prevent accidents and illnesses. Stress and poor posture are also among their topics.

The founder of occupational medicine is regarded as the Italian doctor **Bernardino Ramazzini**. Around the year 1700 he wrote a work on the **diseases of workers**. In it he described the ailments of many trades, from miner to baker. He advised doctors always to ask their patients about their job as well.

Some diseases are caused by dust. Anyone who breathes in **quartz dust** for a long time, such as miners in **tunnel building**, can develop **silicosis**, a scarring of the lungs. Inhaled **asbestos dust** can, after many years, cause a **mesothelioma**, a malignant disease of the lining of the chest or abdomen. In Switzerland, asbestos has been banned since 1990. Many years of loud **noise** leads to **noise-induced hearing loss**, which is why ear protection is so important.

So that harmful substances do not endanger health, there are **limit values**. The **MAK value** gives the **maximum permitted concentration** of a substance in the air at work. Below this value, most people should come to no harm even when working every day. In Switzerland, **Suva** publishes a list of such limit values.

In Switzerland, the **Labour Act** regulates, among other things, **working hours and rest periods** and **health protection** in firms. For recognised **occupational diseases**, **compulsory accident insurance** pays. It covers, for example, treatment and, if necessary, a pension. The country’s largest accident insurer is Suva in Lucerne.

gewusst: More than 300 years ago, Ramazzini already recommended breaks and exercise for people who sit for a long time.
In building the great Alpine tunnels in Switzerland, protection from quartz dust played an important part.

teile.einleitung: Every eye has a small place where it cannot see anything: the blind spot. In everyday life we notice nothing of it. With a simple experiment, though, you can find it yourself.
wichtigste: At the blind spot there are no light-sensitive cells.
There nerve fibres and blood vessels leave the eye, the optic nerve exits.
The brain fills the gap with what can be seen all around.
Every eye has a blind spot, so a person has two.
In the field of view it lies about 15 degrees to the side towards the temple.
Edme Mariotte first described it around 1660.
Octopuses have no blind spot.

abschnitte.text: At the back of the eye lies the **retina** with many **light-sensitive cells**. Their nerve fibres come together at one place and leave the eye there as the **optic nerve**. Blood vessels also enter and leave here. At this place there is no room for sensory cells. So you see nothing there, and this is the **blind spot**.

In everyday life we do not notice a hole in the picture. The **brain fills in** the gap with what can be seen all around. In addition, the other eye usually sees the missing spot. Every eye has exactly **one** blind spot, so a person with two healthy eyes has **two**. They lie at different places in the picture.

On a sheet of paper you draw a **cross** and, a few centimetres to the right of it, a **dot**. Then you close your left eye and look at the cross exactly with your right eye. Now you slowly move the sheet nearer and further away. At a certain distance the dot suddenly **disappears**. The blind spot lies about **15 degrees** to the side of the centre of your gaze, towards the **temple**.

The French physicist **Edme Mariotte** first described the blind spot around **1660**. He showed it at the king’s court. **Octopuses**, on the other hand, have no blind spot. In them the nerve fibres lie behind the sensory cells. They do not have to cross the retina, so no gap arises.

gewusst: The optic nerve exits on the nose side of the retina, but in the field of view the gap lies on the temple side, because the image in the eye is upside down.
Because the other eye covers the gap, you only notice the blind spot if you close one eye.

teile.einleitung: A guide dog is a specially trained dog. It helps blind and severely visually impaired people to move about safely outdoors. Dog and human work together as a team.
wichtigste: A guide dog leads its person safely around obstacles.
Labrador retrievers are often trained.
At work the dog wears a guide harness with a rigid handle.
You do not stroke a working guide dog.
The dog stops in front of stairs and kerbs.
The blind person decides when to cross the road.
The Swiss School for Guide Dogs for the Blind is in Allschwil, canton of Basel-Landschaft.

abschnitte.text: A **guide dog** leads its person safely around **obstacles**, for example around posts, bikes or low branches. In front of **stairs** and **kerbs** it stops. In this way its person knows that a step is coming. Often **Labrador retrievers** are trained. They are calm, friendly and like to learn.

At work the dog wears a **guide harness** with a rigid **handle**. The person holds this handle in their hand. Through it they feel every movement of the dog, for example when it stops or steps aside. When the dog is wearing the harness, it knows: now we are working. Without the harness it may simply be a dog and play.

Crossing the **road** is teamwork. The **blind person** listens closely to the traffic and decides when it is safe. They give the **command**, and the dog then leads them safely across. The person knows the way, the dog watches for obstacles. Traffic lights with a sound signal help as well.

A working guide dog has to **concentrate** completely on the way. That is why you do not stroke, call or feed it. Distraction can become **dangerous** for its person. Anyone who would like to greet the dog asks the person first. Often this is possible during a break.

A young dog first lives with a **foster family**. There it gets to know everyday life: buses, streets, shops and many people. After that the actual **training** begins. A well-known school is the foundation **Swiss School for Guide Dogs for the Blind** in **Allschwil**. Allschwil lies in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.

gewusst: Guide dogs also learn “intelligent disobedience”: they refuse a command if it would be dangerous.
In many shops where dogs are otherwise not allowed, guide dogs may go in.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Office of Public Health, BAG for short in German, is the federal health authority. It looks after the health of the whole population of Switzerland, from health insurance to protection against infectious diseases.
wichtigste: The BAG has its seat in the Bern region.
It belongs to the Federal Department of Home Affairs.
Every year it approves the premiums for basic insurance.
It keeps the list of specialities and the list of analyses.
The Epidemics Act regulates the duty to report certain diseases.
Radiation protection, for example against radon, is also among its tasks.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Office of Public Health** has its head office in the **Bern** region. It belongs to the **Federal Department of Home Affairs** (FDHA). In Switzerland, many health tasks are a matter for the **cantons**, for example hospitals. The **Confederation**, however, is responsible for important areas that affect the whole country. The BAG carries out these tasks.

In Switzerland, every person has to take out **basic insurance**. The BAG has to **approve** the **premiums** of the health insurers every year before they apply. It keeps the **list of specialities**, a list of the medicines that basic insurance pays for. The **list of analyses** says which laboratory tests are reimbursed. With the premium calculator **Priminfo**, you can compare the insurers’ premiums.

The BAG watches how **infectious diseases** spread. The basis for this is the **Epidemics Act**. Among other things it regulates the **duty to report**: doctors and laboratories have to report certain diseases. In this way outbreaks can be recognised early. The BAG also issues recommendations on vaccinations and informs the population.

**Radiation protection** also belongs to the BAG. This includes protection against **radon**, a natural gas from the ground that can build up in buildings. The BAG also sees to it that X-ray machines are used safely. With campaigns it promotes a healthy way of life. This is about, for example, exercise, diet or giving up tobacco.

gewusst: In some Alpine areas of Switzerland, the radon level in houses is especially high.
The list of specialities includes several thousand medicines.

teile.einleitung: Glasses help people who do not see sharply to see clearly again. Their ground lenses steer the light so that it falls into the eye exactly right. Many children and adults wear glasses every day.
wichtigste: Glasses with ground lenses help you to see better.
Short-sighted people see blurred in the distance.
Long-sighted people see blurred up close.
Many older people need reading glasses, because the lens of the eye becomes stiffer.
Glasses are fitted by opticians.
Instead of glasses, you can also wear contact lenses.

abschnitte.text: In the eye, the **cornea** and **lens** focus the light onto the retina. If the eye is a little too long or too short, no sharp picture forms there. A **spectacle lens** redirects the light suitably beforehand. Then the picture falls exactly on the retina again, and you see sharply. Every lens is **ground** exactly for the eye.

Anyone who is **short-sighted** sees near things well, but in the **distance** blurred, for example the board. Lenses that are thinner in the middle help against this. Anyone who is **long-sighted** sees blurred **up close**, for example when reading. For this you need lenses that are thicker in the middle. Many older people need **reading glasses**, because the lens of their eye becomes stiffer and can no longer adjust well to near things.

Glasses consist of the **frame**, the lenses, the **arms** behind the ears and the **bridge**, which rests on the nose. The sight test is often done by an eye doctor or an **optician**. Opticians fit the glasses and sell them. Instead of glasses you can also put **contact lenses** directly on the eye.

If you come in from the cold into a warm house in winter, your glasses **mist up**. The damp, warm air cools on the cold lenses, and tiny droplets of water form. After a short time the misting goes away again. Sunglasses protect the eyes from strong light and UV radiation. For sport there are especially robust **sports glasses**.

gewusst: The first glasses appeared at the end of the 13th century in Italy.
Short-sightedness has become more common in children and young people worldwide in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: An anaesthetic puts people into a deep, painless sleep so that they can be operated on. One of the first anaesthetics was ether. Its public demonstration in Boston in 1846 is seen as the birth of modern anaesthesia.
wichtigste: Anaesthetic ether is the compound diethyl ether.
On 16 October 1846 the first public operation under ether took place in Boston.
The ether was given by the dentist William Morton.
Crawford Long had already operated with ether in 1842.
Ether catches fire easily and is therefore dangerous.
In 1847 James Young Simpson introduced chloroform.

abschnitte.text: In the past, people had to endure operations fully conscious. Surgeons therefore worked as fast as they could. For a long time people looked for a drug that switches pain off. One candidate was **laughing gas**. The dentist **Horace Wells** demonstrated it in public in Boston in 1845. But the patient cried out, probably because the amount was too small. The onlookers thought the whole thing was a fraud.

On **16 October 1846**, a famous demonstration took place at the Massachusetts General Hospital in **Boston**. The dentist **William Morton** had a patient breathe in ether vapour. Then the surgeon removed a growth on the neck. The patient showed no pain. This day is seen as the **birth of modern anaesthesia**. The news spread quickly to Europe.

The American doctor **Crawford Long** had already removed a growth under ether in **1842**. But he only reported it years later. So the fame went to others at first. Soon after the demonstration in Boston, the doctor and writer **Oliver Wendell Holmes** suggested the word **anaesthesia**. It comes from Greek and means “lack of sensation”.

The classic anaesthetic ether is **diethyl ether**. It is a colourless, easily evaporating liquid. If you breathe in its vapours, you become unconscious. But ether has a big disadvantage: it is **easily flammable**. Its vapours form explosive mixtures with air. Open flames and sparks were therefore dangerous in the operating theatre.

As early as **1847**, **James Young Simpson** introduced **chloroform** in Edinburgh. It worked faster and did not burn. But it was more dangerous for the heart and liver. Later, ether and chloroform were replaced by safer drugs. Today specially trained experts, the **anaesthetists**, monitor every anaesthetic closely.

gewusst: 16 October is celebrated in many countries as “Anaesthesia Day”.
The operating theatre of 1846 in Boston has been preserved and is now called the “Ether Dome”.

teile.einleitung: Screen time is the time you spend in front of a phone, tablet, computer or television. Screens are fun and help with learning. Too much of it, though, especially in the evening, can put a strain on sleep, eyes and body.
wichtigste: Screens give off a lot of blue light, which keeps you awake.
About an hour before sleep, it is best to put screens away.
At night the phone is better kept outside the bedroom.
Exciting games in the evening wake up the brain.
After a long time on screens, the eyes often become tired and dry.
A timer helps to keep an eye on the time.
Playing outdoors strengthens muscles and bones.

abschnitte.text: Screens give off a lot of **blue light**. This light tells the body that it is still day. As a result you become tired later. Experts advise putting screens away about **an hour** before sleep. In this way the body can come to rest.

It is not only the light that disturbs sleep. An **exciting game** or a thrilling video stimulates the brain. Afterwards it takes longer until you can fall asleep. Better before falling asleep is a **book**. It does not glow and it calms you.

In the bedroom, **messages**, sounds and light from the phone can disturb sleep. That is why at night it is best kept **outside the bedroom**. For an alarm you can use a simple alarm clock. In this way you sleep more peacefully and are more rested in the morning.

When looking at the screen, you **blink** less often. That is why after a long time the eyes become **tired and dry**. Short breaks help, in which you look into the distance. Enough distance from the screen is also important.

abschnitte.titel: Keeping an eye on the time
abschnitte.text: In front of the screen time often passes faster than you think. A **timer** or alarm clock shows when the agreed time is up. Instead of sitting for hours, **movement in the fresh air** does you good. It strengthens muscles and bones. In the evening you are then pleasantly tired.

gewusst: Many phones and tablets can themselves show how long you have used them in a day.
Candlelight contains almost no blue light and therefore hardly disturbs the body clock.

teile.einleitung: The caecum is a short, blind-ended section at the start of the large intestine, at the lower right of the belly. A thin projection hangs from it, the vermiform appendix. When this becomes inflamed, in everyday speech people talk of appendicitis.
wichtigste: The caecum is the start of the large intestine.
It usually lies in the lower right abdomen.
From the caecum hangs the appendix, also called the vermiform appendix.
The appendix probably supports the immune system in the gut.
An inflammation of the appendix is called appendicitis.
Typical are stomach pains that move into the lower right abdomen.
Appendicitis is often operated on.

abschnitte.text: The **caecum**, in German “Blinddarm” or “blind gut”, lies where the small intestine passes into the large intestine, usually in the lower right abdomen. It has this name because it ends blindly downwards, that is, it has no exit. At its end hangs the **appendix**, a thin tube usually about 8 to 10 centimetres long. Its technical name is appendix, which means “attachment”.

For a long time the appendix was thought to be a useless leftover from evolutionary history. Today we know that it contains a lot of **lymphatic tissue**, which belongs to the defence system. It probably supports the immune system in the gut. It might also serve as a refuge for useful gut bacteria, for example after a bad bout of diarrhoea.

What is called “Blinddarmentzündung” in everyday German is really an inflammation of the appendix, **appendicitis**. It occurs especially often in children and young people. The pains often begin around the belly button and then move into the lower right abdomen. Feeling sick, loss of appetite and a mild fever often come with it.

If you suspect it, you must go quickly to the doctor or hospital. If the inflamed appendix bursts, the inflammation can spread through the whole belly, which is dangerous. Usually the appendix is removed in an **operation**, nowadays often through small cuts with keyhole surgery. In some milder cases, doctors also treat first with antibiotics.

Many plant-eating animals have a very large caecum. In rabbits and horses, bacteria there help to digest the tough plant food. In humans the caecum is comparatively small. Meat eaters such as cats have only a very short caecum.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin attachment on the caecum, the vermiform appendix.
The inflammation of the appendix.
The last section of the gut, in which water is removed from the food pulp.
Tissue in which many defence cells sit.

gewusst: Appendix removal is one of the most common emergency operations on the abdomen.
You can live quite normally without an appendix.

teile.einleitung: The eye is the sense organ with which we see. It catches light and turns it into signals that the brain puts together into pictures. Through our eyes we take in a large part of all the information from our surroundings.
wichtigste: With our eyes we see the world around us.
Without light, the eyes cannot see.
The black hole in the middle of the eye is called the pupil.
The iris determines eye colour.
The eyelid protects the eye when we blink.
The picture that the brain works on is formed on the retina.
Glasses help many people to see sharply again.

abschnitte.text: The eyeball is round and, in adults, about 2.4 centimetres across. At the front lies the clear **cornea**, behind it the coloured **iris** with the pupil in the middle. Behind the pupil sits the lens. The inside is filled with the vitreous humour, a clear, jelly-like mass.

The **pupil** is really a hole through which light falls into the eye, which is why it looks black. The iris is a ring of muscle that makes the pupil bigger or smaller. In the dark the pupil becomes wide, so that more light gets in; in bright light it becomes narrow. The colour of the iris, whether blue, green or brown, depends on the pigment melanin and is inherited.

The cornea and the **lens** focus the light, as in a camera. On the **retina** at the back of the eye, a small upside-down picture is formed. There, millions of sensory cells, the rods and cones, turn the light into nerve signals. The optic nerve carries the signals to the brain, which makes an upright picture from them.

The **eyelid** closes when we blink and protects the eye from dust and injury. We blink about 10 to 20 times a minute. In doing so, tear fluid is spread over the eye, which keeps it moist and clean. Eyelashes and eyebrows keep sweat and dirt away.

In **short-sightedness**, you see near things sharply but distant ones blurred. In long-sightedness it is the other way round. Glasses or contact lenses bend the light so that the picture forms sharply on the retina again. In Switzerland, children’s eyes are often tested already in kindergarten or at school.

Strong sunlight can damage the eyes, especially in snow and on glaciers in the mountains. So you should wear good sunglasses there. You should never look straight at the sun. Anyone who looks at screens for a long time should take regular breaks and look into the distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The opening in the middle of the iris through which light falls into the eye.
The coloured ring in the eye.
The layer at the back of the eye with sensory cells for light.
A clear part of the eye that focuses the light.
The nerve that carries the signals from the eye to the brain.

gewusst: The picture on the retina is upside down; only the brain turns it round.
Every eye has a blind spot, where the optic nerve leaves and there are no sensory cells.
Newborn babies still see quite blurred and only recognise colours bit by bit.

teile.einleitung: The AV node is a small knot of special heart muscle cells. It passes the heart’s electrical rhythm on from the atria to the ventricles and slows it down briefly on the way. In this way the heart works in the right order.
wichtigste: AV stands for atrioventricular, that is, between atrium and ventricle.
It lies at the floor of the right atrium near the septum.
It is also called the Aschoff-Tawara node, after Ludwig Aschoff and Sunao Tawara.
It conducts the excitation much more slowly than the Purkinje fibres.
If the sinus node fails, it beats at about 40 to 60 per minute.
The vagus nerve slows the conduction.
In atrial fibrillation, it lets through only some of the impulses.

abschnitte.text: The heart has its own **conduction system**. The rhythm begins in the **sinus node** in the right atrium. From there the excitation spreads across the atria and reaches the **AV node**. It lies at the floor of the right atrium near the septum between the atria. It was described in 1906 by the Japanese researcher **Sunao Tawara**, who worked with the German pathologist **Ludwig Aschoff**. That is why it is also called the Aschoff-Tawara node.

The AV node conducts the excitation **much more slowly** than other parts of the system, such as the Purkinje fibres in the ventricles. This little pause is useful: the atria have time to contract and push the blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract. After that the excitation runs quickly through the ventricles by way of the **bundle of His**, the **bundle branches** and the Purkinje fibres. On the ECG, the **PQ interval** shows how long the conduction takes.

Normally the sinus node sets the rhythm at about 60 to 80 beats a minute. If it fails, the AV node can step in. Its **own rate** is about **40 to 60 per minute**. That is enough to survive, but slower than normal. The body can also influence the AV node: the **vagus nerve**, part of the parasympathetic system, **slows** the conduction, and the sympathetic system speeds it up.

In **atrial fibrillation**, very many disorderly impulses reach the AV node. Because it cannot be excited for a short time after each impulse, it lets **only some of the impulses through**. So it acts like a filter and protects the ventricles from beating dangerously fast. Some medicines strengthen this braking effect on purpose.

When the conduction is disturbed, it is called an **AV block**. In first-degree AV block, the conduction is only slowed, and the PQ interval is **longer than 0.20 seconds**. In second degree, single beats drop out. In **third-degree AV block**, **no excitation** reaches the ventricles any more. They then beat only with a slow substitute rhythm, and often a **pacemaker** is needed.

gewusst: In 1906 Tawara already presented the AV node and the conduction system in detail in a book.
Without the pause in the AV node, the atria and ventricles would contract almost at the same time.
